parts.label: a
parts.text:
Bilal owns a mobile phone repair shop in Rawalpindi. He pays the electricity bill for his family home from his own savings account, and it is not recorded anywhere in the shop's books. Which accounting concept is being applied?
A business entity
B duality
C going concern
D money measurement
parts.answer: A business entity
parts.working: Business entity: the owner's private transactions are kept separate from the business's records. Money measurement (D) is wrong because the bill can be measured in money; it is left out because it is private, not because it cannot be valued.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A bookshop values a box of last year's diaries at their expected selling price of $140 less selling costs of $20, because this is lower than their cost of $310. Which concept requires this?
A consistency
B matching
C prudence
D realisation
parts.answer: C prudence
parts.working: Prudence: assets must not be overstated and expected losses are recognised as soon as they are foreseen, so inventory is valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value ($120). Realisation (D) concerns when revenue is recognised, not the value of unsold goods.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A large hotel company buys a waste-paper bin for $18. It is expected to last five years, but the cost is charged in full to the statement of profit or loss as general expenses. Which concept justifies this treatment?
A historical cost
B materiality
C going concern
D prudence
parts.answer: B materiality
parts.working: Materiality: the amount is too small to affect users' decisions, so the cost of depreciating it over five years is not worth the effort. Prudence (D) is not the reason, because the bin is not being undervalued out of caution; it is simply insignificant.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A furniture maker's year ends on 31 December 2026. A customer ordered a table on 10 December 2026 and paid in full on 2 January 2027. The table was delivered to and accepted by the customer on 29 December 2026. In which year should the sale be recognised, and which concept applies?
A year ended 31 December 2026; realisation
B year ended 31 December 2027; realisation
C year ended 31 December 2026; going concern
D year ended 31 December 2027; matching
parts.answer: A year ended 31 December 2026; realisation
parts.working: Realisation: revenue is recognised when control of the goods passes to the customer (delivery and acceptance on 29 December 2026), not when cash is received. B wrongly uses the date of payment.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A trader's financial year ends on 31 March 2027. Rent of $1,850 per month is payable for a shop. During the year she paid $20,350, which covered April 2026 to February 2027. What rent expense should appear in the statement of profit or loss for the year ended 31 March 2027?
A $18,500
B $20,350
C $22,200
D $24,050
parts.working: Matching (accruals): the expense is the rent for the 12 months used, 12 × $1,850 = $22,200, whether paid or not; March's $1,850 is accrued. B is the cash paid, which ignores the accrual.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statements about accounting concepts are correct?
1 The consistency concept means that a business can never change its depreciation method.
2 The going concern concept supports valuing non-current assets at cost less depreciation rather than at their forced-sale value.
3 The duality concept means that every transaction has two equal and opposite effects.
4 The money measurement concept means that the skill of a business's workforce is shown as an asset.
A 1 and 2
B 1 and 4
C 2 and 3
D 3 and 4
parts.answer: C 2 and 3
parts.working: 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 1 is wrong: a method may be changed if the new method gives a fairer view, with the change disclosed. Statement 4 is wrong: the skill of workers cannot be measured reliably in money, so it is not recorded.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which item would NOT be recorded in the books of a software company because of the money measurement concept?
A a laptop bought on credit from a supplier
B the loyalty and good morale of its programmers
C a loan received from a bank
D an amount owed by a customer who is unlikely to pay
parts.answer: B the loyalty and good morale of its programmers
parts.working: Morale and loyalty cannot be measured objectively in money, so they are not recorded. D is recorded (it is measurable; an irrecoverable debt or allowance would be used).

stem: Nadia runs a printing business in Karachi. She has owned a large printing press for three years.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by the going concern concept.
parts.answer: The assumption that the business will continue to trade for the foreseeable future and has no intention or need to close down or greatly reduce its operations.
parts.working: 1 mark: continue trading; 1 mark: for the foreseeable future / no intention to liquidate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the going concern concept affects the value of non-current assets in a statement of financial position.
parts.answer: Non-current assets are shown at cost less accumulated depreciation (carrying amount), spread over their useful lives, rather than at what they would fetch if sold immediately (break-up value).
parts.working: 1 mark: cost less depreciation over useful life; 1 mark: not at break-up / forced-sale value because the business is not expected to sell them.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the money measurement concept.
parts.answer: Only transactions and events that can be measured objectively in monetary terms are recorded in the accounting records.
parts.working: 1 mark: only items measurable in money; 1 mark: measured objectively/reliably are recorded.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two items of value to a business that are not recorded because of this concept.
parts.answer: Any two of: skill/experience of the workforce; staff morale; good relations with customers or suppliers; a good location (unless purchased); quality of management.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid non-monetary items.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the duality concept.
parts.answer: Every transaction has two equal and opposite effects on the business, so for every debit entry there is a credit entry of the same amount.
parts.working: 1 mark: two aspects/effects; 1 mark: equal debit and credit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Kamran buys a delivery van costing $14,500 on credit from Pak Motors. State the two effects of this transaction on the accounting equation.
parts.answer: Non-current assets (van) increase by $14,500; liabilities (other payable, Pak Motors) increase by $14,500.
parts.working: 1 mark: assets +14,500; 1 mark: liabilities +14,500. Capital unchanged.

stem: Farah's bakery has a year end of 30 June. On 1 July 2026 electricity of $780 was owing for June 2026. During the year to 30 June 2027 she paid electricity bills of $9,640. On 30 June 2027 electricity of $1,120 was owing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the accounting concept that requires the electricity expense to include amounts not yet paid.
parts.answer: Accruals (matching) concept.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the electricity expense to be shown in the statement of profit or loss for the year ended 30 June 2027.
parts.working: Paid 9,640 − opening accrual 780 (belongs to last year) + closing accrual 1,120 = 9,980. M1 deduct opening accrual, M1 add closing accrual, A1.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Omar sells solar lamps. On the last day of his financial year he sent lamps to a retailer on sale or return. The retailer had not accepted them by the year end. Omar included the lamps in revenue at their selling price of $4,800, which is cost plus 20%. They were not included in closing inventory. His draft profit for the year was $41,350.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the treatment of these goods breaks the realisation concept.
parts.answer: Revenue should only be recognised when control passes to the customer, i.e. when the customer accepts the goods. The goods sent on sale or return have not been accepted, so no sale has taken place.
parts.working: 1 mark: revenue recognised when goods accepted / control passes; 1 mark: applied — not yet accepted, so not revenue.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the corrected profit for the year.
parts.working: Cost = 4,800 × 100/120 = 4,000. Revenue reduced by 4,800; closing inventory increased by 4,000. 41,350 − 4,800 + 4,000 = 40,550. B1 cost, M1 both adjustments, A1.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
At the end of her financial year, Hina, a clothing retailer in Lahore, has the following inventory.
Item                      Cost $       NRV $
Cotton shirts              6,200       9,100
Silk scarves               3,450       2,800
Leather belts              1,980       1,650
Denim jackets              7,400      11,200

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the value of closing inventory.
parts.working: Each line at the lower of cost and NRV: 6,200 + 2,800 + 1,650 + 7,400 = 18,050. M1 lower of cost/NRV line by line, M1 at least two lines correct, A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the accounting concept you have applied and explain why it is applied item by item rather than to the total.
parts.answer: Prudence. If the totals were compared, gains on some items would hide losses on others, so inventory (and profit) would be overstated.
parts.working: 1 mark: prudence; 1 mark: totals would offset expected losses against unrealised gains.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Zubair Engineering bought a machine two years ago for $48,000. It has been depreciated at 10% per year on cost (straight-line). For year 3 the accountant proposes to use 20% per year on the reducing balance instead.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the consistency concept.
parts.answer: Once a business has chosen an accounting method (e.g. a depreciation method), it should use the same method from year to year, so that results can be compared over time.
parts.working: 1 mark: same methods each year; 1 mark: allows comparison between periods.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the depreciation for year 3 under the existing method and under the proposed method.
parts.answer: Straight-line: $4,800. Reducing balance: $7,680.
parts.working: SL = 10% × 48,000 = 4,800. Carrying amount after 2 years = 48,000 − 2 × 4,800 = 38,400; RB = 20% × 38,400 = 7,680. B1 SL, M1 carrying amount, A1 RB.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the effect on profit for year 3 if the method is changed, and state one condition under which a change of method is acceptable.
parts.answer: Profit would fall by $2,880. A change is acceptable if the new method gives a fairer (truer) view of the asset's use, and the change and its effect are disclosed.
parts.working: 1 mark: decrease 2,880 (own figure); 1 mark: fairer presentation/disclosed.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Tariq has decided to close his electronics shop next month. His draft statement of financial position shows: inventory $26,000; equipment (carrying amount) $40,000; trade receivables $15,000; cash $3,800; trade payables $21,400.
If the shop closes: the inventory can be sold for $17,500; the equipment for $22,000; and 10% of the trade receivables will not be collected. Cash and payables are unchanged.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Tariq's capital (net assets) on the going concern basis.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate Tariq's capital if the business is no longer a going concern, and the decrease in capital.
parts.answer: Capital $35,400; decrease $28,000.
parts.working: Inventory 17,500 + equipment 22,000 + receivables 90% × 15,000 = 13,500 + cash 3,800 − payables 21,400 = 35,400. Decrease 63,400 − 35,400 = 28,000. M1 break-up values, M1 receivables 90%, A1 capital, A1 decrease.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the going concern concept no longer applies to Tariq's business.
parts.answer: Tariq intends to close the business within weeks, so it will not continue to trade for the foreseeable future; assets must be valued at what they will realise on sale.
parts.working: 1 mark: closure planned / not foreseeable future; 1 mark: so realisable (break-up) values used.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the prudence concept and the realisation concept work together when a business values its closing inventory.
parts.answer: Inventory is valued at cost (not selling price) because the profit on it is not realised until it is sold — realisation. If the net realisable value falls below cost, the expected loss is recognised now — prudence. So gains wait until realised, losses are recognised when foreseen.
parts.working: 1 mark: cost not selling price; 1 mark: profit only recognised when realised (sold); 1 mark: losses recognised at once / lower of cost and NRV.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether too much prudence can conflict with the aim of giving a true and fair view.
parts.answer: Excessive prudence (e.g. very large allowances for doubtful debts or undervalued assets) understates profit and assets, so statements are no longer neutral or faithful. Profit is moved to later years, breaking matching and making comparison misleading. Some caution is needed so owners do not withdraw unrealised profits. Conclusion: prudence should mean caution, not deliberate understatement.
parts.working: 1 mark each for up to 4 developed points: understatement of profit/assets; not neutral/faithful; shifts profit between periods/affects matching; caution still useful to protect capital; a balanced conclusion.

stem: Ali Traders bought land in 2004 for $85,000. A valuer says it is worth $410,000 today. The business has never revalued the land.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the historical cost concept.
parts.answer: Assets are recorded at their original cost (the price paid to acquire them).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one advantage and one disadvantage of using historical cost for the land bought by Ali Traders.
parts.answer: Advantage: the cost is objective and can be checked against the purchase documents. Disadvantage: the figure is out of date and understates the land's current value, so the SOFP may mislead users.
parts.working: 1 mark advantage (objective/verifiable); 1 mark disadvantage (out of date/understates value).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the materiality concept.
parts.answer: An item is material if leaving it out or misstating it could influence the decisions of users of the financial statements. Immaterial items need not be treated strictly (e.g. small tools may be expensed).
parts.working: 1 mark: could influence users' decisions; 1 mark: immaterial items can be treated in the simplest way.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A stapler costing $25 is material to a small corner shop but not to a multinational bank. Explain this statement.
parts.answer: Materiality is relative to the size of the business: $25 is a large proportion of the shop's profit or assets, but an insignificant fraction of the bank's.
parts.working: 1 mark: relative to size/scale; 1 mark: compared with profit or total assets.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two items, other than small value equipment, for which materiality affects the accounting treatment.
parts.answer: Any two: separate disclosure of large unusual items; whether to record small accruals or prepayments; grouping small expenses into 'sundry expenses'; whether to correct a small error.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

stem: Saima runs a dental clinic in Peshawar. Her year ends on 31 December. On 1 January 2026 insurance of $2,400 had been prepaid for January to September 2026. On 1 October 2026 she paid $3,600 for twelve months' insurance to 30 September 2027.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the insurance expense for the year ended 31 December 2026.
parts.working: Opening prepayment 2,400 (Jan–Sep 2026) + 3/12 × 3,600 = 900 (Oct–Dec) = 3,300. M1, M1, A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the amount of the prepayment at 31 December 2026 and where it appears in the statement of financial position.
parts.answer: $2,700, shown as a current asset (other receivables).
parts.working: 9/12 × 3,600 = 2,700 B1; current asset B1.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Rashid owns a grocery shop. During the year he took goods costing $650 from the shop for his family's use, and paid his home electricity bill of $420 from the business bank account. Both amounts were recorded as business expenses: the goods remained in purchases and the bill was debited to the shop's electricity account. His draft profit for the year was $38,200.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the corrected profit for the year.
parts.working: Goods taken: reduce purchases (cost of sales) by 650 → profit +650. Home electricity removed from expenses → +420. 38,200 + 650 + 420 = 39,270. M1 M1 A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how each item should be recorded, and name the concept that has been broken.
parts.answer: Goods taken: Dr Drawings, Cr Purchases $650. Home electricity: Dr Drawings, Cr Electricity (expense) $420. Concept: business entity.
parts.working: 1 mark each double entry; 1 mark business entity.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Jamal Kitchens' year ends on 30 June. On 20 June 2027 a customer ordered an industrial oven for $8,000 and paid a deposit of $2,000. The oven, which cost Jamal $5,000, was still in the warehouse on 30 June and was delivered on 5 July 2027. The bookkeeper recorded the full $8,000 as revenue, set up a trade receivable for $6,000, and left the oven out of closing inventory. Draft profit was $63,400.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain, with reference to the realisation concept, why this sale should not be included in revenue for the year ended 30 June 2027.
parts.answer: Revenue is recognised when control of the goods passes to the customer. The oven was delivered after the year end (5 July), so the sale belongs to the next year. Receiving the order and deposit does not realise the revenue.
parts.working: 1 mark: control passes on delivery; 1 mark: delivered after year end, so next year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the corrected profit for the year.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how the deposit of $2,000 should be shown in the statement of financial position at 30 June 2027, and state the other correction needed to that statement.
parts.answer: The deposit is a current liability (amount received in advance / contract liability) of $2,000, because the business still owes the customer the oven. The trade receivable of $6,000 recorded for the balance must be removed, and inventory increased by $5,000.
parts.working: 1 mark current liability; 1 mark reason; 1 mark remove receivable / add inventory.

author: HomiLabs

stem: The conceptual framework used for international financial reporting sets out the qualitative characteristics that make financial information useful to investors, lenders and other creditors.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the two fundamental qualitative characteristics of useful financial information.
parts.answer: Relevance: information can make a difference to users' decisions because it has predictive value, confirmatory value, or both (and is material). Faithful representation: information depicts what it claims to — it is complete, neutral and free from error.
parts.working: 1 mark each characteristic named, 1 mark each correct explanation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name two enhancing qualitative characteristics and explain how one of them helps an investor comparing two companies.
parts.answer: Any two of: comparability, verifiability, timeliness, understandability. E.g. comparability: if both companies use similar policies consistently and disclose them, the investor can identify real differences in performance rather than differences caused by accounting methods.
parts.working: 1 mark each name (max 2); 1 mark explanation applied to comparing companies.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Crescent Textiles Limited has made losses for three years and its bank has warned it may withdraw the overdraft.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two indicators that a company may not be a going concern.
parts.answer: Any two: repeated large losses; net current liabilities / unable to pay debts as they fall due; loss of a major customer or supplier; bank refusing to renew loans; loan repayments in default; key licence withdrawn.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two effects on the financial statements if a company is no longer a going concern.
parts.answer: Assets are revalued to realisable (break-up) values, often much lower, e.g. specialised machinery and inventory. Non-current liabilities may become current because they must be repaid on closure. Extra liabilities (e.g. closure costs, redundancy) may need to be recognised. Depreciation over useful life no longer applies.
parts.working: 2 marks each effect: identification + explanation.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each situation, name the accounting concept that is applied or broken.
(i) A taxi company changes from straight-line to reducing balance depreciation each year, choosing whichever gives the higher profit.
(ii) The owner records the business's van at the price paid, not its current market value.
(iii) A wholesaler makes an allowance for a customer who has entered liquidation.
(iv) Commission earned in the final week of the year is included in income although it will be received next month.
parts.answer: (i) consistency (broken); (ii) historical cost (applied); (iii) prudence (applied); (iv) accruals/matching or realisation (applied).
parts.working: 1 mark each. (iv) accept accruals, matching or realisation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the treatment in (i) could mislead users of the financial statements.
parts.answer: Changes in profit would be caused by the switch in method rather than real performance, so year-to-year comparisons are unreliable and profit may be manipulated upwards.
parts.working: 1 mark: not comparable; 1 mark: profit manipulated / not a fair view.

stem: A wholesaler in Faisalabad has trade receivables of $64,000 at the year end. It keeps an allowance for irrecoverable debts of 2.5% of trade receivables. The allowance brought forward is $1,250.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount to be charged to the statement of profit or loss for the allowance for irrecoverable debts.
parts.answer: $350 (increase)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the net figure for trade receivables in the statement of financial position.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the concept that requires an allowance for irrecoverable debts and explain why.
parts.answer: Prudence: receivables should not be overstated, so the expected loss on debts that may not be collected is recognised now. (Accept matching: the expected loss is matched to the year of the sale.)
parts.working: 1 mark concept; 1 mark explanation.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Sofia's draft profit for the year is $54,300. The following have been discovered:
1 Revenue includes goods with a selling price of $3,000 sent on sale or return and not yet accepted. They cost $2,250 and are not in closing inventory.
2 Closing inventory includes goods at cost $1,800 which can only be sold for $1,100.
3 Rent expense includes $1,500 paid for the first month of next year.
4 The school fees of Sofia's daughter, $2,400, were paid from the business bank account and charged to general expenses.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each item, name the accounting concept that has not been applied.
parts.answer: 1 realisation; 2 prudence; 3 accruals (matching); 4 business entity.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare a statement showing the corrected profit for the year.
parts.answer:
Corrected profit $56,750
Draft profit                            54,300
1 Remove sale or return goods          (3,000)
1 Add them to closing inventory          2,250
2 Reduce inventory to NRV                (700)
3 Rent prepaid for next year             1,500
4 Owner's private school fees            2,400
Corrected profit                        56,750
parts.working: 1 mark per correct adjustment line (max 4, item 1 needs both lines); 1 mark corrected profit (own figure).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Kareem is thinking of lending money to a small manufacturing business and is studying its financial statements for the last four years.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why the consistency concept is important to users of financial statements.
parts.answer: 1 It allows a business's results to be compared from year to year, so trends in profit and performance are real and not caused by changes in method. 2 It prevents managers or owners from manipulating profit by switching methods (e.g. inventory valuation or depreciation) to show the result they want. Also accept: helps comparison with other businesses using similar policies.
parts.working: 2 marks per reason: 1 identification + 1 development.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the realisation concept.
parts.answer: Revenue (and profit) is recognised when it is earned — when goods or services have been transferred to the customer — not when cash is received.
parts.working: 1 mark: recognised when earned / control passes; 1 mark: not when cash received.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A customer orders goods on 3 March, receives them on 9 March and pays on 20 April. State the date on which the revenue is recognised.
parts.answer: 9 March (when the goods are delivered to the customer).
parts.working: 1 mark.

stem: Indus Agro Limited revalued its land upwards by $30,000 during the year. The land was not sold. The accountant included the gain in the statement of profit or loss, giving a draft profit for the year of $72,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the corrected profit for the year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain, with reference to accounting concepts, why the revaluation gain should not be included in the profit for the year.
parts.answer: The gain is unrealised: the land has not been sold, so no revenue has been earned (realisation). Prudence means unrealised gains are not reported as profit that could be withdrawn or distributed. The gain is credited to a revaluation reserve in equity (other comprehensive income) instead.
parts.working: 1 mark realisation/unrealised; 1 mark prudence/not available for distribution; 1 mark revaluation reserve.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The managing director argues that showing the land at $30,000 more makes the statements more useful. Evaluate this argument.
parts.answer: For: an up-to-date value is more relevant to users assessing the company's worth and security for loans. Against: valuations are subjective and less verifiable than historical cost; future depreciation charges rise. Conclusion: revaluation in the SOFP is acceptable if done for the whole class and by an independent valuer, but the gain must not go through profit.
parts.working: 1 mark for, 1 mark against, 1 mark reasoned conclusion.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Leila owns a shoe shop in Islamabad. At her year end she has 1,200 pairs of shoes that cost $14 each and normally sell for $22 each. She wants to apply for a bank loan and proposes to value her closing inventory at selling price to show a higher profit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount by which profit would be overstated if Leila used her proposed valuation.
parts.working: At selling price 1,200 × $22 = 26,400; at cost 1,200 × $14 = 16,800; overstatement 9,600. M1 A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise Leila whether she should value her closing inventory at selling price. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Against: the profit on unsold goods has not been realised (realisation); prudence says gains are not anticipated, so inventory should be at the lower of cost and NRV; overstated profit could lead her to withdraw cash the business has not earned; the bank would be misled about her performance; next year's profit would be understated when the goods are sold. For: selling price shows what she expects to receive and may impress the bank. Decision: she should not; she should value at cost ($16,800) unless NRV is lower, and explain her expected margin to the bank separately.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks for points (at least one on each side for full marks), 1 mark for a clear justified decision.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Statement of profit or loss and SOFP

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which item is shown in the equity section of a limited company's statement of financial position?
A 6% loan notes (2033)
B share premium
C corporation tax payable
D dividends paid during the year
parts.answer: B share premium
parts.working: Share premium is a capital reserve and part of equity. Loan notes (A) are a non-current liability; dividends paid (D) appear in the statement of changes in equity as a deduction from retained earnings, not as a separate line in the SOFP.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Statement of profit or loss and SOFP
stem: Shalimar Foods Limited provides the following for the year ended 31 March 2027: revenue $1,840,000; cost of sales $1,104,000; distribution costs $196,000; administrative expenses $248,000; finance costs $36,000; tax $64,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the gross profit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit from operations.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the profit for the year.
parts.working: 292,000 − finance costs 36,000 = 256,000 profit before tax; − tax 64,000 = 192,000. M1 A1.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Statement of profit or loss and SOFP

The company has $300,000 7% loan notes (2031) in issue for the whole year. Only $10,500 of loan note interest has been paid. Tax for the year is estimated at $29,000.

stem: Swat Valley Hotels Limited wants $2 million to build a new wing. Its gearing (non-current liabilities ÷ (equity + non-current liabilities)) is already 58%. Profits are seasonal and fell in each of the last two years after floods. The directors are considering: (1) a rights issue of ordinary shares; (2) a five-year bank loan at 11% interest secured on the hotel; (3) a sale and leaseback of its existing staff accommodation annex.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of each of the three sources of finance for Swat Valley Hotels Limited, and recommend which the directors should use. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Rights issue: no interest or repayment, no security needed, keeps gearing low (already high at 58%); but shareholders may not take up the issue after two poor years; cost of issue; dividends expected later. Bank loan (5 years): quick, interest tax-deductible, owners keep control; but interest and repayments must be met from uncertain seasonal cash flow, raises gearing further, bank may require the hotel as security and may refuse given current gearing. Sale and leaseback of the annex: releases cash from existing assets quickly; leaseback means future lease payments and loss of the asset's future value. Recommendation: a rights issue (or mixed with a smaller loan) because gearing is already high and profits are volatile, so fixed interest increases risk.
parts.working: Level 3 (8–10): balanced discussion of all three sources applied to the hotel (gearing, seasonality, control), clear justified recommendation. Level 2 (4–7): advantages and disadvantages of at least two sources with some application, recommendation given. Level 1 (1–3): generic points about sources of finance, little application.

stem:

parts.answer: Legally it may pay, as dividends come from distributable profits (retained earnings). parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which feature applies to a sole trader?
A The owner has limited liability.
B The business is a separate legal entity from its owner.
C The owner has unlimited liability for the business's debts.
D The business must publish audited financial statements.
parts.answer: C The owner has unlimited liability for the business's debts.
parts.working: A sole trader is not a separate legal person, so the owner is personally liable for all business debts (unlimited liability). A and B describe limited companies.

parts.text:
Which statements about a public limited company are correct?

2 Its shareholders have unlimited liability.

A 1 and 2
B 1 and 3
C 2 and 4

parts.answer: B 1 and 3

parts.text:
A hockey club in Sialkot is run for its members, not to make a profit. Which statement does it prepare instead of a statement of profit or loss, and what is the name of its equivalent of capital?
A income and expenditure account; accumulated fund
B receipts and payments account; retained earnings
C statement of changes in equity; accumulated fund
D income and expenditure account; current account
parts.answer: A income and expenditure account; accumulated fund

stem: Areeba plans to open a small bakery in Multan as a sole trader.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two advantages of operating as a sole trader.
parts.answer: Any two: owner keeps all the profit; full control and quick decisions; easy and cheap to set up; financial affairs are private (no need to publish accounts).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two disadvantages of operating as a sole trader.
parts.answer: Any two: unlimited liability; limited capital (own savings and loans only); heavy workload / no one to share responsibility; business may end if the owner dies or is ill; harder to borrow.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the term limited liability.
parts.answer: Shareholders can lose no more than the amount they have paid (or agreed to pay) for their shares; their personal assets cannot be used to pay the company's debts.
parts.working: 1 mark: loss limited to investment in shares; 1 mark: personal assets protected.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what is meant by saying a limited company is a separate legal entity.
parts.answer: The company exists in law separately from its owners: it can own assets, enter contracts, sue and be sued in its own name, and it continues if shareholders change or die.
parts.working: 1 mark: separate person in law; 1 mark: example (contracts, own assets, continuity).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two differences between a private limited company and a public limited company.
parts.answer: Any two: a private company cannot offer its shares to the general public, a public company can (and may be listed on a stock exchange); private company shares are usually transferred only with the directors' agreement, public company shares are freely traded; a public company usually needs a minimum share capital and stricter disclosure; a private company name ends in 'Limited/(Private) Limited', a public one in 'plc' or equivalent.
parts.working: 2 marks per difference, comparing both types.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one reason why a family business might prefer to remain a private limited company.
parts.answer: The family keeps control because shares cannot be sold to outsiders without approval, so there is no risk of takeover; also fewer disclosure requirements and lower costs.
parts.working: 1 mark reason, 1 mark development.

stem: Usman has run a computer accessories shop in Hyderabad as a sole trader for six years. He wants to open a second branch and start selling online. His brother, who has IT skills, offers to invest $40,000 and become a partner.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Advise Usman whether he should form a partnership with his brother. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: For: extra capital ($40,000) to open the second branch; brother's IT and online-sales skills add expertise; workload and decision-making shared; cover during illness or holidays. Against: profits must be shared; unlimited liability continues — Usman becomes liable for his brother's business decisions; disagreements may arise, especially in a family; slower decisions; partnership may end on death or retirement. Decision: e.g. form the partnership with a written partnership agreement covering profit sharing, interest on capital and salaries, because the capital and skills are needed for the expansion.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for advantages and up to 2 for disadvantages, applied to the case; 1 mark recommendation of a written agreement or other safeguard; 1 mark justified decision.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Zainab and Kiran are partners in an interior design business in Karachi. Turnover has tripled in three years and they have just won a contract to design the interior of a 200-room hotel, which will need expensive materials bought in advance. A cousin is willing to invest money but does not want to take part in running the business or have unlimited liability.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Advise Zainab and Kiran whether they should convert their partnership into a private limited company. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: For conversion: limited liability protects their homes against claims (important given the large contract and its risks); the company is a separate legal entity, so it continues if a partner leaves; easier to raise finance — can issue shares to investors such as their cousin and use loan notes; may appear more credible to large clients. Against: set-up costs and legal formalities; must file accounts publicly (loss of privacy) and may require an audit; profits taxed as a company and owners paid through salaries and dividends; banks may still ask for personal guarantees, reducing the benefit of limited liability; shares in a private company cannot easily be sold. Decision: convert, because the growth in contract size and the need for outside capital make limited liability and access to share finance worth the extra cost.
parts.working: Level 3 (7–8): well-applied points on both sides and a justified decision. Level 2 (4–6): some applied points on both sides or one-sided with a decision. Level 1 (1–3): general features of partnerships/companies.

parts.answer: $36,000. Nasir has limited liability: his loss is limited to the amount paid for his shares (30,000 × $1.20); his personal assets cannot be claimed by the company's creditors.
parts.working: 1 mark amount, 1 mark limited liability, 1 mark personal assets protected.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between ownership and control in a limited company.
parts.answer: Shareholders own the company, but the directors (who may not be shareholders) manage and control it on their behalf.
parts.working: 1 mark owners = shareholders; 1 mark control = directors/managers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two reasons why limited companies must publish annual financial statements.
parts.answer: Because shareholders do not run the company, they need information to judge the directors' performance (stewardship); creditors and lenders need information because their claims are limited to the company's assets (limited liability).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare how owners withdraw profits from (i) a sole trader business and (ii) a limited company.
parts.answer: (i) The sole trader takes drawings, recorded in the capital account. (ii) Shareholders receive dividends declared by the directors out of distributable profits; directors who work in the company also receive salaries treated as expenses.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Compare how the owners' capital is shown in the statement of financial position of a partnership and of a limited company.
parts.answer: Partnership: each partner has a capital account (often fixed) and a current account for profit shares, interest and drawings. Company: equity shows issued share capital and reserves (share premium, retained earnings and other reserves).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

stem: Hassan bought 40,000 ordinary shares of $1 each in a private limited company at $1.25 per share, fully paid. Salman is a general partner in a firm of architects with one other partner.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the maximum amount Hassan could lose as a shareholder, and the maximum Salman could lose as a partner. Explain the difference.
parts.answer: Hassan: $50,000 (40,000 × $1.25 paid). Salman: there is no limit — he could lose his capital and his personal assets, because partners have unlimited liability and are jointly liable for all the partnership's debts (including those caused by the other partner).
parts.working: 1 mark Hassan's 50,000; 1 mark Salman unlimited; 1 mark limited liability explained; 1 mark joint liability/personal assets.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one way in which the law allows a partner to have limited liability, and the condition that applies.
parts.answer: A limited partner (in a limited partnership / LLP structure) may have liability limited to their capital, provided there is at least one general partner with unlimited liability and the limited partner takes no part in managing the business (or the firm is registered as a limited liability partnership).
parts.working: 1 mark limited partner/LLP; 1 mark condition (no management role / at least one general partner / registration).

stem: A school in Abbottabad built an extension to its building costing $40,000. The bookkeeper debited this to repairs and maintenance. Buildings are depreciated at 10% per year on cost, with a full year's charge in the year of acquisition.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the effect of the error on profit for the year.
parts.answer: Profit is understated by $36,000.
parts.working: The 40,000 should be removed from expenses (+40,000) and depreciation of 10% × 40,000 = 4,000 charged; net +36,000. M1 A1.

parts.label: b

stem:
Royal Pharmacy spent the following on its building during the year:
1 Replacing worn roof tiles: $6,800
2 Adding a second floor: $95,000
3 Repainting the shop front: $3,200
4 Installing a new lift (not there before): $28,500
5 Architect's fees for the second floor: $7,400
6 Cleaning after the building work: $1,100

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total capital expenditure and the total revenue expenditure.
parts.answer: Capital $130,900; revenue $11,100
parts.working: Capital: items 2, 4, 5 = 95,000 + 28,500 + 7,400 = 130,900. Revenue: items 1, 3, 6 = 6,800 + 3,200 + 1,100 = 11,100. 1 mark each correct classification group, 1 mark each total.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why item 1 is revenue expenditure while item 2 is capital expenditure.
parts.answer: Replacing worn tiles restores the building to its original condition (maintenance), so it is an expense; adding a floor improves/enlarges the asset and increases its earning capacity for more than one year, so it is capital.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Distinguish between a capital receipt and a revenue receipt, giving one example of each.
parts.answer: Capital receipt: from sale of non-current assets, loans or capital introduced (e.g. proceeds of selling an old van). Revenue receipt: from normal trading (e.g. sales revenue, rent received, commission).
parts.working: 1 mark each with example.

B profit understated; non-current assets overstated

D profit understated; non-current assets understated

parts.label: a

stem: Karakoram Foods Limited has 4,000 shareholders. The company is run by a board of five directors.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the term stewardship in the context of a limited company.
parts.answer: Stewardship is the responsibility of the directors to look after the company's resources (assets) properly on behalf of the shareholders who own it, and to account to them for how those resources have been used.
parts.working: 1 mark: directors manage/safeguard resources for shareholders; 1 mark: accountability/reporting to owners.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two ways in which directors demonstrate good stewardship.
parts.answer: Any two: keeping proper accounting records; preparing annual financial statements that give a true and fair view; safeguarding assets and preventing fraud through internal controls; having the statements audited and presenting them at the annual general meeting; using resources efficiently in shareholders' interests.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two differences between an internal auditor and an external auditor.
parts.answer: Any two: appointment — internal auditor is an employee appointed by management, external auditor is independent and appointed by the shareholders; reporting — internal auditor reports to the directors/audit committee, external auditor reports to the shareholders; purpose — internal audit reviews systems, controls and efficiency for management, external audit gives an opinion on whether the statements give a true and fair view; legal requirement — external audit is required by law for most companies, internal audit is optional; qualification/independence — external auditor must be a registered, independent accountant.
parts.working: 2 marks per difference (both sides compared).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three statutory rights of a company's external auditor.
parts.answer: Any three: right of access at all times to the company's books, records and vouchers; right to require information and explanations from directors and officers; right to receive notice of and attend general meetings; right to speak at general meetings on matters concerning them as auditor; right to make written representations if they are to be removed or not reappointed.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the meaning of the phrase 'a true and fair view'.
parts.answer: The financial statements are free from material misstatement and fairly present the company's financial performance and position, prepared in accordance with accounting standards and the law. It does not mean that every figure is exactly correct.
parts.working: 1 mark: free from material misstatement / faithfully presented; 1 mark: in accordance with standards / not absolute accuracy.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State who is responsible for preparing a company's financial statements.
parts.answer: The directors (not the auditors).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State who appoints the external auditors of a limited company, and to whom they report.
parts.answer: They are appointed by the shareholders (usually at the annual general meeting) and report to the shareholders.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why it is important that the external auditor is independent of the directors.
parts.answer: The auditor checks the statements prepared by the directors; if not independent they might be influenced to accept misstatements, so shareholders could not rely on the opinion.
parts.working: 1 mark: checking directors' work / objective opinion; 1 mark: shareholders' reliance/confidence.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between an unmodified (unqualified) audit opinion and a qualified audit opinion.
parts.answer: Unmodified: the auditor concludes that the financial statements give a true and fair view in all material respects. Qualified: the auditor concludes that the statements give a true and fair view except for the effects of a specific matter, which is material but not pervasive (a material misstatement, or an inability to obtain enough evidence about one area).
parts.working: 2 marks each: meaning + key words ('true and fair', 'except for', material but not pervasive).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the three types of modified audit opinion and state when each is given.
parts.answer: Qualified opinion ('except for'): a misstatement or lack of evidence that is material but not pervasive. Adverse opinion: misstatements are material and pervasive, so the statements do not give a true and fair view. Disclaimer of opinion: the auditor cannot obtain sufficient appropriate evidence and the possible effects are material and pervasive, so no opinion is expressed.
parts.working: 1 mark each type named; 1 mark each correct circumstance.

parts.text: Calculate the misstatement as a percentage of profit before tax, correct to two decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the type of audit opinion the auditor is likely to give. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: A qualified ('except for') opinion. The overstatement of inventory is material (well above the 5% threshold the firm uses) but it affects only one area of the statements, so it is not pervasive; the rest of the statements give a true and fair view.
parts.working: 1 mark qualified; 1 mark material (with reference to the figure); 1 mark not pervasive / limited to inventory.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Pak Agro Exports Limited has no internal audit department. Last year losses from undetected errors and staff fraud were estimated at $140,000. The finance director proposes an internal audit department costing $95,000 a year, which is expected to reduce such losses by 60%. The external auditor has said it may be able to rely on some of the internal auditors' work.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the expected annual saving in losses and the net annual cost or benefit of the internal audit department.
parts.answer: Saving $84,000; net annual cost $11,000

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise the directors whether they should set up the internal audit department. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Against: on these figures it costs $11,000 a year more than it saves; the saving is only an estimate; internal auditors are employees, so they are less independent than the external auditor and cannot replace the external audit. For: it reviews and tests internal controls continuously, deterring fraud as well as detecting it; it can improve the efficiency of operations and the reliability of records for management; the external auditor may rely on its work, which could reduce the external audit fee and close the $11,000 gap; it helps the directors show good stewardship of shareholders' assets. Decision: e.g. set it up, because the net cost is small and the non-financial benefits (stronger controls, possible lower audit fee) are likely to outweigh it.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for points against (using the $11,000 figure), up to 3 marks for points in favour applied to the company, 1 mark for a justified decision.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Mehran Retail Limited runs 45 supermarkets across Pakistan and has set up an internal audit department.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain three functions of an internal audit department.
parts.answer: Reviewing and testing internal controls (e.g. authorisation of purchases, segregation of duties) to see that they work; checking the accuracy and reliability of accounting records and reports to management; detecting and preventing fraud and error; reviewing the efficiency and value for money of operations; checking compliance with laws, regulations and company policies; helping the external auditor, who may rely on its work.
parts.working: 2 marks each: function identified (1) + explanation (1), max 3 functions.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two limitations of an external audit.
parts.answer: Auditors test samples of transactions, not every one, so some errors may go undetected; many figures rely on judgement and estimates (e.g. depreciation, allowances, provisions), so the opinion is reasonable not absolute assurance; auditors rely on information and explanations from management, which may be incomplete or deliberately misleading (collusion/fraud); the audit is of past information and is out of date when published; time and cost limits.
parts.working: 2 marks each: limitation + explanation.

stem: During the year, the directors of Lahore Builders Limited: (1) bought land for $1.3 million from a company owned by the managing director's brother; an independent valuer had valued it at $1.0 million, and the transaction was not disclosed in the annual report; (2) increased their own bonuses by 40% while reducing the dividend per share from 12 cents to 8 cents; (3) published the annual report four months later than usual. The company's profit for the year rose by 12% and the directors set up an internal audit department.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether the directors of Lahore Builders Limited have carried out their stewardship responsibilities properly. Conclude with a judgement.
parts.answer: Against good stewardship: buying land from a company owned by the managing director's brother at 30% above valuation is a conflict of interest and may waste shareholders' funds; failure to disclose the related party transaction; directors' bonuses increased while dividends cut — possible self-interest; the delay in publishing accounts reduces accountability. For: profits rose by 12%; they set up an internal audit department and kept proper records; the land may have strategic value. Judgement: overall the directors have not fully discharged their stewardship duty because of the undisclosed related-party purchase and the bonus/dividend issue, although operational performance improved.
parts.working: Level 3 (7–8): balanced discussion applied to the case with a justified judgement. Level 2 (4–6): some applied points, may be one-sided, some judgement. Level 1 (1–3): general statements about stewardship.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why shareholders of a large company need an external audit.
parts.answer: Ownership is separated from control: shareholders do not run the company and cannot check the records themselves. The directors prepare the statements and could present results favourably to protect bonuses or reputation. An independent expert's opinion that the statements are true and fair gives shareholders confidence when assessing directors' stewardship and making decisions (buy/sell/vote). It also helps deter fraud and error.
parts.working: 1 mark each for four points, or 2 marks each for two developed points.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State four items normally included in an external auditor's report.
parts.answer: Any four: title and addressee (the shareholders); the auditor's opinion; basis for opinion (statement that the audit was done under auditing standards and the auditor is independent); key audit matters (for listed companies); material uncertainty related to going concern, if any; responsibilities of the directors for the financial statements; responsibilities of the auditor; auditor's name, signature, address and date.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

stem: After a cashier at Sadiq Motors Limited was found to have stolen $18,000 over two years, a shareholder complained at the annual general meeting that the auditors 'should have found the fraud'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the responsibility of (i) the directors and (ii) the external auditor in relation to fraud.
parts.answer: (i) The directors are primarily responsible for preventing and detecting fraud, by setting up and monitoring internal controls and a culture of honesty. (ii) The auditor must plan and perform the audit to obtain reasonable assurance that the statements are free from material misstatement whether caused by fraud or error; they are not required to find all fraud, but must report material fraud they discover to the appropriate level of management/shareholders.
parts.working: 2 marks each part.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State four responsibilities of the directors of a limited company relating to its financial records and statements.
parts.answer: Any four: keep adequate accounting records; prepare annual financial statements that give a true and fair view and follow accounting standards; select suitable accounting policies and apply them consistently; make reasonable judgements and estimates; safeguard the company's assets; take reasonable steps to prevent and detect fraud; assess whether the company is a going concern; file the statements as required by law.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two threats to the independence of an external auditor.
parts.answer: Self-interest: e.g. the auditor owns shares in the client or depends heavily on its fees, so may avoid a qualified opinion. Self-review: the audit firm also prepares the accounts it audits. Familiarity: a long relationship or family ties with directors. Intimidation: directors threaten to remove the auditor. Advocacy: the auditor promotes the client's interests.
parts.working: 2 marks each: threat named + example/explanation.

stem: A flood destroyed the head office of Sindh Rice Mills Limited, including most sales and inventory records for the year. Revenue, trade receivables and closing inventory together make up most of the figures in the financial statements. The directors have estimated these figures, but there is no supporting evidence for the auditor to test.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the type of audit opinion the auditor should give. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: A disclaimer of opinion. The auditor cannot obtain sufficient appropriate evidence for revenue, receivables and inventory, which affect most of the statements, so the possible effects are both material and pervasive. The auditor therefore does not express an opinion. A qualified opinion would only be suitable if the lack of evidence affected a limited area, and an adverse opinion needs evidence that the statements are actually misstated.
parts.working: 1 mark disclaimer; 1 mark inability to obtain evidence; 1 mark material; 1 mark pervasive; 1 mark distinguishing from qualified/adverse.

author: HomiLabs

stem: The bank has withdrawn all loans from Margalla Shoes Limited and the directors have decided to put the company into liquidation shortly after the year end. However, they have prepared the financial statements on a going concern basis and refuse to change them or to disclose the planned liquidation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the type of audit opinion the auditor should give. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: An adverse opinion. The company is not a going concern (bank has withdrawn finance, directors intend to liquidate), but the statements are prepared on a going concern basis, so assets are at cost less depreciation rather than realisable values and liabilities may be misclassified. This misstatement is material and affects the statements as a whole (pervasive), so they do not give a true and fair view. It is not a disclaimer because the auditor has sufficient evidence.
parts.working: 1 mark adverse; 1 mark basis of preparation wrong; 1 mark material; 1 mark pervasive; 1 mark sufficient evidence/not a disclaimer.

author: HomiLabs

stem: The internal auditor of Indus Hardware Limited attended the year-end inventory count. The inventory records show a book value of $145,600. The physical count, valued at cost, is $138,950.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the inventory shortage and express it as a percentage of the book value, correct to two decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest three possible causes of the shortage.
parts.answer: Any three: theft by staff or customers; goods sent out without being invoiced; recording errors (e.g. purchases recorded twice); damaged goods thrown away and not recorded; count errors; goods returned to suppliers not recorded.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one internal control that would reduce the risk of this happening again.
parts.answer: E.g. regular surprise inventory counts by staff independent of the storekeeper; restricted access to the store; goods-out notes authorised for every dispatch.
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the term segregation of duties.
parts.answer: Dividing the stages of a transaction between different people so that no one person controls it from start to finish; this makes fraud harder because it would need collusion, and errors are more likely to be spotted.
parts.working: 1 mark meaning; 1 mark benefit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two examples of segregation of duties in the purchases system of a company.
parts.answer: Any two: the person who orders goods is not the person who receives them; the person who records invoices is not the person who authorises payment; the person who signs payments is not the person who keeps the purchases ledger; a different person reconciles supplier statements.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Other than shareholders, name two groups who rely on a company's audited financial statements, and explain why each relies on the audit.
parts.answer: Any two: banks/lenders — deciding whether to lend and checking loan covenants, need assurance figures are reliable; suppliers — deciding whether to give credit; tax authorities — assessing tax payable; potential investors — deciding whether to buy shares; employees/trade unions — job security and pay negotiations; government/regulators.
parts.working: 1 mark each group; 1 mark each reason linked to reliability.

stem: Thar Coal Services Limited reports profit before tax of $1,150,000. Its mining equipment cost $3,600,000 and has a useful life of 12 years with no residual value, but the directors have decided not to charge any depreciation on it this year. The external auditor disagrees. The directors tell shareholders that "the auditor is responsible for getting the figures right".

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the straight-line depreciation for the year, the corrected profit before tax, and the misstatement as a percentage of the reported profit before tax, correct to two decimal places.
parts.answer: Depreciation $300,000; corrected profit before tax $850,000; misstatement 26.09%

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the directors' statement is wrong, and state with reasons the audit opinion likely to be given if the directors refuse to charge depreciation.
parts.answer: The directors are responsible for preparing financial statements that give a true and fair view; the auditor only examines them and gives an independent opinion on them. The misstatement (26.09% of profit) is material, but it is confined to one item (depreciation, carrying amount of equipment and retained earnings) rather than the statements as a whole, so it is not pervasive. The auditor is therefore likely to give a qualified ('except for') opinion.
parts.working: 1 mark directors prepare; 1 mark auditor gives opinion only; 1 mark material with reference to figure; 1 mark qualified because not pervasive.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Swat Marble Limited has 2,500 shareholders, none of whom work in the business. This year its external auditor gave a qualified audit opinion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the external auditor's report is addressed to the shareholders rather than to the directors.
parts.answer: The auditor is appointed by, and acts for, the shareholders, who own the company but do not manage it. The report gives them an independent opinion on the statements the directors have prepared, so it is a check on the directors' stewardship.
parts.working: 1 mark appointed by / acts for shareholders; 1 mark checks directors' stewardship for owners who do not run the company.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State three possible consequences for Swat Marble Limited of receiving a qualified audit opinion.
parts.answer: Any three: shareholders lose confidence in the directors and may vote against their reappointment; the share price may fall; banks may refuse loans or charge higher interest; suppliers may reduce credit; potential investors may be put off; the company's reputation may suffer.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: At the annual general meeting of Kohat Cement Limited, shareholders must vote on reappointing Khan & Co as external auditors. Khan & Co received an audit fee of $85,000 and a further $240,000 for consultancy, including designing the company's new computerised accounting system. The same audit partner has led the audit for 11 years.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate non-audit fees as a percentage of the total fees received from the company, correct to one decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise the shareholders whether they should vote to reappoint Khan & Co as auditors. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Against: non-audit fees are almost three times the audit fee (about 74% of total), creating a self-interest threat — the firm may be reluctant to qualify its opinion and risk losing lucrative consultancy work; the firm designed the new accounting system, so it would be auditing its own work (self-review threat); the audit partner has been in charge for 11 years (familiarity threat). For: the firm knows the business well, which may make the audit efficient and cheaper; no evidence of any wrongdoing; changing auditors has costs. Decision: shareholders should not reappoint unless safeguards are put in place (e.g. rotate the audit partner, stop providing system design/consultancy, or have a separate team); otherwise appoint a new independent firm.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for independence threats applied, up to 2 marks for points in favour, 1 mark for safeguards, 1 mark for a justified decision.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how publishing an audited annual report helps the directors carry out their stewardship responsibility.
parts.answer: The annual report shows shareholders how the directors have used the company's resources and what results they achieved; the audit gives independent assurance that this account is true and fair; shareholders can then question directors and vote on their reappointment at the AGM, so the directors are held accountable.
parts.working: 1 mark: reports use of resources/results; 1 mark: independent assurance; 1 mark: accountability (AGM/votes).

stem: The honorary auditor of the Peshawar Squash Club checks the treasurer's records for the year. Cash in hand at the start was $3,850. Receipts recorded were: subscriptions $46,200; event ticket sales $18,750; donations $9,500. All recorded payments, supported by receipts, totalled $61,400. The cash counted at the year end was $11,280.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount of cash that should be held at the year end, and the amount missing.
parts.answer: Should hold $16,900; missing $5,620

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two controls the club committee could introduce to improve the stewardship of its funds.
parts.answer: Any two developed: all receipts banked intact and promptly, with numbered receipts issued; two signatories required for payments; regular bank reconciliations reviewed by someone other than the treasurer; an independent honorary auditor checks the accounts annually; monthly reports to the committee comparing receipts with members' list.
parts.working: 2 marks each: control + how it protects funds.

author: HomiLabs

stem: The directors of Faisal Textiles Limited each receive a bonus equal to 2% of the year's profit before tax. This year the directors postponed essential machine maintenance and changed the estimated useful life of machinery from 8 to 15 years, increasing profit by $1.2 million.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss the conflict of interest between the directors and the shareholders of Faisal Textiles Limited, and suggest how the shareholders could reduce the risk that the directors act in their own interest.
parts.answer: Conflict: the directors' bonus depends on annual profit, so they have an incentive to boost short-term profit (e.g. by delaying maintenance, cutting training, or choosing accounting estimates that increase profit), while shareholders want long-term growth in value and reliable statements; directors also control the information shareholders receive. Ways to reduce it: link part of pay to long-term targets or share price over several years (or pay part in shares); appoint independent non-executive directors and an audit committee; keep a strong independent external audit; require clear disclosure of directors' remuneration and related-party transactions; vote on remuneration at the AGM.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for explaining the conflict with reference to the case, up to 3 marks for suitable safeguards explained.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
During the audit of Chitral Tea Limited, the auditor identified the following errors in the draft statement of financial position, which shows net assets of $2,460,000:
• Damaged inventory not yet written down to net realisable value: effect on net assets −$36,000
• Accrued audit fee not recorded: effect on net assets −$18,000
• Prepaid rent omitted: effect on net assets +$12,500

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the corrected net assets of the company.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The directors agree to make all the corrections. State the type of audit opinion that is likely to be given and explain why.
parts.answer: An unmodified opinion: once the misstatements have been corrected, the statements give a true and fair view in all material respects, so there is no reason to modify the opinion.
parts.working: 1 mark unmodified; 1 mark explanation.

author: HomiLabs

stem: The directors of Hala Ceramics Limited propose that the company's internal audit department, which reports to the finance director, should take over the work of the external auditor. This would save the external audit fee of $120,000 a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the directors' proposal.
parts.answer: Against: internal auditors are employees who report to the finance director, so they are not independent of the people whose statements they would check; shareholders, lenders and other users need an independent opinion that the statements give a true and fair view; an external audit is normally a legal requirement for a limited company, so it cannot simply be replaced; the external auditor is appointed by and reports to the shareholders, whereas internal audit serves management. For: the saving of $120,000 a year; internal auditors know the business well. Conclusion: reject the proposal; keep both, and instead let the external auditor rely on the internal auditors' work where appropriate, which may reduce the fee.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks for points (at least one in favour for full marks) applied to the company, 1 mark for using the $120,000 or the reporting line, 1 mark for a justified conclusion.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A delivery van was bought for $48,000. It is expected to be used for 6 years and then sold for $6,000. The straight-line method is used. What is the annual depreciation charge?
A $7,000
B $8,000
C $6,000
D $9,000
parts.working: (48,000 − 6,000) ÷ 6 = $7,000. $8,000 ignores the residual value; $9,000 wrongly adds the residual value to cost.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A machine was bought at the start of year 1 for $80,000. It is depreciated at 25% per annum using the reducing balance method. What is the depreciation charge for year 3?
A $11,250
B $20,000
C $15,000
D $33,750
parts.working: Year 1: 25% × 80,000 = 20,000 (CA 60,000). Year 2: 25% × 60,000 = 15,000 (CA 45,000). Year 3: 25% × 45,000 = $11,250. $20,000 is the straight-line style charge on cost; $33,750 is the carrying amount at the end of year 3.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A business with a year end of 31 December bought equipment for $36,000 on 1 April 2025. Depreciation is charged at 20% per annum on cost, calculated on a monthly basis. What is the depreciation charge for the year ended 31 December 2025?
A $5,400
B $7,200
C $1,800
D $6,000
parts.working: 20% × 36,000 = 7,200 per year; April to December = 9 months; 7,200 × 9/12 = $5,400. $7,200 charges a full year; $1,800 charges only 3 months.

stem: Hamza Printers, Lahore, bought a printing machine on 1 January 2024 for Rs 1,250,000. Installation cost Rs 50,000. The machine is expected to last 5 years and then be sold for Rs 100,000. The straight-line method is used and the financial year ends on 31 December.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the annual depreciation charge.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the carrying amount of the machine at 31 December 2026.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the accounting concept applied when depreciation is charged, and explain how it is applied.
parts.answer: Matching (accruals) concept: the cost of the machine is spread over the years in which it helps to earn revenue.
parts.working: 1 mark for naming matching/accruals; 1 mark for explaining that the cost is charged against the revenue of the periods that benefit from the asset.

author: HomiLabs

stem: SwiftDrop, a courier business in Nairobi, bought a delivery van for $40,000. It uses the reducing balance method at 40% per annum.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the depreciation charge for each of the four years using the reducing balance method.
parts.working: 40% × 40,000 = 16,000; 40% × 24,000 = 9,600; 40% × 14,400 = 5,760; 40% × 8,640 = 3,456. M1 for applying 40% to the carrying amount, A2 all four correct (A1 for two or three correct).

parts.label: b
parts.text: The van will be worth $5,184 after four years. Calculate the annual charge if the straight-line method were used instead.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the reducing balance method may be more suitable for the van.
parts.answer: A van loses more of its value in its early years, and repair costs rise as it gets older, so a high early charge gives a more even total cost each year.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: van loses most value early; carrying amount closer to resale value; maintenance rises with age so depreciation + repairs is more even; van used most heavily when new.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the effect on profit for year 1 of using the reducing balance method instead of the straight-line method.
parts.answer: Profit is $7,296 lower.
parts.working: 16,000 − 8,704 = 7,296 (M1); profit lower/decreases (A1).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Mehran Engineering has a financial year ending 31 March. At 1 April 2024 its machinery cost $150,000 and the provision for depreciation was $42,000. A further machine costing $60,000 was bought on 1 October 2024. Machinery is depreciated at 10% per annum on cost, on a monthly basis. No machinery was sold.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the depreciation charge for each of the years ended 31 March 2025 and 31 March 2026.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare the provision for depreciation of machinery account for the two years, balancing it at the end of each year.
parts.answer:
Closing balances: 31 March 2025 $60,000; 31 March 2026 $81,000.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Al-Noor Motors, a garage in Karachi, uses the revaluation method for its loose tools. On 1 January 2025 the tools were valued at Rs 84,000. During the year tools costing Rs 37,500 were bought and paid by bank. On 31 December 2025 the tools were valued at Rs 96,300.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the depreciation of loose tools for the year.
parts.working: Opening valuation 84,000 + purchases 37,500 − closing valuation 96,300 (M1) = Rs 25,200 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare the loose tools account for the year ended 31 December 2025.
parts.answer:
Loose tools account

parts.working: B1 opening valuation debit; B1 purchases debit; B1 depreciation credit and closing valuation c/d.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two reasons why the revaluation method is used for loose tools rather than the straight-line method.
parts.answer: Loose tools are many low-cost items, so keeping a record of each one is impractical; they are lost, broken or replaced often, so a yearly valuation reflects their real use.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: many small items; low individual cost; no record of each item's cost/life; frequent loss, breakage or theft; useful lives vary/unpredictable.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Rukhsana runs a tailoring workshop in Peshawar and owns sewing machines and a delivery motorcycle.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two causes of depreciation of non-current assets.
parts.answer: Wear and tear through use; obsolescence (also: passage of time, depletion).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: wear and tear; obsolescence (new technology/fashion); passage of time (e.g. lease); depletion (e.g. a quarry).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the effect on the financial statements if a business does not provide for depreciation.
parts.answer: Expenses are understated so profit is overstated, and non-current assets are overstated in the statement of financial position.
parts.working: 1 mark profit overstated (expenses too low); 1 mark non-current assets/capital overstated.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State three figures needed to calculate a straight-line depreciation charge.
parts.answer: Cost of the asset, expected residual value, expected useful life.
parts.working: All three for 2 marks; two correct for 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Oakfield Dental Clinic depreciates office equipment at 20% per annum on cost. A full year's depreciation is charged in the year of purchase and none in the year of disposal. On 1 January 2025 equipment at cost was $90,000; none of it was fully depreciated. On 3 March 2025 new equipment was bought for $14,000. On 30 November 2025 an item bought in 2022 for $8,000 was sold for $2,500.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the depreciation charge for office equipment for the year ended 31 December 2025.
parts.working: Equipment held at year end at cost: 90,000 − 8,000 + 14,000 = 96,000 (M1 M1). 20% × 96,000 = $19,200 (A1). Full year on the new item, nothing on the item sold.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit or loss on the disposal of the item sold.
parts.answer: Loss $700
parts.working: Depreciation charged 2022, 2023, 2024 = 3 × 1,600 = 4,800 (M1). Carrying amount = 8,000 − 4,800 = 3,200 (A1). Proceeds 2,500 → loss $700 (A1).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Cloudline Data, a web-hosting company in Singapore, bought server equipment for $125,000. It expects to sell the equipment for $27,000 after three years.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the annual reducing balance rate that reduces the cost to the residual value in exactly three years. Give your answer as a whole-number percentage.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the depreciation charge for year 2.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the carrying amount at the end of year 2.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the business chose the reducing balance method for this equipment.
parts.answer: The equipment (e.g. computer servers) becomes out of date quickly and loses most of its value early, so a higher charge in early years matches its fall in value and use.
parts.working: 1 mark for identifying early loss of value/obsolescence; 1 mark for linking to matching cost with benefit.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Lumière Bakery, in Montreal, bought an oven for $50,000 at the start of year 1. Its policy is to depreciate the oven at 20% per annum using the reducing balance method. Years 1 and 2 were correct, but in year 3 the bookkeeper charged 20% of the original cost.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the correct depreciation charge for year 3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the effect of the error on the profit for year 3.
parts.answer: Profit understated by $3,600
parts.working: Charged 10,000, should be 6,400; difference 3,600 (M1); profit understated (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the effect of the error on the statement of financial position at the end of year 3.
parts.answer: Accumulated depreciation overstated by $3,600, so the carrying amount of non-current assets (and capital) is understated by the same amount.
