author: HomiLabs

stem: A freelance designer in Dhaka buys a laptop for $2,400 and depreciates it at 30% per annum using the reducing balance method.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the depreciation charge for each of the first two years.
parts.answer: Year 1 $720; year 2 $504

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the carrying amount at the end of year 2.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the reducing balance method suits a laptop.
parts.answer: Laptops become obsolete quickly and lose most value in the first years, so a larger charge early matches the fall in value.
parts.working: 1 mark obsolescence/early loss of value; 1 mark matching charge with benefit/value.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Farhan is opening a furniture workshop in Sialkot and will apply for a bank loan after his first year. He buys a CNC machine for $90,000, expected to last 5 years with a residual value of $10,000. He can use the straight-line method or the reducing balance method at 35% per annum. Profit before depreciation for year 1 is expected to be $60,000. He wants to choose the method that shows the higher profit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit for year 1 under each method.
parts.answer: Straight-line $44,000; reducing balance $28,500

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise Farhan which method he should use. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Advice should favour the method that best reflects how the machine is used, applied consistently, rather than the one that flatters the loan application (e.g. reducing balance if the machine loses value fast).
parts.working: Points for SL: higher year-1 profit by $15,500; simple; suits even use. Points for RB: matches heavy early use/fall in value; more prudent; profits more even when repairs rise. Consistency concept: once chosen, the method must be kept, so a switch later to boost profit is not allowed; a bank will look at cash flow and security, not only profit; choosing a method only to impress the bank misleads users. Up to 4 marks for points (max 3 one side), 2 marks for a justified decision.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Zainab Fashions, Faisalabad, bought shop fittings for Rs 360,000 on 1 July 2025. Its year ends on 31 December. Fittings are depreciated at 12.5% per annum on cost, calculated monthly.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the depreciation charge for the years ended 31 December 2025 and 31 December 2026.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The owner says, 'Depreciation means I am saving money to replace the fittings.' Explain why this is not correct.
parts.answer: Depreciation is a non-cash expense: it reduces profit but no money is set aside, so cash is not saved unless the owner chooses to keep it in a separate fund.
parts.working: 1 mark non-cash/book entry; 1 mark no cash set aside/does not create a replacement fund.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A machine cost $30,000. Accumulated depreciation on it was $18,000 when it was sold for $9,500 cash. What was the result of the disposal?
A Loss of $2,500
B Profit of $9,500
C Profit of $2,500
D Loss of $20,500
parts.answer: A Loss of $2,500
parts.working: Carrying amount = 30,000 − 18,000 = 12,000. Proceeds 9,500 < 12,000 → loss of $2,500. 'Profit of $2,500' reverses the comparison; 'Loss of $20,500' ignores the accumulated depreciation.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A business part-exchanged an old vehicle for a new one with a list price of $45,000. The old vehicle had cost $32,000 and had accumulated depreciation of $22,400. A Profit of $2,400
B Loss of $2,400
C Profit of $12,000
D Loss of $20,000
parts.answer: A Profit of $2,400
parts.working: Carrying amount = 32,000 − 22,400 = 9,600. Allowance 12,000 − 9,600 = profit $2,400. 'Loss of $20,000' compares the allowance with cost, ignoring depreciation.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Greenleaf Accountants, Cape Town, sold an old office computer server for $7,200 cash. It had cost $18,000 and accumulated depreciation was $11,250.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Takumi Textiles, Osaka, bought a machine on 1 January 2022 for $64,000. It is depreciated at 25% per annum using the reducing balance method, with a full year's charge in the year of purchase and none in the year of sale. The machine was sold on 1 January 2025 at a loss of $3,800.

parts.label: a

parts.label: b

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Mei owns a catering business in Kuala Lumpur. Her old van has a carrying amount of $11,500. She needs a new van with a list price of $58,000.
Option 1: the dealer gives a trade-in allowance of $13,000 on the old van and Mei pays the balance.
Option 2: Mei sells the old van privately for $15,500 after paying $600 for advertising, and the dealer gives her a 4% trade discount on the new van because there is no trade-in.

parts.label: a

parts.answer: Option 1 $45,000; option 2 $40,780

parts.label: b

parts.answer: Option 2 saves $4,220 in cash, but Mei must weigh the time, risk and delay of a private sale.

parts.working: Carrying amount = 400,000 − 80,000 = 320,000; 500,000 − 320,000 = $180,000. $100,000 compares with cost and ignores the accumulated depreciation.

stem: Daraz Storage Ltd bought land for $250,000 in 2020. In 2024 the land was revalued to $320,000 and the increase was credited to a revaluation reserve. In 2026 the land was revalued to $230,000. Land is not depreciated.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how the decrease in value in 2026 is treated.
parts.answer: Decrease $90,000: $70,000 debited to the revaluation reserve; $20,000 charged as an expense in the statement of profit or loss.
parts.working: 320,000 − 230,000 = 90,000 (M1); 70,000 against reserve, remaining 20,000 to profit or loss (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare the journal entry for the 2026 revaluation. A narrative is not required.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the whole decrease is not taken to the revaluation reserve.

parts.working: 1 mark reserve only contains the previous surplus on this asset; 1 mark fall below cost is a loss charged to profit (prudence).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Aster Ltd owns land bought for $180,000. A professional valuer now values it at $260,000. The directors decide to show the land at the new value.

parts.label: c

A 30.00%

C 70.00%

author: HomiLabs

author: HomiLabs

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem: Blue Lagoon Laundry, Colombo, had revenue of $1,260,000 for 2025. The carrying amount of its non-current assets at 31 December 2025 was $420,000. Its non-current asset turnover for 2024 was 2.40 times.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem: Shifa Pharmacy, Rawalpindi, has an annual cost of sales of Rs 1,095,000 and holds average inventory of Rs 150,000. The owner wants to reduce inventory turnover to 35 days with no change in cost of sales.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the reduction in average inventory needed to reach 35 days.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State two risks to the pharmacy of holding less inventory.
parts.answer: Running out of medicines that patients need, losing customers to other pharmacies; losing bulk-buying discounts.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: stock-outs/lost sales; loss of customer goodwill (patients need medicines urgently); loss of bulk discounts; more frequent ordering costs; supplier delays.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A company has 1,200,000 ordinary shares of $0.50 each. Its profit for the year was $540,000 and it has no preference shares. What is its earnings per share?
A 45 cents
B 90 cents
C 22.5 cents
D 4.5 cents
parts.answer: A 45 cents
parts.working: 540,000 ÷ 1,200,000 shares = $0.45 = 45 cents. 90 cents wrongly divides by the nominal value of the share capital ($600,000) instead of the number of shares.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A company's equity is $600,000 and its only non-current liability is a loan of $200,000. It issues a further $100,000 of debentures to buy machinery. Gearing = non-current liabilities ÷ (equity + non-current liabilities) × 100. What is the gearing ratio after the issue?
A 33.33%
B 25.00%
C 50.00%
D 42.86%
parts.working: 300,000 ÷ (600,000 + 300,000) × 100 = 33.33%. 25.00% is the gearing before the issue; 50.00% divides debt by equity only (300,000 ÷ 600,000).

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem: Andes Coffee plc has 4,000,000 issued ordinary shares of $1 each and no preference shares. For the year: profit for the year $1,320,000; ordinary dividends paid $480,000. The market price of one share is $4.62.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the earnings per share.
parts.answer: 33 cents

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the price earnings ratio.
parts.answer: 14.00 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the dividend cover.
parts.answer: 2.75 times

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the dividend yield, to two decimal places.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Explain what the price earnings ratio shows an investor.
parts.answer: It shows how many years of current earnings the share price represents; a high P/E means the market expects profits to grow (or sees the share as low risk).
parts.working: 1 mark price paid per $1 of earnings / years to recover price; 1 mark high = confidence/expected growth.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem:
Extract from the statement of financial position of Baltic Fisheries Ltd at 31 March 2026:
                                 $
Ordinary share capital   2,000,000
Share premium              400,000
Retained earnings        1,100,000
8% debentures (2032)     1,500,000
Profit from operations for the year was $690,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the gearing ratio, to two decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the interest cover, to two decimal places.
parts.answer: 5.75 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why both lenders and ordinary shareholders are interested in the gearing ratio.
parts.answer: Lenders: a high gearing means more risk that interest and capital will not be repaid. Shareholders: high gearing means fixed interest is paid before dividends, so dividends are more volatile, although returns can be higher when profits rise.
parts.working: 1 mark lenders' risk of non-payment/security; 1 mark shareholders: interest paid first, dividends at risk; 1 mark development (higher gearing magnifies returns in good years / ability to borrow more).

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem:
Ayesha, a retired teacher in Lahore, wants regular income from shares. She is choosing between two companies:
                           Crescent Foods plc   Delta Tech plc
Profit for the year                  $900,000       $1,560,000
Ordinary shares in issue            3,000,000        6,000,000
Ordinary dividends paid              $450,000         $312,000
Market price per share                  $3.60            $3.90
Dividend cover                      2.0 times        5.0 times
Gearing                                   45%              15%

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the dividend yield for each company, to two decimal places.
parts.answer: Crescent 4.17%; Delta 1.33%

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the price earnings ratio for each company.
parts.answer: Crescent 12.00; Delta 15.00

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise Ayesha which company's shares she should buy. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Crescent suits her need for regular income (higher yield), but its high gearing makes the dividend less safe; a justified decision either way.
parts.working: Crescent: yield 4.17% v 1.33%; pays out half its profit. Against Crescent: gearing 45% – interest comes first, dividend cover only 2.0. Delta: low gearing 15%, cover 5.0 so dividend is safe, higher P/E suggests market expects growth – but low income now. 1 mark per point to 3 (both sides needed for 3), 1 mark decision linked to her need for income.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem: Kilimanjaro Tea Ltd: at 31 December 2024 long-term loans were $800,000 and equity was $1,200,000 (gearing 40.00%). At 31 December 2025 long-term loans were $500,000 and equity was $1,500,000. Gearing = non-current liabilities ÷ (equity + non-current liabilities) × 100.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the gearing ratio at 31 December 2025.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether the company is high or low geared in 2025 and give one advantage to ordinary shareholders of the change since 2024.
parts.answer: Low geared (below 50%). Less interest has to be paid, so more profit is available for dividends and the risk of not paying a dividend is lower.
parts.working: 1 mark low geared; 1 mark advantage (less interest/lower risk/more profit for dividends).

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem:
Pacifica Bottling plc has 5,000,000 ordinary shares of $1 each, equity of $7,500,000 and no borrowings. It needs $2,000,000 for a new production line, after which profit from operations is expected to be $1,400,000 a year. Ignore taxation.
Option 1: issue 1,000,000 ordinary shares at $2 each.
Option 2: borrow $2,000,000 with a 7% long-term loan.
Gearing = non-current liabilities ÷ (equity + non-current liabilities) × 100.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the expected earnings per share under each option, to two decimal places (in cents).
parts.answer: Option 1 23.33 cents; option 2 25.20 cents

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the gearing ratio under option 2.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise the directors which option to choose. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Option 2 gives higher EPS and keeps control with existing shareholders; gearing of 21.05% is still low, so the loan is affordable unless profits are uncertain.
parts.working: For loan: EPS 25.20c v 23.33c; no dilution of control; interest cover 10 times. Against: fixed interest must be paid even if profit falls; capital must be repaid; gearing rises. 1 mark per point (max 2), 1 mark decision.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which user of a business's financial statements is most interested in its liquid (acid test) ratio?
A A supplier deciding whether to offer 30 days' credit
B A shareholder comparing dividend yields
C The tax authority checking the profit figure
D A competitor comparing gross margins
parts.answer: A A supplier deciding whether to offer 30 days' credit
parts.working: A trade supplier wants to know whether the business can pay its short-term debts on time, which the liquid ratio measures. Shareholders are more interested in returns and dividends.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem: Bilal owns Sunrise Poultry Farm near Sheikhupura. He employs a farm manager and twelve workers and wants to borrow money from a bank to build a new shed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two internal users of the financial statements of Sunrise Poultry Farm.
parts.answer: The owner (Bilal) and the farm manager/employees.
parts.working: 1 mark each: owner; managers; employees (internal).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what the bank would look for in the financial statements before lending to the farm.
parts.answer: Whether the farm makes enough profit and cash to pay interest and repay the loan, and what assets could be offered as security.
parts.working: 1 mark profitability/cash flow to repay; 1 mark security/gearing/existing debts.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the farm's employees are interested in its financial statements.
parts.answer: To judge job security and whether the farm can afford pay rises.
parts.working: 1 mark job security/continuity; 1 mark ability to pay wages/pay rises/bonuses.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem: Hira owns a shoe retailer with two shops in Karachi. She compares her ratios with those of a large shoe retailer in Madrid that publishes its financial statements online, to decide whether her business is doing well.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain three limitations of using ratio analysis to compare the two businesses.
parts.answer: Different accounting policies (e.g. depreciation methods, inventory valuation) make ratios not comparable; historical cost and different inflation and currency conditions in Pakistan and Spain distort figures; ratios ignore non-financial factors such as location, brand and staff skills.
parts.working: For each of three limitations: 1 mark identifying, 1 mark explaining in context. Accept: different policies; different year ends/seasonal timing; historical cost/inflation; different sizes and markets; ratios are based on past data; window dressing at the year end; non-financial factors ignored; no single 'correct' ratio.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem:
Kiran owns a clothing boutique in Hyderabad (Sindh). Her ratios are:
                                2024      2025
Gross margin                     38%       41%
Profit margin                    14%       10%
Return on capital employed       22%       17%
Current ratio                1.9 : 1   1.8 : 1
Trade receivables turnover   34 days   29 days

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two ratios that show an improvement in 2025.
parts.answer: Gross margin (rose from 38% to 41%) and the trade receivables turnover (fell from 34 to 29 days).
parts.working: 1 mark each with direction stated.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the profit margin fell although the gross margin rose.
parts.answer: Operating expenses (such as rent, wages or advertising) rose faster than gross profit, so a smaller share of revenue was left as profit.
parts.working: 1 mark expenses rose; 1 mark faster than gross profit / as % of revenue.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two actions Kiran could take to improve her profit margin.
parts.answer: Cut operating expenses such as advertising or energy; move to cheaper premises or renegotiate rent.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two sensible expense-control or revenue actions.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem:
Liang owns a bicycle shop in Kunming and has asked a bank for a five-year loan. At 31 December 2025: inventory $64,000; trade receivables $41,000; cash $3,000; current liabilities $72,000. Other information:
                               Liang   Industry average
Return on capital employed       21%                15%
Interest cover               6 times            5 times
Current ratio                      ?           1.80 : 1
Liquid ratio                       ?           1.00 : 1

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate, to two decimal places, Liang's (i) current ratio and (ii) liquid (acid test) ratio.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise the bank whether it should grant the loan. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Profitability is strong (ROCE 21% v 15%), but liquidity is weak (0.61 v 1.00), so the bank may lend only with security or conditions.
parts.working: For: ROCE above the industry; interest cover 6 times. Against: both liquidity ratios below the industry average; may struggle to meet repayments in cash. Other: security available, purpose of loan, owner's record. 1 mark per point (max 3, both sides), 1 mark justified decision.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem:
Meridian Furniture plc has two divisions. The directors can invest in only one of them.
                           North $     South $
Revenue                  2,400,000   1,500,000
Profit from operations     288,000     270,000
Capital employed         1,600,000   1,800,000
Profit margin               12.00%      18.00%

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate for each division, to two decimal places: (i) the asset turnover (revenue ÷ capital employed), (ii) the return on capital employed.
parts.answer: North: asset turnover 1.50 times, ROCE 18.00%. South: asset turnover 0.83 times, ROCE 15.00%.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise the directors which division should receive the investment. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: North earns the higher ROCE through efficient use of assets, though South has the better margin; a justified choice, usually North.
parts.working: North: higher ROCE 18% v 15%; uses assets more intensively (1.50 v 0.83). South: higher profit margin 18% v 12% – if extra capital raises its sales, it may gain more. Non-financial: market growth, competition, capacity. 1 mark per point (max 3, both sides), 1 mark decision.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem: Tendai sells farm supplies in Harare. In 2025 he increased the credit period for customers from 30 to 60 days to win more business; his trade receivables turnover in 2024 was 38 days and the business now has a bank overdraft. For 2025: credit sales $730,000; credit purchases $511,000; trade receivables $122,000; trade payables $42,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate for 2025, to the nearest whole day: (i) the trade receivables turnover, (ii) the trade payables turnover.
parts.answer: (i) 61 days (ii) 30 days

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise Tendai whether to continue offering 60 days' credit. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Longer credit raised sales but customers now pay 31 days after Tendai pays suppliers, which has caused the overdraft; he should probably return to shorter credit or offer cash discounts.
parts.working: For keeping: sales grew; competitive; customer loyalty. Against: receivables days 38 → 61 while payables 30, overdraft interest, higher risk of irrecoverable debts. 1 mark per point (max 3, both sides), 1 mark decision.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem:
Omar holds shares in Granite Peak Cement plc, which has 7,000,000 ordinary shares in issue.
                                2024         2025

Ordinary dividends paid   $1,050,000   $1,050,000
Market price per share         $3.00        $2.40

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the dividend cover for each year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the dividend yield for each year, to two decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise Omar whether to keep his shares. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: The higher yield is only because the share price fell; with cover of 1.20 the dividend is at risk, so Omar should consider selling unless he expects profits to recover.
parts.working: For keeping: yield up to 6.25%; dividend maintained; price may recover. Against: EPS fell 30c → 18c; cover 1.20 – dividend barely covered, may be cut; falling price shows market concern. 1 mark per point (max 3, both sides), 1 mark decision.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem: Esi runs a homeware shop in Kumasi. For 2025: cost of sales $384,000; inventory 1 January 2025 $40,000; inventory 31 December 2025 $56,000. In 2024 the rate of inventory turnover was 12 times.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of inventory turnover for 2025.
parts.answer: 8.00 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two possible reasons why the rate of inventory turnover has fallen from 12 times.
parts.answer: Sales have slowed (fewer customers); Esi bought too much inventory or some lines are out of fashion.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: lower demand/sales; overbuying/bulk purchases; slow-moving or obsolete lines; higher selling prices reduced sales; new competitor.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise Esi whether she should sell her slow-moving inventory at reduced prices. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Selling at a discount releases cash and storage space and avoids obsolescence, but lowers the gross margin and may train customers to wait for sales; a justified decision.
parts.working: For: cash released, less risk of obsolescence/damage, lower storage cost, turnover improves. Against: lower gross margin, damages brand image, customers wait for discounts. 1 mark per point (max 3), 1 mark decision.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem:
Yusuf owns a restaurant in Dubai. At the start of 2025 he introduced a premium menu.
                        2024 $      2025 $
Revenue              1,250,000   1,400,000
Cost of sales          500,000     616,000
Operating expenses     450,000     560,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the gross margin for each year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit margin for each year.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise Yusuf whether he should keep the new premium menu. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: The menu raised revenue by 12% but profit fell from $300,000 to $224,000 because food and staff costs rose faster; he should change it unless prices can rise or costs be cut.
parts.working: For: revenue up 150,000; new customers/reputation; may take time to pay off. Against: GM down 4 points, PM down 8 points, profit down 76,000; expenses up 110,000. 1 mark per point (max 3), 1 mark decision.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem: Divya runs an electrical wholesaler in Chennai. Her current assets are inventory $60,000, trade receivables $80,000 and cash $10,000. Current liabilities are trade payables $40,000 and a bank overdraft $60,000 (current ratio 1.50 : 1; liquid ratio 0.90 : 1). A debt factor offers to buy all her trade receivables for $76,000 cash. Divya would use the cash to repay the overdraft in full.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate, to two decimal places, the current ratio and the liquid ratio after the proposal.
parts.answer: Current ratio 2.15 : 1; liquid ratio 0.65 : 1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise Divya whether to accept the factor's offer. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: The overdraft disappears and the current ratio rises, but the liquid ratio falls and the business loses $4,000 and control of debt collection; a justified decision.
parts.working: For: overdraft repaid, no overdraft interest, immediate cash, no irrecoverable debt risk. Against: cost 4,000 (5%); liquid ratio falls 0.90 → 0.65; customers dealt with by a third party; one-off – future receivables still slow. 1 mark per point (max 3), 1 mark decision.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem:
Directors of Dune Solar Ltd review the last three years. For 2025: profit from operations $840,000; equity $4,200,000; non-current liabilities $1,400,000.
                                2023      2024      2025
Return on capital employed       19%       17%         ?
Gearing                          10%       18%       25%
Current ratio                1.9 : 1   1.6 : 1   1.3 : 1

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the return on capital employed for 2025, to two decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether the company's financial position has improved over the three years.
parts.answer: No: profitability has fallen (ROCE 19% → 15%), borrowing has risen (gearing 10% → 25%) and liquidity has weakened (current ratio 1.9 → 1.3), although gearing is still low and the borrowing may be funding growth.
parts.working: ROCE falling each year: less return per $ invested (1–2 marks). Gearing up: more risk, more interest, but still below 50% (1–2). Current ratio down: possible liquidity pressure, still above 1 (1–2). Balanced point: new investment may not yet have produced profit (1). Conclusion (1). Max 6.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
The treasurer of Riverside Tennis Club provides these balances at 1 January 2025:
                                 $
Clubhouse                  180,000
Equipment                   24,500
Bar inventory                3,800
Subscriptions in arrears     1,200
Subscriptions in advance       900
Bank                         6,700
Electricity accrued            450
Bar suppliers (payables)     2,100

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the accumulated fund of the club at 1 January 2025.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the meaning of the term 'accumulated fund'.
parts.answer: It is the club's capital: the excess of its assets over its liabilities, built up from past surpluses (and capital receipts) that belong to the members.
parts.working: 1 mark equivalent of capital / assets − liabilities; 1 mark built up from accumulated surpluses.

at 1 January 2025: subscriptions in arrears $1,400; subscriptions in advance $600

at 31 December 2025: subscriptions in arrears for 2025 $1,100; subscriptions received in advance for 2026 $1,350

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the subscriptions account for the year ended 31 December 2025.
parts.answer:
Subscriptions income transferred to the income and expenditure account: $37,350.
Subscriptions account
Dr                                                                                                   Cr

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why some clubs do not include subscriptions in arrears as income until they are received.
parts.answer: Prudence: members who have not paid may leave the club and never pay, so the income is uncertain and should not be recognised (nor shown as an asset) until cash is received.
parts.working: 1 mark prudence; 1 mark uncertainty of collection/members may leave.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Highland Golf Society was formed on 1 January 2022. Life membership fees are credited to a life membership account and transferred to the income and expenditure account in equal amounts over 10 years, starting in the year the fee is received. Life membership fees received were: 2022 $9,000; 2023 $6,000; 2024 $12,000; 2025 $7,500.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount transferred from the life membership account to the income and expenditure account for 2025.
parts.working: All fees received 2022–2025 are still within their 10 years: 10% × (9,000 + 6,000 + 12,000 + 7,500) (M1) = $3,450 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the balance on the life membership account at 31 December 2025.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why life membership fees are not treated as income in full in the year they are received.
parts.answer: Matching: the fee pays for membership over many years, so it is spread over the years in which members use the club; taking it all at once would overstate the surplus in one year.
parts.working: 1 mark matching/accruals; 1 mark fee covers future years / avoids distorting one year's surplus.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Cedar Hill Chess Club started on 1 January 2025 with 240 members. The annual subscription is $150. By 31 December 2025, 12 members had not paid their 2025 subscription and 9 members had already paid their 2026 subscription.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the subscriptions income for 2025.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the cash received for subscriptions during 2025.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State how the subscriptions in arrears and in advance are shown in the statement of financial position at 31 December 2025.
parts.answer: Arrears $1,800: current asset. In advance $1,350: current liability.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Lakeside Rowing Club's year ends on 31 March. At 31 March 2026 its accumulated fund was $158,400. The surplus for the year was $12,600. During the year the club received a legacy (a gift in a former member's will) of $20,000, which was credited directly to the accumulated fund.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the accumulated fund at 1 April 2025.
parts.working: Closing fund = opening fund + surplus + legacy (M1). Opening = 158,400 − 12,600 − 20,000 (M1) = $125,800 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the legacy was credited directly to the accumulated fund rather than to the income and expenditure account.
parts.answer: It is a one-off capital receipt, not a regular revenue income; including it would overstate the surplus from normal activities and mislead members about whether subscriptions cover running costs.
parts.working: 1 mark capital/non-recurring receipt; 1 mark would distort the year's surplus.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one item, other than a deficit, that would reduce the accumulated fund.
parts.answer: A decrease in the value of assets with no change in liabilities, e.g. a downward revaluation of the clubhouse charged to the fund.
parts.working: 1 mark for any valid item (e.g. downward revaluation; loss of an uninsured asset).

author: HomiLabs

stem: The new treasurer of Al-Huda Community Sports Club, Quetta, has prepared only a receipts and payments account. Members have asked for an income and expenditure account instead.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain three differences between a receipts and payments account and an income and expenditure account.
parts.answer: R&P is a summary of the cash book; I&E follows the accruals basis. R&P includes capital items such as buying equipment; I&E has revenue items only. R&P ends with a cash/bank balance (an asset); I&E ends with a surplus or deficit. I&E includes non-cash items such as depreciation.
parts.working: For each of three differences: 1 mark identifying, 1 mark developing. Accept: cash v accruals basis; capital and revenue items v revenue only; closing balance v surplus/deficit; no depreciation/accruals in R&P; R&P covers all years' amounts received (e.g. arrears) v I&E for the current year only.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Ravi Riverside Cricket Club, Lahore. Information for 2025:
                                          Rs
Subscriptions received               412,000
Profit on bar (already calculated)    86,500
Match fees received                   38,000
Bank interest received                 4,200
Ground maintenance paid              145,000
Coach fees paid                      120,000

parts.text: Calculate the difference in annual income to the club between running the bar itself and accepting the franchise.
parts.answer: The club would receive $1,300 a year less from the franchise.
parts.working: Current bar profit 9,800 − franchise fee 8,500 (M1) = $1,300 less (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise the committee whether to accept the franchise offer. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Although the club loses $1,300 a year, the franchise gives a guaranteed income and removes risks and the workload on volunteers; a justified decision.
parts.working: For franchise: fixed, certain income; no inventory, theft or wage risk; volunteers freed; professional service. Against: $1,300 less; club loses control of prices and opening hours; profit could grow if run well; tied for 3 years. 1 mark per point (max 4, both sides), 1 mark decision.

parts.answer: 12 years

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the amount credited to the income and expenditure account each year for one life member, and compare it with the annual subscription.
parts.answer: $240 a year, which is $40 more than the annual subscription of $200.

parts.text: Advise the committee whether to introduce life membership. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Life membership brings in cash now for the new courts and secures members, but the club loses income from long-serving members (after 12 years they pay nothing) and must still provide services; a justified decision.
parts.working: For: immediate cash; loyal members; less collection effort/arrears; income spread $240 a year for 10 years. Against: members staying more than 12 years cost the club income; costs rise with inflation but the fee is fixed; club still serves them after the fee has been fully transferred. 1 mark per point (max 4), 1 decision.

At 31 August 2026 the sales ledger control account of Margalla Office Supplies showed a debit balance of $84,620. The total of the list of balances extracted from the sales ledger was $82,585. The following errors were found.
1 The sales journal was undercast by $900.
2 A credit note for $340 was entered in the customer's account but was omitted from the sales returns journal.
3 A discount allowed of $125 was credited to a customer's account twice.
4 An irrecoverable debt of $760 was written off in the customer's account but not in the control account.
5 A customer's balance of $1,280 was omitted from the list of balances.
6 A contra of $430 was recorded in the customer's account but not in the control account.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare a statement showing the corrected sales ledger control account balance.
parts.answer:
Balance per control account                            84,620
Add (1) sales journal undercast                           900
Less (2) credit note omitted from returns journal       (340)
Less (4) irrecoverable debt not entered                 (760)
Less (6) contra not entered                             (430)
Corrected balance                                      83,990
parts.working: 1 mark each for items 1, 2, 4 and 6 correctly adjusted; own figure total.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare a statement showing the corrected total of the list of sales ledger balances.
parts.answer:
Total of list                                          82,585
Add (3) discount credited twice                           125
Add (5) balance omitted                                 1,280
Corrected total                                        83,990
The corrected totals agree.
parts.working: 1 mark each for items 3 and 5; 1 mark corrected total $83,990 agreeing with (a).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one type of error that would not be revealed by comparing the control account with the list of balances.
parts.answer: For example an error of commission: an invoice posted to the wrong customer's account.
parts.working: 1 mark for any valid error.

1 The purchases journal was overcast by $1,000.
2 Goods returned to a supplier, $560, were debited to the supplier's account as $650.
3 Discounts received of $215 were recorded in the suppliers' accounts but not in the control account.
4 A supplier's credit balance of $2,140 was entered in the list as $1,240.
5 A payment of $1,780 to a supplier was entered on the credit side of the supplier's account.
6 A contra of $670 was entered in the control account twice.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare a statement showing the corrected purchases ledger control account balance.
parts.answer:
Balance per control account (credit)                   63,410
Less (1) purchases journal overcast                   (1,000)
Less (3) discounts received not entered                 (215)
Add (6) contra debited twice                              670
Corrected balance                                      62,865
parts.working: 1 mark each for items 1, 3 and 6 (direction must be right: a credit balance is reduced by debits); 1 mark own figure total. Items 2, 4 and 5 do not affect the control account.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare a statement showing the corrected total of the list of purchases ledger balances.
parts.answer:
Total of list                                                65,435
Add (2) returns overstated by $90                                90
Add (4) balance listed as $1,240 instead of $2,140              900
Less (5) payment credited instead of debited (2 × $1,780)    (3,560)
Corrected total                                              62,865
parts.working: 1 mark each for items 2, 4 and 5 (item 5 must be doubled); 1 mark total agreeing with (a).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A trader finds two errors in her sales ledger records.
1 The sales journal was overcast by $500.
2 An invoice for $120 was credited to the customer's account instead of being debited.
What adjustments are needed to the sales ledger control account balance and to the total of the list of customers' balances?
A control account: decrease $500; list: increase $240
B control account: decrease $500; list: increase $120
C control account: increase $500; list: decrease $240
D control account: no change; list: increase $740
parts.answer: A control account: decrease $500; list: increase $240
parts.working: The overcast journal total is posted only to the control account, so its debit balance is $500 too high. The individual invoices were posted correctly except the $120 invoice, which was credited instead of debited, so the customer's balance is understated by 2 × $120 = $240. B forgets to double the reversal.

On 31 January 2026 the bank statement of Tamarind Catering, Chennai, showed an overdraft of $2,380. The following items explain the difference from the cash book.
1 Cheques of $4,120 paid to suppliers had not been presented.
2 A lodgement of $3,560 had not been credited by the bank.
3 Bank charges of $140 had not been entered in the cash book.
4 A credit transfer of $920 from a customer had not been entered in the cash book.
5 A cheque payment of $715 had been recorded in the cash book as $175.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the updated (correct) cash book balance at 31 January 2026.
parts.answer: Overdraft $2,940
parts.working: Work back from the bank statement: −2,380 − 4,120 + 3,560 = (2,940). M1 unpresented cheques deducted; M1 lodgement added; A1 overdraft 2,940.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the cash book balance before the corrections were made.
parts.answer: Overdraft $3,180
parts.working: Updated = original − 140 + 920 − 540, so original = −2,940 + 140 − 920 + 540 = (3,180). M1 reversing the three items; M1 the error of $540 (715 − 175) treated correctly; A1 overdraft 3,180.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why an overdraft is shown as a debit balance on the bank statement but as a credit balance in the cash book.
parts.answer: The bank statement is prepared from the bank's point of view: the customer owes the bank, so the customer is a debtor (debit). In the business's cash book the overdraft is money owed to the bank, a liability (credit).
parts.working: 1 mark each point.

parts.answer: Any two explained: timing differences such as unpresented cheques (entered in the cash book but not yet paid by the bank) or lodgements not yet credited; items the bank has entered that the business does not yet know about, such as bank charges, interest, standing orders, direct debits, credit transfers or dishonoured cheques; errors in the cash book or by the bank.
parts.working: 1 mark for each reason, 1 mark for each explanation (2 × 2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two benefits of preparing a bank reconciliation statement regularly.
parts.answer: Any two: errors in the cash book or by the bank are found quickly; the cash book is brought up to date; fraud is more likely to be detected; stale (old unpresented) cheques can be identified; it confirms the bank balance shown in the statement of financial position.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

(ii) A credit sale to A. Khan was debited to the account of A. Khanum.
(iii) A purchase invoice for $1,290 was entered in the purchases journal as $1,920 and posted from there.
(iv) Cash received from a customer was debited to the customer's account and credited to the cash account.
parts.answer: (i) error of principle; (ii) error of commission; (iii) error of original entry; (iv) complete reversal of entries
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why none of these errors is revealed by the trial balance.
parts.answer: In each case the debit entry equals the credit entry, so the totals of the trial balance still agree.
parts.working: 1 mark: equal debits and credits; 1 mark: totals still agree / no suspense account needed.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Correction of errors and suspense account
stem:
The trial balance of Hunza Apricot Traders at 31 December 2025 did not agree, and a suspense account was opened with a credit balance of $2,460. The draft profit was $31,250. Three errors were found, after which the suspense account was closed.
1 Insurance paid of $760 was credited to the insurance account.
2 Interest received of $290 was entered in the bank account but not posted to the interest received account.
3 The sales account was undercast by an amount not yet known.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the suspense account, showing the amount by which the sales account was undercast as the balancing figure.
parts.answer:
Suspense account
Dr                                  $ | Cr                                  $
Interest received                 290 | Difference in trial balance     2,460
Sales                           3,690 | Insurance                       1,520
                                3,980 |                                 3,980
parts.working: 1 mark opening credit balance; 1 mark insurance 2 × 760 = 1,520 credit; 1 mark interest 290 debit; 1 mark sales undercast $3,690.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the corrected profit for the year.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Ayesha has just started work as an accounts assistant at a pharmacy chain in Islamabad. She believes that because her trial balance agrees, her ledger accounts must be correct.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two purposes of preparing a trial balance.
parts.answer: Any two: to check the arithmetical accuracy of double entry (debits = credits); to provide a summary of balances from which the financial statements are prepared; to help locate errors.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain three types of error that a trial balance will not reveal. Give an example of each.
parts.answer: Any three with an example: omission (a transaction not recorded at all); commission (posted to the wrong account of the same type); principle (posted to the wrong class of account, e.g. capital expenditure as revenue); original entry (wrong amount in the book of prime entry); complete reversal; compensating errors.
parts.working: 1 mark per error type with a correct example.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which cost is a direct cost for a business that makes wooden tables?
A timber used to make the tables
B rent of the factory
C salary of the factory supervisor
D depreciation of the cutting machines
parts.answer: A timber used to make the tables
parts.working: Timber can be traced directly to each table. Factory rent, supervision and depreciation (B, C, D) are production overheads: they are incurred for the factory as a whole and cannot be traced to a single table.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A semi-variable cost is $13,000 when 2,000 units are made and $22,000 when 5,000 units are made. What will the cost be when 6,500 units are made?
A $19,500
B $26,500
C $28,600
D $42,250
parts.working: Variable cost per unit = 9,000 ÷ 3,000 = $3; fixed element = 13,000 − 2,000 × 3 = 7,000. At 6,500 units: 7,000 + 6,500 × 3 = 26,500. C treats the whole cost as variable (22,000 ÷ 5,000 × 6,500).

stem: Mehran Bakery, Lahore, had the following costs in June 2026: flour $18,400; packaging for each loaf $2,300; wages of bakers $26,500; depreciation of ovens $1,900; bakery rent $3,200; wages of the delivery van driver $2,750.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Classify each of the following costs as direct materials, direct labour, production overhead or non-production overhead.
(i) flour
(ii) wages of bakers
(iii) depreciation of ovens
(iv) wages of the delivery van driver
parts.answer: (i) direct materials (ii) direct labour (iii) production overhead (iv) non-production (distribution) overhead
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the prime cost for the month.
parts.working: Prime cost = direct materials + direct labour = 18,400 + 2,300 + 26,500 = 47,200. M1 (packaging included as a direct material, rent excluded) A1.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
The production costs of Northern Plastics, Abbottabad, for five months were:
Month          Units  Total cost $
January        4,200        31,860
February       5,600        38,020
March          3,500        28,780
April          6,100        40,220
May            4,800        34,500

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the high–low method to calculate the variable cost per unit.
parts.working: (40,220 − 28,780) ÷ (6,100 − 3,500) = 11,440 ÷ 2,600 = $4.40. M1 using the highest and lowest output (not the highest and lowest cost) A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the fixed cost per month.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the expected total cost for a month in which 7,000 units are made.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State one limitation of the high–low method.
parts.answer: It uses only two observations, which may not be typical; the forecast for 7,000 units is outside the range of the data and assumes cost behaviour stays the same.
parts.working: 1 mark for any valid limitation.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Punjab Uniform Company receives an order for 500 school uniforms. Costs for the order are: direct materials $6,250; direct labour 550 hours costing $4,400; a design royalty of $350 payable for this order. Production overheads are absorbed at $8 per direct labour hour. Administration and selling overheads are charged at 15% of production cost.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare a cost statement for the order showing prime cost, production cost and total cost.
parts.answer:
Direct materials                                6,250
Direct labour                                   4,400
Direct expenses (design royalty)                  350
Prime cost                                     11,000
Production overheads (550 hours × $8)           4,400
Production cost                                15,400
Administration and selling (15%)                2,310
Total cost                                     17,710
parts.working: 1 mark prime cost; 1 mark overhead absorbed; 1 mark production cost; 1 mark administration and total cost.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total cost per uniform.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the selling price per uniform if the company wants a profit margin of 25% on the selling price. Give your answer to the nearest cent.
parts.working: Cost is 75% of the price: 35.42 ÷ 0.75 = 47.23. M1 dividing by 0.75 (not multiplying by 1.25) A1.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Taj Ceramics, Gujrat, makes tiles. Variable cost is $7.50 per unit. General fixed costs are $18,000 per month. One quality supervisor, paid $3,600 per month, is needed for every 2,500 units (or part of 2,500 units) produced each month.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total monthly cost at outputs of 4,000, 5,000 and 6,000 units.
parts.working: Supervisors needed: 2, 2 and 3. 1 mark each total.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the cost per unit at each output.
parts.working: 2 marks all correct, 1 mark for two correct.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the cost per unit falls by much less between 5,000 and 6,000 units than between 4,000 and 5,000 units.
parts.answer: The supervisors' cost is a stepped fixed cost. Above 5,000 units a third supervisor is needed, so fixed costs rise by $3,600 and the benefit of spreading fixed costs over more units is partly lost.
parts.working: 1 mark: stepped fixed cost identified; 1 mark: extra supervisor at 6,000 units increases total fixed cost.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A food processing company in Nairobi records three costs at two levels of output.
Cost      1,000 units $  3,000 units $
X                 6,000          6,000
Y                 4,500         13,500
Z                 5,000          9,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Classify each cost X, Y and Z by its behaviour. Give a reason for each.
parts.answer: X is fixed (total unchanged when output changes); Y is variable (total rises in proportion: $4.50 per unit at both outputs); Z is semi-variable (rises with output but not in proportion: it has a fixed element).
parts.working: 1 mark each with reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total of the three costs at an output of 2,400 units.
parts.working: X 6,000; Y 2,400 × 4.50 = 10,800; Z: variable 2 per unit, fixed 3,000, so 3,000 + 2,400 × 2 = 7,800. Total 24,600. 1 mark each cost.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Shoaib Shoes, Sialkot, values its inventory of finished shoes at production cost.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between product costs and period costs. Give one example of each for a shoe manufacturer.
parts.answer: Product costs are the costs of making the goods (direct materials, direct labour, production overheads); they are included in the value of inventory and charged as cost of sales when the goods are sold, e.g. leather. Period costs are not part of production (administration, selling and distribution); they are charged in full against profit in the period in which they are incurred, e.g. sales staff salaries.
parts.working: 1 mark each definition, 1 mark each valid example.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Bengal Shirts, Dhaka, recorded total overheads of $186,000 in a month with 12,000 machine hours and $221,000 in a month with 15,500 machine hours. A new customer offers to buy 2,000 shirts at $11 each. Each shirt needs direct materials $3.20, direct labour $2.40 and 0.5 machine hours. The factory has spare capacity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the variable overhead per machine hour and the fixed overhead per month.
parts.answer: Variable $10 per machine hour; fixed $66,000 per month

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total variable cost of the special order.
parts.working: Materials and labour 2,000 × 5.60 = 11,200; variable overhead 1,000 hours × 10 = 10,000; total 21,200. M1 A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise the company whether it should accept the order. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Accept, subject to the points below. Revenue 22,000 − variable cost 21,200 = contribution $800; fixed overhead does not change, so profit rises by $800. However the margin is very small; check there is spare machine capacity, that regular customers will not demand the same low price, and whether the order may lead to future work.
parts.working: 1 mark contribution calculated; 1 mark relevant non-financial point(s); 1 mark clear decision consistent with the analysis.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Prices of raw materials have risen steadily during the year. Compared with AVCO, what is the effect of using FIFO?
A higher closing inventory and higher gross profit
B higher closing inventory and lower gross profit
C lower closing inventory and higher gross profit
D lower closing inventory and lower gross profit
parts.answer: A higher closing inventory and higher gross profit
parts.working: Under FIFO the oldest (cheapest) units are issued first, so closing inventory is valued at the latest, higher prices. Cost of sales is lower, so gross profit is higher. B forgets that a higher closing inventory reduces cost of sales.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A business had an opening inventory of 200 units costing $5 each. It bought 300 units at $6 each and then 250 units at $6.40 each. It then issued 450 units. Using FIFO, what is the value of the closing inventory?
A $1,600
B $1,760
C $1,900
D $1,920
parts.working: 300 units remain: the latest 250 at $6.40 = 1,600 and 50 at $6 = 300, total 1,900. B is a weighted average value (1,760); A values the closing units at the oldest prices.

stem:
Kashmir Carpet Weavers records the following movements of wool in January.
Date    Details
1 Jan   Opening inventory 400 kg at $8.00 per kg
6 Jan   Received 600 kg at $8.50 per kg

20 Jan  Received 500 kg at $9.00 per kg

author: HomiLabs

stem:
SunPower Traders, Bahawalpur, sells solar panels.
1 Apr opening inventory 20 panels at $150
5 Apr bought 40 panels at $160
14 Apr sold 45 panels at $240 each
22 Apr bought 30 panels at $170
29 Apr sold 35 panels at $250 each

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the value of closing inventory on 30 April using FIFO.
parts.working: 10 panels remain, all from the 22 April purchase: 10 × 170 = 1,700. M1 A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the value of closing inventory on 30 April using AVCO (perpetual). Give your answer to the nearest cent.
parts.working: After 5 Apr: 60 units, 9,400, average 156.67; 14 Apr issue 45 → balance 15 units 2,350. After 22 Apr: 45 units 7,450, average 165.56; 29 Apr issue 35 → balance 10 units = 7,450 × 10/45 = 1,655.56. 1 mark each stage.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the gross profit for April under each method.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Falcon Pharma Distributors uses AVCO. Its profits and closing inventory values were:
                                Year 1 $  Year 2 $
Profit for the year (AVCO)        71,200    84,000
Closing inventory: AVCO           45,900    50,100
Closing inventory: FIFO           48,600    52,300
Opening inventory for year 1 was the same under both methods.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit for year 1 if FIFO had been used.
parts.working: Higher closing inventory raises profit: 71,200 + (48,600 − 45,900) = 73,900. M1 A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit for year 2 if FIFO had been used.
parts.working: Opening inventory is also higher under FIFO, which reduces profit: 84,000 + (52,300 − 50,100) − (48,600 − 45,900) = 83,500. M1 closing adjustment; M1 opening adjustment; A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The directors receive a bonus based on profit and want to change from AVCO to FIFO. Advise them whether they should make this change. Justify your answer.
parts.answer:
Points for: FIFO is allowed by IAS 2; inventory in the statement of financial position is closer to current prices; profit would have been higher in year 1.
Points against: the consistency concept means a method should be changed only if the new one gives a fairer view, and the change must be disclosed; over time total profit is the same (year 2 would be lower); changing to raise bonuses is unethical and misleading to users.
Decision: do not change merely to increase the bonus.
parts.working: 1 mark points for/against using figures; 1 mark consistency/IAS 2; 1 mark justified decision.

stem: Rania is choosing a method of valuing the inventory of spare parts for her motorcycle repair business in Amman.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two advantages of the FIFO method of inventory valuation.
parts.answer: Any two: follows the usual physical flow of goods; closing inventory is valued at recent prices; easy to understand; no averages need to be recalculated; acceptable under IAS 2.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one advantage of the AVCO method.
parts.answer: Any one: it smooths out price changes so that issue prices and profits fluctuate less; all units of the same item are given the same value.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why a company preparing financial statements under international standards may not use LIFO.
parts.answer: IAS 2 Inventories does not allow LIFO.
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which is a feature of a just-in-time (JIT) system of inventory management?
A raw materials are delivered in small quantities as they are needed
B large buffer inventories are held in case of supplier delays
C materials are bought in bulk to obtain trade discounts
D suppliers are chosen only on the basis of the lowest price
parts.answer: A raw materials are delivered in small quantities as they are needed
parts.working: JIT aims to hold little or no inventory, so deliveries arrive in small batches just before they are used. B and C describe the opposite approach; under JIT suppliers are chosen for reliability and quality, not only price (D).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statements about just-in-time inventory management are correct?
1 It reduces the cost of storing inventory.
2 It increases the risk that production will stop.
3 It makes it easier to obtain bulk-purchase discounts.
4 It depends on reliable suppliers.
A 1, 2 and 4
B 1 and 3 only
C 2, 3 and 4
D 3 and 4 only
parts.answer: A 1, 2 and 4
parts.working: Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct. Statement 3 is wrong: JIT orders are small and frequent, so bulk-purchase discounts are usually lost.

stem: Indus Auto Parts, Karachi, assembles brake units for car manufacturers. It currently keeps three months' inventory of components in a rented warehouse.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two advantages to the business of adopting a just-in-time system.
parts.answer: Any two explained: lower holding costs (storage space, insurance, security); less working capital tied up in inventory, improving cash flow; less risk of obsolescence, damage or theft; storage space can be used for production; close links with suppliers can improve quality.
parts.working: 1 mark each advantage, 1 mark each explanation in context.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Green Valley Foods, Mardan, holds average inventory of raw materials of $240,000. Annual holding costs are 18% of average inventory. Under a proposed JIT system average inventory would fall to $40,000. There would be 500 extra deliveries a year costing $12 each, and suppliers would increase prices by 1% on annual purchases of $1,200,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the expected net annual saving from introducing JIT.
parts.answer:
Holding cost saved: (240,000 − 40,000) × 18%       36,000
Less extra delivery costs: 500 × $12              (6,000)
Less price increase: 1% × 1,200,000              (12,000)
Net annual saving                                  18,000
parts.working: M1 A1 holding cost saving; B1 delivery costs; B1 price increase; A1 net saving.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise the managers whether to introduce JIT. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: The saving of $18,000 supports JIT. But the company must be confident of its suppliers' reliability, since a late delivery would stop production; demand must be steady; and the 1% price rise may grow. Decision: introduce JIT if suppliers can guarantee delivery, perhaps keeping a small buffer at first.
parts.working: 1 mark use of the figure; 1 mark non-financial factor(s); 1 mark justified decision.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Atlas Bicycles, Lahore, is considering JIT for its components. Average inventory would fall from $380,000 to $120,000; holding costs are 20% a year of average inventory. The number of orders would rise from 12 to 150 a year, each costing $85 to process. The production manager expects JIT to cause 4 days of production stoppage a year, losing contribution of $6,500 per day.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the expected net annual financial effect of adopting JIT.
parts.answer:
Holding cost saved: (380,000 − 120,000) × 20%          52,000
Less extra ordering costs: (150 − 12) × $85          (11,730)
Less expected lost contribution: 4 × $6,500          (26,000)
Net annual saving                                      14,270
parts.working: 1 mark holding cost; 1 mark ordering cost (138 extra orders); 1 mark stoppage cost; 1 mark net saving.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of days of stoppage per year at which JIT would no longer be worthwhile.
parts.answer: More than 6.20 days, i.e. 7 or more whole days

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise the directors whether to adopt JIT. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: For: a net saving is expected; less cash tied up in inventory. Against: the saving depends heavily on the stoppage estimate; only about two more days of stoppage would remove it; supplier reliability and transport links must be checked. Decision consistent with these points, e.g. adopt only with a supplier guarantee or penalty clause.
parts.working: 1 mark for points for and against; 1 mark justified decision.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A furniture manufacturer in Chiang Mai, Thailand, is thinking of changing to JIT for its supplies of timber and fittings.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two conditions that must exist for a just-in-time system to work successfully.
parts.answer: Any two explained: reliable suppliers that can deliver at short notice; suppliers located close by or good transport links; high and consistent quality of materials (no time to replace faulty items); stable, predictable demand and production schedules; good communication/IT links with suppliers; a flexible, well-trained workforce.
parts.working: 1 mark each condition, 1 mark each explanation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one effect of JIT on the working capital of a business.
parts.answer: Less money is tied up in inventory, so cash is released (current assets fall).
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Pearl Electronics, Penang, holds average inventory of $300,000. Under JIT this would fall to $60,000. The warehouse no longer needed could be rented out for $2,500 per month. Insurance is 1.5% of average inventory. Annual losses from obsolete inventory would fall from $9,000 to $1,500. A supplier liaison officer would be employed at a salary of $22,000 a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net annual benefit of introducing JIT.
parts.answer:
Rent from warehouse: 12 × $2,500                       30,000
Insurance saved: 1.5% × (300,000 − 60,000)              3,600
Obsolescence losses saved: 9,000 − 1,500                7,500
Less salary of supplier liaison officer              (22,000)
Net annual benefit                                     19,100
parts.working: 1 mark each item; total own figure.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two risks of introducing JIT for this business.
parts.answer: Any two: late or failed deliveries stopping production; loss of bulk discounts; supplier price rises once the firm depends on them; sudden increases in demand cannot be met; quality problems.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Sindhri Juices, Multan, makes mango juice. Fresh mangoes are available locally only from June to August; the company freezes pulp in a large cold store so that it can make juice all year. Bottles and cartons are bought from a nearby supplier who can deliver daily. The directors have read that JIT reduces costs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Advise the directors whether Sindhri Juices should adopt just-in-time purchasing for fresh mangoes. Justify your answer.
parts.answer:
For JIT: less fresh fruit wasted through spoilage; lower cold-storage costs; less cash tied up; fruit used fresher, improving quality.
Against JIT: mangoes are available only in a short season, so supply cannot be called off all year; prices rise sharply out of season; weather can disrupt harvests and transport; juice production must run at full capacity during the season.
Possible compromise: JIT for packaging and bottles, which can be supplied all year, but bulk buying and pulp storage for mangoes.
Decision: do not adopt JIT for mangoes.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for points for; up to 2 marks for points against (in context); 1 mark for a compromise or further analysis; 1 mark justified decision.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A worker is paid $12 per hour for a basic week of 40 hours. Overtime is paid at time-and-a-half. In one week she works 44 hours. What is her gross pay?
A $528
B $552
C $576
D $792
parts.working: 40 × 12 + 4 × 18 = 480 + 72 = 552. A pays all hours at the basic rate; C pays the overtime at double time.

stem: A garment workshop in Karachi pays machinists $0.85 per garment with a guaranteed minimum of $360 per week. Output in one week was: Asif 520 garments, Bilal 390 garments, Chen 465 garments.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the gross pay of each worker for the week.
parts.working: Asif 520 × 0.85 = 442.00; Bilal 390 × 0.85 = 331.50, below the minimum so paid 360.00; Chen 465 × 0.85 = 395.25. 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total labour cost and the labour cost per unit produced. Give the cost per unit to the nearest cent.
parts.working: Total 1,197.25 ÷ 1,375 units = 0.87. 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one reason for paying a guaranteed minimum wage.
parts.answer: Gives workers security of income when output is low for reasons outside their control (machine breakdown, shortage of materials); may be required by law.
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Hassan runs a repair workshop for air-conditioning units in Doha and is deciding how to pay his technicians.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage to the employer of paying workers a time rate rather than a piece rate.
parts.answer: Advantage (any one explained): quality is not sacrificed for speed; pay is simple to calculate; suitable where output cannot be measured. Disadvantage (any one explained): no incentive to work faster, so supervision is needed; labour cost per unit rises when output falls.
parts.working: 1 mark advantage, 1 mark explanation; 1 mark disadvantage, 1 mark explanation.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Workers at Rose Valley Packaging, Swat, are paid $14 per hour plus a bonus of 50% of the time saved, valued at the hourly rate. The standard time is 0.4 hours per unit. In one week both Farida and Gul worked 38 hours. Farida produced 110 units and Gul produced 92 units.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the gross pay of each worker for the week.
parts.answer: Farida $574; Gul $532
parts.working: Farida: standard time 110 × 0.4 = 44 hours, time saved 6 hours, bonus 50% × 6 × 14 = 42; pay 532 + 42 = 574. Gul: standard time 92 × 0.4 = 36.8 hours, no time saved, pay 38 × 14 = 532. 2 marks each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the labour cost per unit for each worker. Give your answers to the nearest cent.
parts.answer: Farida $5.22; Gul $5.78
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Discuss whether the bonus scheme benefits the company.
parts.answer: Benefit: the faster worker's cost per unit is lower even after the bonus, because time saved is shared 50:50. Drawback: workers may rush and quality may fall; slow workers still receive full time-rate pay, so there is no penalty.
parts.working: 1 mark each point.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Twelve production workers at Margalla Furniture each worked 45 hours last week. The basic week is 40 hours at $10 per hour, and overtime is paid at time-and-a-half. The overtime was needed because of a general increase in orders, not for any particular job.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total gross wages for the week.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how much of the gross wages should be treated as direct labour and how much as production overhead.
parts.answer: Direct labour $5,400; production overhead $300
parts.working: All hours at basic rate are direct: 12 × 45 × $10 = 5,400. The overtime premium 12 × 5 × $5 = 300 is overhead because the overtime was due to the general level of work. 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain when the overtime premium would be treated as a direct cost.
parts.answer: When the overtime is worked at the specific request of a customer or for a particular job, the premium can be traced to that job and is charged to it as direct labour.
parts.working: 1 mark specific job/customer; 1 mark charged directly to that job.

topic: Company financial statements and IAS adjustments
stem:
The draft profit for the year ended 31 December 2025 of Ravi Valley Cement plc was $286,400. The following matters have not been dealt with correctly.
1 Inventory with a cost of $24,000 has a net realisable value of $17,500.
2 Machinery bought on 1 January 2025 for $60,000 has not been depreciated. The policy is 10% per annum straight-line.
3 The company has $200,000 6% debentures. Interest for the second half of the year has not been paid or accrued.
4 An interim dividend of $15,000 was debited to administrative expenses.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare a statement showing the corrected profit for the year ended 31 December 2025.
parts.answer:
Draft profit for the year                                   286,400
Less inventory written down to NRV (24,000 − 17,500)        (6,500)
Less depreciation on new machinery (10% × 60,000)           (6,000)
Less debenture interest accrued (200,000 × 6% × 6/12)       (6,000)
Add interim dividend wrongly charged as an expense           15,000
Corrected profit for the year                               282,900
parts.working: 1 mark each adjustment, total own figure.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why an interim dividend paid must not be included in the statement of profit or loss.
parts.answer: A dividend is a distribution (appropriation) of profit to the owners, not an expense of earning profit. It is deducted from retained earnings in the statement of changes in equity.
parts.working: 1 mark: appropriation/distribution to shareholders; 1 mark: shown in the SOCE / retained earnings.

2 An ordinary dividend paid of $42,000 was debited to finance costs.
3 A customer's debt of $3,800 is irrecoverable and must be written off.
4 Trade receivables before the write-off were $193,800. The allowance for doubtful debts, currently $2,900, is to be 2% of trade receivables after the write-off.
5 Insurance of $2,600 paid for October 2026 was charged as an expense.
6 Kitchen equipment (cost $24,000, accumulated depreciation $20,500) was sold for $5,000 cash. The proceeds were credited to revenue and no other entries were made.

parts.label: a

Less loan interest accrued (12,000 − 7,500)           (4,500)
Add dividend wrongly charged to finance costs          42,000
Less irrecoverable debt                               (3,800)
Less increase in allowance (3,800 − 2,900)              (900)
Add insurance prepaid                                   2,600
Less disposal proceeds wrongly in revenue             (5,000)
Add gain on disposal (5,000 − 3,500)                    1,500
Corrected profit                                      450,600
parts.working: 1 mark each: interest (12,000 − 7,500 = 4,500); dividend; irrecoverable debt; allowance (2% × 190,000 = 3,800, increase 900); prepayment; disposal (remove 5,000 from revenue, add gain 5,000 − 3,500 = 1,500: net −3,500). Corrected profit $450,600.
