stem: The directors of Kalash Mountain Resorts plc are preparing the financial statements and are unsure how to deal with a number of uncertain items.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the following terms as used in IAS 37: (i) a provision, (ii) a contingent liability.
parts.answer: (i) A liability of uncertain timing or amount. (ii) A possible obligation whose existence depends on uncertain future events, or a present obligation that is not probable or cannot be measured reliably.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the three conditions that must be met before a provision is recognised.
parts.answer: There is a present obligation (legal or constructive) from a past event; an outflow of resources to settle it is probable; a reliable estimate of the amount can be made.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State how a probable contingent asset is treated.
parts.answer: It is disclosed in a note but not recognised in the statement of financial position.
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Company financial statements and IAS adjustments
subtopic: Provisions, contingencies and events after the reporting period
stem:
Indus Ferries plc has the following matters at 31 March 2026.
1 A passenger is suing the company for injuries suffered on one of its ferries in January 2026. The lawyers say the company will probably lose, and estimate damages of $85,000.
2 The company has guaranteed a $200,000 bank loan of a supplier. The supplier has had some cash-flow difficulties; the company's advisers consider a default possible but not probable.
3 The company is claiming $40,000 compensation from a shipyard for late delivery of a ferry. The lawyers think the claim will probably succeed, but the shipyard has not agreed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each matter, state how it should be treated in the financial statements for the year ended 31 March 2026. Give reasons.
parts.answer:
1 Recognise a provision of $85,000: present obligation from a past event, outflow probable, reliable estimate. Charge to profit or loss; show as a liability.
2 Disclose as a contingent liability in a note only: an outflow is possible, not probable.
3 Do not recognise; disclose as a contingent asset in a note because the inflow is probable but not virtually certain.
parts.working: 1 mark treatment and 1 mark reason for each matter.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The draft profit before dealing with these matters was $520,000. Calculate the revised profit.
parts.working: Only the provision affects profit.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Company financial statements and IAS adjustments
subtopic: Provisions, contingencies and events after the reporting period
stem:
The draft profit of Saddar Electronics plc for the year ended 31 March 2026 is $310,000. The financial statements will be authorised for issue on 30 June 2026. These events occurred after the year end.
1 20 April 2026: a customer who owed $18,000 at 31 March 2026 was declared bankrupt; nothing will be received.
2 5 May 2026: a fire destroyed inventory worth $60,000 in the warehouse.
3 12 May 2026: goods held in inventory at 31 March 2026 at a cost of $25,000 were sold for $19,000, with selling costs of $1,000.
4 1 June 2026: the directors proposed a final dividend of $40,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Classify each event as adjusting or non-adjusting and state how each should be treated.
parts.answer:
1 Adjusting: confirms the customer could not pay at the year end; write off $18,000.
2 Non-adjusting: the condition (fire) arose after the year end; disclose in a note if material.
3 Adjusting: gives evidence of NRV at the year end; write inventory down to 18,000.
4 Non-adjusting: no obligation existed at the year end; disclose in a note, no liability.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the revised profit for the year ended 31 March 2026.
parts.working: 310,000 − 18,000 − (25,000 − 18,000) = 285,000. 1 mark each adjustment, 1 mark answer (non-adjusting events ignored).

author: HomiLabs

topic: Company financial statements and IAS adjustments
subtopic: Provisions, contingencies and events after the reporting period
stem:
Crescent Appliances plc sold 12,000 washing machines in 2025 with a one-year warranty. Past experience shows that 80% need no repairs, 15% need minor repairs costing $40 each and 5% need major repairs costing $250 each. The warranty provision brought forward from 2024 is $180,000. At 31 December 2025 the provision should equal the expected cost of repairs on the machines sold in 2025. The draft profit is $960,000. In addition:
• a former employee is suing the company for $70,000; lawyers believe the claim will possibly, but not probably, succeed
• the company's insurer has confirmed in writing that it will pay $15,000 for flood damage costs already charged as an expense in 2025; nothing has been recorded.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the warranty provision required at 31 December 2025.
parts.working: 12,000 × (15% × 40 + 5% × 250) = 12,000 × 18.50. M1 expected value; M1 both outcomes; A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the amount to be charged in the statement of profit or loss for the warranty provision.
parts.answer: $42,000 (increase in the provision)
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how the lawsuit and the insurance claim should be treated.
parts.answer: Lawsuit: an outflow is only possible, so it is disclosed as a contingent liability, not provided for. Insurance: the inflow is virtually certain (written confirmation), so it is no longer contingent and is recognised as a receivable and income of $15,000.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the revised profit for the year.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Company financial statements and IAS adjustments
stem: Neelum Mineral Water plc has 2,000,000 ordinary shares of $0.50 each. Profit for the year ended 31 December 2025 was $380,000 and retained earnings at that date are $1,150,000. An interim dividend of $0.04 per share has been paid. The directors propose a final dividend of $0.12 per share. The company has cash of $90,000 and plans to extend its factory next year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total cost of the proposed final dividend.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the dividend cover for the year if the final dividend is paid. Give your answer to two decimal places.
parts.answer: 1.19 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise the directors whether they should pay the proposed final dividend. Justify your answer.
parts.answer:
For: retained earnings of $1,150,000 mean the dividend is legally possible; shareholders expect a return and the share price may fall if it is cut; a stable dividend signals confidence.
Against: cash is only $90,000, so the company would need to borrow about $150,000, adding interest; dividend cover of 1.19 is low, so most of this year's profit is paid out; the factory extension planned for next year needs funds.
Decision: pay a reduced final dividend (for example $0.05 per share, $100,000) or delay payment until cash allows.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for points for, up to 2 marks for points against (using figures), 1 mark for a justified decision.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Company financial statements and IAS adjustments
stem:
Tarbela Engineering plc has 1,500,000 ordinary shares of $1 each, share premium of $400,000, retained earnings of $900,000 and cash of $260,000. The directors are considering two options.
Option A: pay a cash dividend of $0.15 per share.
Option B: make a bonus issue of 1 share for every 5 held, using the share premium account, and pay no cash dividend.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show the effect of each option on share capital, share premium, retained earnings, total equity and cash.
parts.answer:
Cash dividend   Bonus issue
Ordinary share capital        no change     +$300,000
Share premium                 no change     −$300,000
Retained earnings             −$225,000     no change
Total equity                  −$225,000     no change
Cash                          −$225,000     no change
parts.working: Option A: 1,500,000 × 0.15 = 225,000. Option B: 1,500,000 ÷ 5 = 300,000 shares × $1 = $300,000 from share premium. 1 mark each correct column pair (share capital/premium; retained earnings; total equity; cash).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise the directors which option they should choose. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Cash dividend: rewards shareholders with cash and meets their income expectations, but leaves only $35,000 cash, which may cause liquidity problems. Bonus issue: no cash leaves the company and reserves are kept for growth; shareholders receive more shares, but the share price will fall in proportion, so they gain no real wealth and may be disappointed. Decision: e.g. a bonus issue (or a smaller cash dividend) because cash is needed for operations.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two relevant points, 1 mark use of figures, 1 mark justified decision.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Company financial statements and IAS adjustments
stem: While preparing the financial statements for the year ended 31 December 2025, the accountant of Kirthar Foods plc discovered that closing inventory at 31 December 2024 had been overstated by $36,000 because of a counting error. This is a material error. Retained earnings at 1 January 2025, as previously reported, were $512,000. The draft profit for 2025, calculated using the incorrect opening inventory, is $148,000. Dividends of $50,000 were paid in 2025.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the restated retained earnings at 1 January 2025.
parts.working: 512,000 − 36,000: the 2024 profit was overstated by the overstatement of closing inventory. M1 A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the corrected profit for 2025.
parts.working: Opening inventory for 2025 was overstated, so cost of sales was too high: 148,000 + 36,000. M1 A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the retained earnings at 31 December 2025.
parts.working: 476,000 + 184,000 − 50,000 = 610,000. The error has reversed itself by the end of 2025. M1 A1.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain how IAS 8 requires a material prior period error to be corrected.
parts.answer: It is corrected retrospectively: the comparative figures for the prior period are restated and the opening balance of retained earnings is adjusted in the statement of changes in equity, rather than putting the correction through the current year's profit.
parts.working: 1 mark retrospective/restate comparatives; 1 mark adjust opening retained earnings.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Company financial statements and IAS adjustments
stem: In 2026 the auditors of Swat Marble plc found that a machine bought on 1 July 2024 for $80,000 had been debited to repairs in 2024. The company depreciates machinery at 20% per annum straight-line, with a time apportionment in the year of purchase. The error is material. The year end is 31 December. Retained earnings at 1 January 2026, as previously reported, were $645,000. The draft profit for 2026 is $210,000 (no depreciation has been charged on the machine).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the restated retained earnings at 1 January 2026.
parts.working: 2024: profit understated by 80,000 − depreciation 8,000 (6 months) = 72,000; 2025: depreciation 16,000 omitted. 645,000 + 72,000 − 16,000 = 701,000. 1 mark each step.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the corrected profit for 2026.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the carrying amount of the machine at 31 December 2026.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the correction for 2024 and 2025 is not included in the profit for 2026.
parts.answer: Including it would distort the 2026 profit and make comparison with earlier years misleading. IAS 8 requires material prior period errors to be corrected retrospectively through opening retained earnings, with comparatives restated.
parts.working: 1 mark distortion/comparability; 1 mark IAS 8 retrospective treatment.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Company financial statements and IAS adjustments
stem:
Solaris Devices plc, Islamabad, spent the following in the year ended 30 June 2026.
1 Salaries of scientists investigating new battery materials, with no particular product in view: $42,000
2 Testing a prototype of a new solar phone charger (all IAS 38 development criteria are met): $68,000
3 Market research carried out before the charger project was approved: $9,000
4 Designing tools for production of the new charger (criteria met): $25,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount to be charged as an expense and the amount to be recognised as an intangible asset for the year.
parts.answer: Expense $51,000; intangible asset $93,000
parts.working: Research (1) and market research before approval (3) are expensed: 51,000. Development meeting all criteria (2) and (4) is capitalised: 93,000. 1 mark per item correctly treated.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two of the criteria that development expenditure must meet before it can be recognised as an asset under IAS 38.
parts.answer: Any two: technically feasible to complete; intention to complete and use or sell; ability to use or sell; probable future economic benefits (a market exists); adequate technical, financial and other resources to complete; expenditure can be measured reliably.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Company financial statements and IAS adjustments
stem: Medisonic plc capitalised development costs of $180,000 for a new ultrasound scanner in 2024. Commercial production began on 1 January 2025 and the costs are amortised straight-line over the expected sales life of 5 years. At 31 December 2026 a competitor launched a cheaper scanner, and the recoverable amount of the development costs was estimated at $90,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amortisation charge for 2026.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the carrying amount of the development costs at 31 December 2026 before any impairment.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the impairment loss at 31 December 2026.
parts.working: 108,000 − recoverable amount 90,000. M1 A1.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the total charge in the statement of profit or loss for 2026 relating to the development costs.
parts.working: Amortisation plus impairment.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Explain why capitalised development costs are amortised.
parts.answer: Matching: the costs are spread over the periods that benefit from sales of the product; the asset has a limited useful life, so its carrying amount should fall as the benefits are used up.
parts.working: 1 mark matching; 1 mark finite life/benefits consumed.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Ittehad Steel Fabricators, Lahore, makes gates, railings and window grilles in batches. It is introducing activity based costing (ABC).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a cost driver.
parts.answer: The factor that causes the cost of an activity to be incurred, so that the cost changes with the level of that factor.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Suggest a suitable cost driver for each of the following activities.
(i) setting up machines for a new batch
(ii) buying materials from suppliers
(iii) inspecting finished goods
(iv) despatching goods to customers
parts.answer: (i) number of set-ups (ii) number of purchase orders (iii) number of inspections (iv) number of despatches/deliveries
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Mehran Pharmaceuticals has identified the following activities for the coming year.
Activity                  Cost $  Expected driver volume
Machine set-ups           84,000             120 set-ups
Quality inspection        56,000       1,400 inspections
Material handling         37,500         2,500 movements

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost driver rate for each activity.
parts.answer: Machine set-ups $700 per set-up; quality inspection $40 per inspection; material handling $15 per movement

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a cost pool.
parts.answer: The total of all the overhead costs caused by one activity, collected together before being charged to products using the cost driver rate.
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A company uses these cost driver rates: $700 per set-up, $40 per inspection and $15 per material movement. Product K needs 18 set-ups, 260 inspections and 400 material movements to make 5,000 units.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total overhead charged to product K using ABC.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the overhead cost per unit of product K.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Karachi Sweets makes boxes of mithai (20,000 boxes a year) and celebration cakes (6,000 cakes a year). Its overheads have been analysed as follows.
Activity           Cost $  Cost driver           Mithai    Cakes
Batch set-ups      45,000  Number of set-ups         40      110
Quality checks     30,000  Number of checks         200      400
Packing            27,000  Packing hours          1,500    1,200

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost driver rate for each activity.
parts.answer: Batch set-ups 45,000 ÷ 150 = $300 per set-up; Quality checks 30,000 ÷ 600 = $50 per check; Packing 27,000 ÷ 2,700 = $10 per packing hour
parts.working: 1 mark each rate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the overhead cost per box of mithai and per cake.
parts.working: 1 mark each product total, 1 mark each cost per unit (to 2 decimal places).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Chiniot Woodcraft makes 4,000 chairs and 1,000 tables a year. Direct costs per unit are: chair materials $22, labour $15; table materials $95, labour $48. Each chair takes 0.5 machine hours and each table 2 machine hours. Overheads are:
Activity              Cost $  Cost driver           Chairs   Tables
Machine operation     96,000  Machine hours          2,000    2,000
Machine set-ups       36,000  Number of set-ups         20       40
Order processing      18,000  Number of orders         100       50

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the overhead cost per chair and per table using activity based costing.
parts.answer:
Machine operation 96,000 ÷ 4,000 = $24 per machine hour; Machine set-ups 36,000 ÷ 60 = $600 per set-up; Order processing 18,000 ÷ 150 = $120 per order
Chairs: 2,000 × 24 + 20 × 600 + 100 × 120 = $72,000; ÷ 4,000 units = $18.00 per unit
Tables: 2,000 × 24 + 40 × 600 + 50 × 120 = $78,000; ÷ 1,000 units = $78.00 per unit
parts.working: 1 mark rates; 1 mark chairs total; 1 mark tables total; 1 mark per-unit figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total cost per chair and per table.
parts.answer: Chair $55; table $221
parts.working: Chair 22 + 15 + 18; table 95 + 48 + 78. 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the selling price of each product if the business adds a mark-up of 40% on total cost.
parts.answer: Chair $77.00; table $309.40
parts.working: Total cost × 1.4. 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Lahore Leather makes 8,000 standard bags and 1,500 designer bags a year. Direct costs are $24.45 per standard bag and $89.60 per designer bag. Overheads are:
Activity            Cost $  Cost driver              Standard  Designer
Design              60,000  Design hours                  100       400
Cutting set-ups     42,000  Number of set-ups              30        70
Inspection          33,000  Number of inspections         900       600

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the overhead cost per unit of each bag using activity based costing.
parts.answer:
Design 60,000 ÷ 500 = $120 per design hour; Cutting set-ups 42,000 ÷ 100 = $420 per set-up; Inspection 33,000 ÷ 1,500 = $22 per inspection
Standard: 100 × 120 + 30 × 420 + 900 × 22 = $44,400; ÷ 8,000 units = $5.55 per unit
Designer: 400 × 120 + 70 × 420 + 600 × 22 = $90,600; ÷ 1,500 units = $60.40 per unit
parts.working: 1 mark rates; 1 mark product totals; 1 mark per-unit figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the selling price of each bag needed to give a profit margin of 20% of selling price.
parts.answer: Standard $37.50; designer $187.50
parts.working: Total cost: standard 24.45 + 5.55 = 30.00; designer 89.60 + 60.40 = 150.00; divide by 0.8. 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A competitor sells a similar designer bag for $175. Advise Lahore Leather whether it should reduce the price of its designer bag to $175. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: At $175 the margin would fall to (175 − 150) ÷ 175 = 14.29%, still a profit of $25 per bag. For: keeps market share; ABC shows the true cost is $150, so the bag is still profitable. Against: lower margin; the brand may justify a higher price (quality, design); other customers may expect discounts. Decision e.g. match the price only if volumes rise, or keep $187.50 and stress quality.
parts.working: 1 mark revised margin/profit; 1 mark points for and against; 1 mark justified decision.

author: HomiLabs

stem: The purchasing department of Faisalabad Garments has annual costs of: staff salaries $38,000; stationery and postage $2,400; purchasing software $5,600. It expects to place 920 purchase orders in the year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost driver rate for the purchasing activity.
parts.answer: $50 per purchase order

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the purchasing cost charged to the hospital uniforms product line, which needed 140 purchase orders.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the number of purchase orders is a more suitable basis than direct labour hours for charging purchasing costs.
parts.answer: Purchasing cost is caused by the number of orders placed, not by how long workers spend making the products.
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Margalla Medical Centre, Islamabad, treats 6,000 outpatients and 1,200 day-surgery patients a year. It has analysed its support costs as follows.
Activity       Cost $  Cost driver             Outpatient  Day surgery
Admissions     72,000  Number of admissions         6,000        1,200
Theatre       240,000  Theatre hours                    0        1,600
Laboratory     54,000  Number of tests              4,500        1,500

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost driver rate for each activity.
parts.answer: Admissions 72,000 ÷ 7,200 = $10 per admission; Theatre 240,000 ÷ 1,600 = $150 per theatre hour; Laboratory 54,000 ÷ 6,000 = $9 per test
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the overhead cost per patient for each type of patient.

stem:
Penang Circuits makes three electronic modules. Annual data:
                                  X        Y        Z
Output (units)               10,000    5,000    2,000
Selling price per unit $         30       48      120
Direct costs per unit $          16       22       31
Overheads:
Activity               Cost $  Cost driver                 X        Y        Z
Set-ups               150,000  Number of set-ups          10       30       60
Component handling     90,000  Components handled      6,000    9,000   15,000
Testing               120,000  Test hours                500      700    1,200

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the overhead cost per unit of each product using activity based costing.
parts.working: 1 mark rates; 1 mark each product (3).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit or loss per unit of each product.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise the directors what action they should take on product Z. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Z makes a loss of $8.50 per unit because it uses a large share of set-ups and testing for low output. Options: raise the price above $128.50 (break-even cost), make Z in larger batches to cut set-ups, or redesign to reduce testing. Before dropping Z, check which overheads would actually be saved and whether customers buy Z with X and Y. Decision: e.g. raise price/reduce set-ups rather than drop at once.

stem: A commercial bank in Lahore wants to find the cost of each service it provides to customers.

parts.text:

stem: Swift Filters, Gujranwala, makes 24,000 oil filters a year in batches of 400. Each batch needs one machine set-up costing $600 and four inspections costing $45 each. Each filter costs $40 to make, and inventory holding costs are 15% a year of the average value held.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the batch-related cost per unit with the current batch size of 400 units.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the batch-related cost per unit if the batch size is increased to 1,000 units.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the net annual saving from the larger batch size, after allowing for higher inventory holding costs.
parts.working: Saving 46,800 − 18,720 = 28,080; extra holding cost: average inventory rises by (1,000 − 400) ÷ 2 = 300 units × $40 × 15% = 1,800; net 26,280. M1 A1.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Advise the managers whether to increase the batch size. Justify your answer.

parts.working: 1 mark point(s) using figures/qualitative; 1 mark decision.

author: HomiLabs

stem:

                Customer A  Customer B

author: HomiLabs

stem: Al-Rawdah Printing, Riyadh, is pricing a job for a customer. Direct costs are $2,400. The job needs 2 press set-ups (rate $180 per set-up), 6 hours of design (rate $45 per design hour) and 3 deliveries (rate $60 per delivery).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Nairobi Business College runs a full-time course (300 students) and a weekend course (600 students). Fees are $900 per full-time student and $260 per weekend student. Tutor costs are $280 and $110 per student respectively. Other costs are:
Activity       Cost $  Cost driver             Full-time  Weekend
Enrolment      36,000  Number of enrolments          300      600
Classrooms    180,000  Room hours                  8,000    4,000
Assessment     42,000  Scripts marked              2,400    1,800

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the overhead cost per student for each course using activity based costing.
parts.answer:
Enrolment 36,000 ÷ 900 = $40 per enrolment; Classrooms 180,000 ÷ 12,000 = $15 per room hour; Assessment 42,000 ÷ 4,200 = $10 per script
Full-time: 300 × 40 + 8,000 × 15 + 2,400 × 10 = $156,000; ÷ 300 students = $520.00 per student
Weekend: 600 × 40 + 4,000 × 15 + 1,800 × 10 = $102,000; ÷ 600 students = $170.00 per student
parts.working: 1 mark each rate (3); 1 mark each cost per student (2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit or loss per student for each course.
parts.answer: Full-time $100 profit; weekend $20 loss
parts.working: Full-time 900 − 280 − 520; weekend 260 − 110 − 170. 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Ravi Valves wants to win a contract to supply 3,000 valves a year at a market price of $64 each, with a profit margin of at least 10% of selling price. Direct costs are $41 per valve. Production uses 24 set-ups at $900 each, 300 inspections at $30 each and 1,500 machine hours at $20 per hour.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the current total cost per unit of the valve.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the maximum cost per unit that allows a 10% margin at a price of $64.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate how many set-ups must be eliminated if the cost reduction is to come entirely from set-ups.
parts.answer: 12 set-ups (from 24 to 12)

parts.label: d
parts.text: Discuss whether this reduction is realistic.
parts.answer: Halving set-ups means producing in batches twice as large, which increases inventory and holding costs and may not suit customer delivery schedules; set-up time might instead be cut by better tooling, or savings found in inspections.
parts.working: 1 mark each point.

author: HomiLabs

stem: The owner of a spice-grinding and packing business in Hyderabad has heard about activity based costing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two features of activity based costing.
parts.answer: Any two: overheads are collected in cost pools by activity; each pool has its own cost driver; costs are charged to products according to their use of each activity; recognises that some costs are driven by batches or complexity, not volume.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two features of a business for which activity based costing is likely to be most useful.
parts.answer: Any two: overheads are a large part of total cost; many different products or services; products differ greatly in complexity, batch size or support needed; a competitive market where accurate prices matter.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Pine View Hotel, Murree, sold 9,000 standard room-nights and 2,000 suite room-nights last year. Its support costs were:
Activity         Cost $  Cost driver            Standard    Suite
Housekeeping     96,000  Cleaning hours            6,000    2,000
Laundry          28,000  Kilograms washed         20,000   15,000
Reception        18,000  Number of check-ins       2,800      800

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost driver rate for each activity.
parts.answer: Housekeeping 96,000 ÷ 8,000 = $12 per cleaning hour; Laundry 28,000 ÷ 35,000 = $0.80 per kg; Reception 18,000 ÷ 3,600 = $5 per check-in
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the overhead cost per room-night for each type of room.
parts.working: 1 mark each total; 1 mark each cost per room-night.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Seaside Snacks, Gwadar, uses ABC. Product Z has annual revenue of $180,000 and direct costs of $102,000. ABC charges it with set-up costs $36,000, inspection costs $18,000 and facility costs $40,000 (factory rent and insurance, shared on floor area). If Z were discontinued, all its set-up and inspection costs would be saved, but the facility costs would not change.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit or loss of product Z using activity based costing.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the effect on the company's total profit if product Z is discontinued.
parts.answer: Profit falls by $24,000
parts.working: Lost revenue 180,000; saved direct costs 102,000, set-ups 36,000 and inspections 18,000; facility costs continue. 180,000 − 156,000 = 24,000 reduction. M1 avoidable costs; M1 facility cost excluded; A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise the directors whether to discontinue product Z. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Do not discontinue on these figures: Z contributes $24,000 towards facility costs that would still be paid. Consider raising its price or reducing set-ups. Also consider whether the space could be used for a more profitable product and the effect on customers who buy other products.
parts.working: 1 mark use of the figure; 1 mark other factor; 1 mark decision.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
An online homeware retailer in Karachi has these activity cost rates: picking $0.40 per item, packing $1.20 per parcel, returns $3.50 per return, customer calls $2.00 per call. Monthly data:
                    Small orders  Large orders
Parcels (orders)          20,000         2,500
Items picked              20,000        20,000
Returns                      800           300
Customer calls             3,000         1,500

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total monthly activity cost of small orders and of large orders.
parts.answer: Small $40,800; large $15,050

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the activity cost per order for each type.
parts.answer: Small $2.04; large $6.02
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The retailer currently adds a flat handling charge of $3 to every order. Explain why this is unfair.
parts.answer: Large orders cost about three times as much to handle as small orders, so small-order customers pay more than their cost and large-order customers pay less than their cost (cross-subsidy).
parts.working: 1 mark each point.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Zamzam Bottling budgeted set-up costs of $120,000 for 200 set-ups and inspection costs of $60,000 for 1,500 inspections. Actual results were: 215 set-ups costing $126,500; 1,420 inspections costing $61,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the budgeted cost driver rate for each activity.
parts.answer: Set-ups $600; inspections $40
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the overhead absorbed and the amount over- or under-absorbed for each activity.
parts.answer: Set-ups: absorbed $129,000, over-absorbed $2,500. Inspections: absorbed $56,800, under-absorbed $4,200
parts.working: 215 × 600; 1,420 × 40. 1 mark each figure.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the net effect on profit of the over- and under-absorption.
parts.answer: Net under-absorption $1,700, reducing profit

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one reason for the under-absorption of inspection costs.
parts.answer: Actual inspection costs were higher than budgeted (e.g. higher inspector wages) while fewer inspections were carried out than budgeted.
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Medicare Tablets makes a vitamin product in batches of 250 packs. Each batch needs one set-up (rate $500) and two inspections (rate $40 each). Each pack needs 0.2 machine hours (rate $30 per hour).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the ABC overhead cost per unit.
parts.working: Batch costs (500 + 2 × 40) ÷ 250 = 2.32; machine 0.2 × 30 = 6.00; total 8.32. 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the batch-related overhead per unit would fall if batches of 500 units were made.
parts.answer: Set-up and inspection costs are incurred per batch, so they are spread over more units.
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Shahrah Motors, Lahore, assembles 10,000 City motorcycles (1.5 machine hours each, direct cost $410) and 3,000 Sport motorcycles (3 machine hours each, direct cost $690) a year. Overheads:
Activity                Cost $  Cost driver                     City    Sport
Purchasing             210,000  Number of purchase orders      1,200    1,800
Engineering changes     96,000  Number of changes                  8       24
Assembly line          480,000  Machine hours                 15,000    9,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the ABC overhead cost per motorcycle for each model.
parts.answer:
Purchasing 210,000 ÷ 3,000 = $70 per order; Engineering changes 96,000 ÷ 32 = $3,000 per change; Assembly line 480,000 ÷ 24,000 = $20 per machine hour
City: 1,200 × 70 + 8 × 3,000 + 15,000 × 20 = $408,000; ÷ 10,000 units = $40.80 per unit
Sport: 1,800 × 70 + 24 × 3,000 + 9,000 × 20 = $378,000; ÷ 3,000 units = $126.00 per unit
parts.working: 1 mark each rate (3); 1 mark each per-unit figure (2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the selling price of each model using a mark-up of 25% on total cost.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Kohinoor Paints sells 12,000 tins a year at $18 each to a hardware chain, delivered in 12 monthly deliveries. The chain now wants weekly deliveries (52 a year) with no change in total volume or price. ABC rates: delivery $140 per delivery; order processing $35 per order (one order per delivery); quality certificate $20 per delivery.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the annual activity cost of supplying the customer under the present arrangement.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the annual activity cost if the customer's request is accepted.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the increase in price per unit needed to keep the profit from this customer unchanged.
parts.answer: $0.65 per unit (price rises to $18.65)
parts.working: Extra cost 7,800 ÷ 12,000 units. M1 A1.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Advise the company how to respond to the customer's request.
parts.answer: Accept only if the price rises by about $0.65 a unit (or a delivery charge of $195 per extra delivery is made); otherwise profit falls by $7,800. Consider the value of keeping a large customer and whether deliveries can be combined with other customers' routes.
parts.working: 1 mark use of figures; 1 mark justified advice.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Quetta Woollens absorbs all its production overheads using a single rate per direct labour hour. The finance director suggests changing to activity based costing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two advantages of activity based costing compared with traditional absorption costing.
parts.answer: Any two explained: more accurate product costs because overheads are charged according to what causes them; better pricing decisions, avoiding over-pricing high-volume and under-pricing low-volume products; identifies costly activities that can be controlled or reduced; better information for decisions about products and customers.
parts.working: 1 mark each advantage, 1 mark each explanation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one limitation of activity based costing.
parts.answer: Any one: expensive and time-consuming to set up and run; choice of cost drivers can be subjective; some costs (e.g. factory rent) have no clear driver and still have to be apportioned; still based on historical/budgeted data.
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Sargodha Agro Tools makes Alpha (20,000 units, 1 direct labour hour each) and Beta (2,000 units, 2 direct labour hours each). Total overheads are $240,000, analysed as:
Activity           Cost $  Cost driver            Alpha     Beta
Set-ups           100,000  Number of set-ups         10       40
Order handling     60,000  Number of orders          50      100
Machining          80,000  Machine hours         15,000    5,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the overhead cost per unit of each product using a single absorption rate per direct labour hour.
parts.answer: Alpha $10.00; Beta $20.00
parts.working: 240,000 ÷ 24,000 hours = $10 per hour; Alpha 1 hour, Beta 2 hours. M1 A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the overhead cost per unit of each product using activity based costing.
parts.working: 1 mark set-up and order rates; 1 mark machining rate; 1 mark each per-unit figure (2).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the two methods give such different results.
parts.answer: Beta is made in small batches with many set-ups and orders, but uses few labour hours. Absorption on labour hours ignores this, so Beta is under-costed and high-volume Alpha over-costed.
parts.working: 1 mark: low-volume/complex product uses more batch-level activities; 1 mark: labour hours do not reflect this.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Spice Route, Karachi, sells 50,000 packs of ground spices (direct cost $2.00 each, 0.1 machine hours each) and 4,000 gift hampers (direct cost $30.00 each, 0.25 machine hours each). Overheads of $180,000 are currently absorbed on machine hours. An ABC analysis shows:
Activity             Cost $  Cost driver            Packs  Hampers
Set-ups              72,000  Number of set-ups         12       36
Packaging design     48,000  Design hours              20       60
Machining            60,000  Machine hours          5,000    1,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the overhead cost per unit of each product using the current machine-hour rate.
parts.answer: Packs $3.00; hampers $7.50
parts.working: 180,000 ÷ 6,000 hours = $30; packs 0.1 hours, hampers 0.25 hours.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the overhead cost per unit of each product using activity based costing.
parts.answer:
Set-ups 72,000 ÷ 48 = $1,500 per set-up; Packaging design 48,000 ÷ 80 = $600 per design hour; Machining 60,000 ÷ 6,000 = $10 per machine hour
Packs: 12 × 1,500 + 20 × 600 + 5,000 × 10 = $80,000; ÷ 50,000 units = $1.60 per unit
Hampers: 36 × 1,500 + 60 × 600 + 1,000 × 10 = $100,000; ÷ 4,000 units = $25.00 per unit
parts.working: 1 mark rates; 1 mark each per-unit figure.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the selling price of each product under each method, using a mark-up of 30% on total cost.
parts.answer: Machine-hour rate: packs $6.50, hampers $48.75. ABC: packs $4.68, hampers $71.50
parts.working: 1 mark each method.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Discuss the consequences for the business of continuing to price using the machine-hour rate.
parts.answer: Packs are over-priced ($6.50 against an ABC-based $4.68), so the business may lose sales of its main product to competitors. Hampers are under-priced ($48.75 against $71.50), so they may sell well but could be making a loss. Overall profit may fall and wrong products be promoted.
parts.working: 1 mark packs over-priced/lost sales; 1 mark hampers under-priced/possible losses.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Tulip Cosmetics produced 10,000 units of a face cream and sold 8,000 units in its first year. There was no opening inventory. Production overhead per unit is $12 under traditional absorption costing and $9 under activity based costing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the overhead included in the closing inventory under each method.
parts.answer: Absorption $24,000; ABC $18,000
parts.working: Closing inventory 10,000 − 8,000 = 2,000 units; × $12 and × $9. 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the effect on reported profit for the year of using ABC instead of absorption costing.
parts.answer: Profit is $6,000 lower under ABC, because $3 less overhead per unit is carried forward in closing inventory, so more of the year's overhead is charged against this year's profit.
parts.working: 1 mark amount; 1 mark explanation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State when the two methods would give the same profit.
parts.answer: When there is no change in the level of inventory (production equals sales), since total overhead charged is the same.
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Indus Packaging plc makes 40 product lines, from high-volume standard cartons to small custom orders that need special design and many machine set-ups. Overheads are 60% of total cost and are absorbed using a single direct labour hour rate. The company has recently lost two large contracts for standard cartons to competitors that charged lower prices, while custom orders have increased. A new ABC system would cost $45,000 to install.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Advise the directors whether they should replace absorption costing with activity based costing. Justify your answer.
parts.answer:
For ABC: overheads are 60% of total cost, so how they are charged matters; the 40 product lines vary greatly in batch size and the custom orders need many set-ups and design hours, so labour-hour absorption is likely to distort costs; recent loss of high-volume contracts suggests these are over-priced; ABC would give better pricing and show which customers and products are profitable.
Against ABC: the $45,000 system cost and staff time; drivers must be chosen and data collected continually; some costs (rent) still have to be apportioned; staff may resist change; benefits are not certain.
Decision: introduce ABC (perhaps first in the custom-order area) because the potential to correct pricing outweighs the cost.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for points for; up to 2 marks for points against (in context); 1 mark use of case data; 1 mark justified decision.

parts.text:
A trader provides the following figures for the year.

Carriage outwards                  1,900
Inventory at end of year          16,800

B $83,000
C $87,600

parts.working: Cost of sales = 14,200 + 86,500 − 2,300 + 1,400 − 16,800 = 83,000. Carriage outwards is a selling expense, not part of cost of sales (A adds it); C adds the returns instead of deducting them; D leaves out carriage inwards.

subtopic: Statement of profit or loss and SOFP

parts.label: a
parts.text:
During the year the owner of a shoe shop took shoes costing $650 for her family. No entry has been made. Which entry records this?
A Debit purchases, credit drawings
B Debit capital, credit inventory
C Debit drawings, credit purchases
D Debit drawings, credit revenue at cost
parts.answer: C Debit drawings, credit purchases
parts.working: Goods taken for own use are drawings, recorded at cost, and they reduce the goods available for sale, so purchases is credited. A reverses the entry. D credits revenue, which would treat the goods as a sale; B uses the closing inventory account, which is not adjusted during the year.

stem: Daniyal's capital at 1 January 2026 was $58,000. On 1 July 2026 he paid a further $7,500 of his savings into the business bank account. Profit for the year ended 31 December 2026 was $21,300. During the year he withdrew $14,400 in cash and took goods costing $900 for his own use.

Capital

Add profit for the year                     21,300

stem:
A factory has budgeted production overheads of $180,000 for the year. Budgeted activity is 30,000 direct labour hours and 12,000 machine hours. It makes two products:

parts.working: B1 each.

Labour hour basis: P $42.00, Q $34.00
Machine hour basis: P $37.50, Q $50.50
parts.working: 1 mark for each cost.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Purpose and features of absorption costing

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by absorption costing.
parts.answer: A costing method in which all production costs – direct costs plus a share of fixed and variable production overheads – are charged to each unit, using overhead absorption rates.
parts.working: 1 mark: all production costs including fixed overheads; 1 mark: charged to units / cost units via absorption rates.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two reasons why a business uses absorption costing.
parts.answer: Any two: IAS 2 requires inventory in the financial statements to include production overheads; it helps set prices that cover all costs; it recognises that fixed overheads are needed to produce output; it shows the full cost of jobs for quotations.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two differences between absorption costing and marginal costing.
parts.answer: Any two: absorption costing includes fixed production overheads in unit cost, marginal costing charges them as period costs; inventory is valued higher under absorption costing; profits differ when inventory levels change; marginal costing shows contribution, absorption costing does not.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

stem: In its first year Kestrel Ltd made 10,000 units and sold 8,500 units at $40 each. Variable production cost was $18 per unit. Fixed production overheads were $80,000, absorbed on the normal output of 10,000 units. Fixed selling and administration costs were $45,000. There was no opening inventory.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit using absorption costing.
parts.working: B1 full cost 26 per unit; B1 cost of sales 221,000; B1 profit 74,000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit using marginal costing.
parts.working: B1 contribution 187,000; B1 profit 62,000.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the two profits are different.
parts.answer: Under absorption costing 1,500 units of closing inventory carry $8 each of fixed overhead ($12,000) forward to next year; under marginal costing all $80,000 is charged this year. So absorption profit is $12,000 higher.
parts.working: 1 mark: fixed overhead in closing inventory; 1 mark: 1,500 × 8 = 12,000.

subtopic: Partnership or sole trader acquired by a company
stem: Farid is a sole trader whose business has made an average profit of $46,000 a year. Zenith Ltd offers to buy his business for 200,000 ordinary shares of $1 each, valued at $1.50 per share. Farid would be employed by Zenith Ltd as branch manager at a salary of $30,000 a year. Zenith Ltd has paid a dividend of $0.09 per share for the last three years.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Farid's expected annual income if he accepts the offer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise Farid whether he should accept the offer. Justify your answer.
parts.answer:
For: expected income $48,000 is $2,000 more than now; a fixed salary is less risky than trading profit; shares are worth $300,000 and can be sold; limited liability; fewer working hours and responsibilities.
Against: dividends are not guaranteed and may fall; the share price may fall; he loses control and becomes an employee who can be dismissed; he is a small minority shareholder with little say; the gain of $2,000 is small.
Decision: e.g. accept, because income rises and risk falls, provided he is satisfied with the dividend record and a service contract.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for points for, up to 3 marks for points against (max 5 for points); 1 mark for a justified decision.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two advantages and two disadvantages for two sole traders of merging their businesses to form a partnership.
parts.answer:
Advantages (any two): more capital; shared workload and skills; economies of scale (bulk buying); losses and risks shared; cover for holidays and illness.
Disadvantages (any two): profits shared; decisions must be agreed and disputes may arise; unlimited liability for the other partner's actions; loss of independence.

Summary statements of cash flows of Marble Furniture Ltd:
                                             2026       2025
                                                $          $
Net cash from operating activities         38,000     92,000
Net cash used in investing activities   (145,000)   (30,000)
Issue of debentures                       100,000          –
Dividends paid                           (40,000)   (40,000)
At 31 December 2026 the company had a bank overdraft of $21,000. Profit for the year rose by 15% in 2026. Inventories and trade receivables both rose sharply during 2026, and the investing outflow was for a new factory.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net change in cash and cash equivalents for 2026 and the balance at 1 January 2026.
parts.answer: Decrease of $47,000; balance at 1 January 2026 $26,000 (in hand)
parts.working: B1 net decrease 47,000; B1 opening 26,000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise the shareholders whether they should be concerned about the company's cash position. Justify your answer.
parts.answer:
Concerns: operating cash flow fell from $92,000 to $38,000 although profit rose 15% – profit is tied up in inventories and receivables (poor working-capital control); cash moved from $26,000 in hand to a $21,000 overdraft; dividends of $40,000 were paid that exceed operating cash; the new debentures add interest costs and must be repaid.
Reassurance: the outflow was mainly a one-off investment in a new factory, financed largely by long-term debentures (matching long-term finance to long-term assets); the factory should raise future profits and cash; the company is still profitable.
Decision: some concern – the investment is sensible, but management must improve credit control and inventory levels and may need to cut the dividend until operating cash flow recovers.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for concerns using figures; up to 2 marks for reassuring points; 1 mark for a justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three uses of a statement of cash flows to the shareholders and managers of a company.
parts.answer: Any three: shows how cash was generated and used; shows whether operating activities generate enough cash to pay interest, tax and dividends; helps assess liquidity and the ability to pay debts; shows how investment was financed; helps forecast future cash flows; cash figures are hard to manipulate and easy to compare.

parts.label: b

parts.answer: Profit is based on the accruals concept and includes non-cash items such as depreciation and provisions, so a profitable business can still run out of cash. The statement of cash flows shows actual cash movements and liquidity.
parts.working: 1 mark: profit uses accruals/non-cash items; 1 mark: cash flows show liquidity/actual cash.

stem: Ivory Ltd made a profit from operations of $120,000 for 2026, but its bank balance fell sharply. Its statement of cash flows shows: depreciation $26,000; increase in inventories $48,000; increase in trade receivables $61,000; decrease in trade payables $19,000; net cash from operating activities $18,000; net cash used in investing activities $200,000; net cash from financing activities $50,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net change in cash and cash equivalents for 2026.
parts.answer: Decrease of $132,000

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using the figures, explain three reasons why Ivory Ltd's cash fell although it was profitable.
parts.answer:
1 Working capital absorbed cash: inventories rose by $48,000 and receivables by $61,000, so much of the profit is tied up in unsold goods and unpaid customer balances.
2 Suppliers were paid faster: payables fell by $19,000, another outflow not shown in profit.
3 Heavy investment: $200,000 was spent on non-current assets, only $50,000 of which was financed by long-term financing; the rest came from existing cash.
(Depreciation of $26,000 reduced profit without any cash outflow, which partly offset these.)
parts.working: For each of three reasons: 1 mark for identifying it and 1 mark for supporting it with figures from the question.

subtopic: Missing figures and statements from incomplete records

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Rukhsana does not keep full accounting records. Her business net assets were $25,000 at the start of the year and $31,400 at the end. During the year she took drawings of $8,200 and paid $3,000 of her own savings into the business bank account. What was her profit for the year?
A $1,200
B $6,400
C $11,600
D $17,600
parts.working: Profit = closing capital − opening capital + drawings − capital introduced = 31,400 − 25,000 + 8,200 − 3,000 = $11,600. D adds the capital introduced instead of deducting it; the extra $3,000 came from Rukhsana's savings, not from trading.

parts.working: Credit sales = receipts + discounts allowed + irrecoverable debts + closing receivables − opening receivables = 61,300 + 1,150 + 480 + 8,950 − 7,420 = $64,460. B ignores discounts allowed and irrecoverable debts, which also reduce what customers owe.

Goods were stolen from a shoe shop in Peshawar shortly before the year end. Opening inventory was $14,200, purchases were $63,800 and revenue was $84,000. All goods are sold at a mark-up of 40% on cost. The inventory remaining at the year end cost $9,450. What was the cost of the goods stolen?

C $18,150

Trade receivables: 1 July 2025 $6,300; 30 June 2026 $7,150
Received from credit customers $82,400; discounts allowed $900
Cash sales $19,600
Purchases for the year (from suppliers' invoices) $63,050; discounts received $700
Inventory: 1 July 2025 $9,400; 30 June 2026 $10,250
General expenses paid $8,300; $400 was owing at 30 June 2026 (nothing owing a year earlier)
Rent paid $9,600, which includes $800 for July 2026
Shop fixtures cost $24,000 and are depreciated at 10% per year using the straight-line method.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total revenue for the year.
parts.working: M1 credit sales; A1 total revenue.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare Farah's statement of profit or loss for the year ended 30 June 2026.
parts.answer:
Farah: Statement of profit or loss for the year ended 30 June 2026
                                     $         $
Revenue                                  103,750
Less cost of sales
  Opening inventory              9,400
  Purchases                     63,050
                                72,450
  Less closing inventory      (10,250)
                                        (62,200)
Gross profit                              41,550
Add discounts received                       700
                                          42,250
Less expenses
  General expenses               8,700
  Rent                           8,800
  Discounts allowed                900
  Depreciation of fixtures       2,400
                                        (20,800)
Profit for the year                       21,450
parts.working: Cost of sales 62,200 (1); gross profit 41,550 (1OF); discounts received added (1); general expenses 8,700 and rent 8,800 (1); discounts allowed and depreciation 2,400 (1); profit $21,450 (1OF).

subtopic: Missing figures and statements from incomplete records
stem:
Kamal repairs bicycles in Multan. He has no bank statements for the last month and wants his statement of financial position at 31 March 2026. He gives you:
Equipment at cost $30,000; accumulated depreciation at 1 April 2025 $9,000. Depreciation is 20% per year, reducing balance.
Inventory $5,620; trade receivables $2,840; rent prepaid $350
Trade payables $3,910; electricity owing $260
Bank loan $8,000, repayable in 2030
Capital at 1 April 2025 $18,400; profit for the year (after depreciation) $14,700; drawings $11,200

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the depreciation charge for the year and the carrying amount of the equipment at 31 March 2026.
parts.answer: Depreciation = (30,000 − 9,000) × 20% = $4,200; carrying amount = $16,800
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare Kamal's statement of financial position at 31 March 2026. The bank balance is the balancing figure.
parts.answer:
Kamal: Statement of financial position at 31 March 2026

  Less accumulated depreciation                 (13,200)

subtopic: Missing figures and statements from incomplete records
stem: A furniture workshop in Chiniot keeps incomplete records. The carrying amount of its machinery was $42,000 at 1 January 2025 and $51,300 at 31 December 2025. Depreciation for the year was $8,900. During the year a machine was sold for $3,200, making a profit on disposal of $700. All other machinery bought was paid for by bank transfer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the carrying amount of the machine sold.
parts.working: M1 proceeds less profit; A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the cost of machinery bought during the year.
parts.answer: Opening 42,000 − disposal 2,500 − depreciation 8,900 + additions = closing 51,300; additions = 51,300 − 42,000 + 8,900 + 2,500 = $20,700
parts.working: M1 add back depreciation; M1 add back carrying amount of disposal; A1 OF.

stem:

stem:

Cheques received from credit customers $96,500, including one of $300 that was later dishonoured

subtopic: Missing figures and statements from incomplete records
stem:
Nikhil runs a mobile food van in Colombo. His capital at 1 January 2025 was $27,400. For 2025 his profit was $18,250 and his drawings were $13,600. At 31 December 2025 his other balances were:
Furniture $9,800
Motor vehicle $17,500
Inventory $7,350
Trade receivables $4,120
Trade payables $5,930
Electricity owing $290
He has lost his bank statements.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Nikhil's capital at 31 December 2025.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the bank balance at 31 December 2025 and state whether it is an asset or a liability.
parts.answer: Capital = assets − liabilities. Assets other than bank 38,770; liabilities 6,220. Bank = 32,050 − 38,770 + 6,220 = −500: an overdraft of $500, a current liability.
parts.working: M1 use of accounting equation; A1 amount; 1 mark liability (overdraft).

subtopic: Missing figures and statements from incomplete records
stem:
Ramón runs a sports shop in Buenos Aires. He did not count inventory at 30 September 2026. His gross margin is 35% on all sales. For the year to 30 September 2026:
Opening inventory $8,200; purchases $52,600; revenue $76,000
Wages paid $21,450. Wages owing: start of year $380; end of year $470.
The wages paid include $1,200 that Ramón paid to himself.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the value of closing inventory at 30 September 2026.
parts.working: M1 cost of sales; M1 opening + purchases − cost of sales; A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the wages expense for the year.
parts.working: M1 accrual adjustments; M1 remove owner's amount (drawings, not wages); A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one reason why the closing inventory found in (a) may differ from the true figure.
parts.answer: The 35% margin is an average; if some goods were sold at a discount, damaged, stolen or sold at different margins, actual inventory will differ from the estimate.
parts.working: 1 mark reason; 1 mark development.

stem:

stem: The inventory records of a pottery shop in Multan for last year were lost. Revenue was $45,000, purchases were $31,600 and closing inventory was $6,900. All goods are sold at a mark-up of 50%.

parts.label: a

parts.answer: Average inventory = (5,300 + 6,900) ÷ 2 = 6,100; turnover = 30,000 ÷ 6,100 = 4.92 times

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A trader adds a mark-up of 25% to the cost of all goods. What is his gross margin?
A 20%
B 25%
C 31.25%
D 33⅓%
parts.working: Cost 100, selling price 125, gross profit 25. Margin = 25 ÷ 125 = 20%. B confuses margin with mark-up: the mark-up is profit as a percentage of cost, but margin is profit as a percentage of selling price.

stem: Tariq sells second-hand books from a small shop in Lahore. He keeps a cash book and files his invoices, but has no ledgers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two reasons why a small trader might keep incomplete records rather than a full double-entry system.
parts.answer: Any two: lack of bookkeeping knowledge; saves time; saves the cost of a bookkeeper or software; the business is small with few transactions.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two disadvantages to the trader of keeping incomplete records.
parts.answer: Any two, developed: (1) no trial balance, so arithmetical errors are hard to find; (2) no detailed statement of profit or loss, so the trader cannot see which expenses are rising; (3) theft or loss of cash or goods may go unnoticed; (4) harder to get a bank loan or satisfy tax authorities without reliable statements.
parts.working: 1 mark for each disadvantage and 1 mark for each explanation, max 2 disadvantages.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A trader keeps no books. At the start and end of each year she simply lists her business assets and liabilities. Which can be found from these two lists alone, with no other details?
A the gross profit for the year
B the owner's capital at each year end
C the profit for the year
D the cost of goods stolen during the year
parts.answer: B the owner's capital at each year end
parts.working: Capital = assets − liabilities, so a statement of affairs at each date gives the capital. C is wrong because profit from the change in capital also needs the drawings and any capital introduced, which the lists of assets and liabilities do not show.

stem: Idris owns a furniture workshop in Chiniot. Five years ago he had four customers who paid in cash; now he has 35 credit customers and six employees. He keeps a cash book only, and an accountant prepares his statements from statements of affairs each year. Last year cash differences of $1,800 could not be explained. Idris wants a bank loan of $40,000 to buy a new machine. A part-time bookkeeper would cost $3,000 per year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Advise Idris whether he should change to a full double-entry bookkeeping system. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: A reasoned recommendation, e.g. Idris should change to full double entry (or computerised accounts): the business has grown, a bank loan is wanted and the cost is small compared with the benefits. Either decision accepted if justified.
parts.working: For (max 4): bank needs reliable statements for the $40,000 loan; full detail of expenses lets him control costs; control accounts and trial balance help find errors and fraud (cash differences of $1,800 last year); detailed receivables records help chase the 35 credit customers; accounting software can automate entries. Against (max 4): cost of a bookkeeper ($3,000 per year) or software and training; time taken from running the workshop; incomplete records have produced a profit figure so far; an accountant could still prepare statements from his records at year end. Decision with justification linked to the figures (1). Max 7: at most 5 for one-sided answers.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A firm in Sialkot makes footballs. The cost card for one ball shows: direct materials $14, direct labour $9, variable overhead $4, fixed overhead absorbed $6. The normal selling price is $45. The firm has spare capacity and is offered a one-off order. What is the lowest price per ball it could accept without reducing its profit?
A $23
B $27
C $33
D $45
parts.working: Only the marginal (variable) cost is extra: 14 + 9 + 4 = $27. Fixed overhead will be paid anyway, so C ($33 full cost) is not the minimum; any price above $27 adds contribution.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Material is in short supply. Product X earns contribution of $24 per unit and uses 4 kg of material; product Y earns $30 and uses 6 kg; product Z earns $18 and uses 2 kg. In what order should production be ranked?
A X, Y, Z
B Y, X, Z
C Z, X, Y
D Z, Y, X
parts.answer: C Z, X, Y
parts.working: Contribution per kg: X 24 ÷ 4 = $6, Y 30 ÷ 6 = $5, Z 18 ÷ 2 = $9, so Z, X, Y. B ranks by contribution per unit, which ignores the scarce resource.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A component costs $18 per unit in variable costs to make. Fixed overhead of $7 per unit is absorbed, which includes a supervisor's salary of $12,000 per year that would be saved if the component were bought in. 4,000 components are needed each year and a supplier offers them at $20.50 each. What is the effect on annual profit of buying instead of making?
A decrease of $10,000
B increase of $2,000
C increase of $12,000
D increase of $18,000
parts.answer: B increase of $2,000
parts.working: Relevant cost of making = 4,000 × 18 + 12,000 = 84,000. Buying = 4,000 × 20.50 = 82,000. Profit rises by $2,000. A ignores the salary saved; D compares with the full cost of $25, but the rest of the absorbed overhead is not saved.

stem: A business in Sialkot makes school bags. Costs per bag: materials $8.50, labour $6.00, variable overhead $1.50. Fixed costs are $48,000 per month. Normal monthly output is 12,000 bags, sold at $25 each, and there is spare capacity of 3,000 bags. A charity offers to buy 2,000 bags at $19 each; it would need special delivery costing $1,400 in total.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the marginal cost of one bag.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the change in monthly profit if the order is accepted.
parts.answer: Contribution per bag 19 − 16 = $3; 2,000 × 3 = 6,000; less delivery 1,400 = increase of $4,600
parts.working: M1 contribution per unit; M1 deduct extra delivery cost; A1. Fixed costs ignored (no change).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two non-financial factors the business should consider before accepting the order.
parts.answer: Any two: existing customers may ask for the lower price; whether the order may lead to repeat business; effect on quality and staff workload; reliability of the new customer; damage to brand image if sold cheaply.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Noor Ceramics makes three products. Material costs $5 per kg and only 13,000 kg is available next month. Fixed costs are $52,000 per month.
Product    Price $  Material kg  Labour $  Var. overhead $  Max demand
Alpha           60            4        15                5       1,500
Beta            85            7        18                6       1,000
Gamma           48            2        16                4       2,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the contribution per kg of material for each product and rank the products.
parts.answer: Alpha: contribution 20, per kg 5.00; Beta: contribution 26, per kg 3.71; Gamma: contribution 18, per kg 9.00. Ranking: Gamma 1st, Alpha 2nd, Beta 3rd.
parts.working: M1 contribution per unit (material at $5 per kg); M1 ÷ kg; A1 ranking.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare the production plan that maximises profit. Make whole units only.
parts.answer: Gamma 2,000 units (4,000 kg); Alpha 1,500 units (6,000 kg); Beta 3,000 kg ÷ 7 = 428 units (2,996 kg).
parts.working: M1 meet full demand in ranking order; M1 remaining material to Beta; A1 428 units.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the profit from this plan.
parts.working: M1; A1 OF.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A workshop in Gujranwala makes two kinds of pump. Next month only 15,000 skilled labour hours are available. Fixed costs are $150,000 per month.
Pump    Price $  Variable cost $  Labour hours per unit  Maximum demand
P            90               54                      3           4,000
Q           120               78                      2           2,500
The variable cost includes labour at the normal rate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the contribution per labour hour for each product and state which should be made first.
parts.answer: P: 36 ÷ 3 = $12 per hour; Q: 42 ÷ 2 = $21 per hour. Make Q first.
parts.working: 1 mark both figures; 1 mark ranking.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of each product to make and the profit for the month. Make whole units only.
parts.working: M1 Q at full demand; M1 P with remaining hours; M1 total contribution; A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Workers will work overtime at a premium of $6 per hour above the normal rate. Calculate the extra profit if overtime is used to meet the full demand for P.
parts.answer: Extra P = 4,000 − 3,333 = 667 units, contribution 667 × 36 = 24,012. Total hours for 4,000 P = 12,000; normal hours available for P = 10,000, so overtime = 2,000 hours (the 1 spare normal hour is used first). Premium = 2,000 × 6 = 12,000. Extra profit = 24,012 − 12,000 = $12,012
parts.working: M1 extra contribution less overtime premium on the overtime hours only; A1 $12,012 (accept $12,006 if all 2,001 hours are treated as overtime).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A company in Gujrat makes three ceiling fans. Its statement for last year shows:
                             Standard $  Deluxe $  Premium $
Revenue                         180,000    95,000    140,000
Variable costs                  110,000    70,000     84,000
Fixed costs (apportioned)        40,000    32,000     36,000
Profit/(loss)                    30,000   (7,000)     20,000
The fixed costs would not change if a product were dropped. The directors want to stop making the Deluxe fan because it makes a loss.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the contribution earned by each product.
parts.answer: Standard $70,000; Deluxe $25,000; Premium $56,000
parts.working: 2 marks all correct; 1 mark two correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total profit if the Deluxe fan is discontinued.
parts.answer: Current profit 43,000; Deluxe contribution lost 25,000; new profit = $18,000
parts.working: M1 fixed costs unchanged; A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain whether the Deluxe fan should be discontinued.
parts.answer: No: it earns a positive contribution of $25,000 towards the fixed costs, which would still have to be paid; profit would fall by that amount.
parts.working: 1 mark decision; 1 mark reason based on contribution.

stem: Rehman Motors makes 10,000 units a year of component K. Cost per unit: materials $6.40, labour $5.20, variable overhead $1.80, fixed overhead absorbed $4.60. A supplier offers component K at $15.50 per unit. If the company buys it in, the space freed can be rented out for $18,000 per year and a supervisor earning $9,000 per year would no longer be needed. Other fixed overheads would not change.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the relevant annual cost of making the component.
parts.working: M1 variable costs only; A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the net annual cost of buying the component and state whether the company should make or buy it.
parts.answer: 155,000 − 18,000 rent − 9,000 salary saved = $128,000. Buying is cheaper by $6,000, so buy.
parts.working: M1 purchase cost less rent; M1 less salary saved; A1 decision.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two non-financial factors to consider before buying from the supplier.
parts.answer: Any two: reliability of delivery; quality control; loss of skills/jobs and staff morale; dependence on one supplier who may raise prices; confidentiality of design.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

stem: A factory in Lahore has 20,000 machine hours a month. It makes one product, selling 8,500 units a month at $40 each; variable cost $22 per unit; 2 machine hours per unit. A customer asks for 2,000 units of a modified version at $30 each. Each needs 2 machine hours and has a variable cost of $21. A one-off design cost of $2,500 would be paid. Demand for the normal product is unchanged.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the spare machine hours and the number of units of the normal product that must be given up.
parts.answer: Spare = 3,000 hours; order needs 4,000 hours; 1,000 hours short = 500 normal units.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the effect on profit of accepting the order.
parts.answer: Order contribution 2,000 × (30 − 21) = 18,000; lost contribution 500 × 18 = 9,000; design cost 2,500; increase in profit = $6,500
parts.working: M1 order contribution; M1 lost contribution; M1 design cost; A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the minimum price per unit at which the order would be worth accepting.
parts.working: M1 variable cost + opportunity and specific costs per unit; A1.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Mirza Ltd makes electric kettles. It sells 8,000 kettles a year at $35 each. Variable cost is $21 per kettle and fixed costs are $80,000 a year. The directors are considering two options for next year:
Option 1: reduce the price to $32; sales are expected to rise to 10,500 kettles.
Option 2: keep the price at $35 and spend $18,000 on advertising; sales are expected to rise to 9,600 kettles.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Advise the directors which option, if either, they should choose. Justify your answer with calculations.
parts.answer: Current profit $32,000; Option 1 profit $35,500; Option 2 profit $36,400. On profit alone Option 2 is better by $900, but the difference is small, so either option can be recommended with justification.
parts.working: Calculations (max 3): current profit 14 × 8,000 − 80,000 = 32,000; Option 1: 11 × 10,500 − 80,000 = 35,500; Option 2: 14 × 9,600 − 98,000 = 36,400. Points (max 3): Option 1 break-even 7,273 units, margin of safety 10,500 − 7,273 = 3,227; Option 2 break-even 7,000 units, margin of safety 2,600; the lower price may start a price war and lower brand image; Option 1 needs extra capacity and workload for 2,500 more units; advertising results are uncertain but could have longer-lasting effects; the sales forecasts are estimates. Decision with reason (1).

stem: A shop in Doha sells water filters at $50 each. Variable cost is $30 per filter and fixed costs are $90,000 per month. It sells 6,000 filters per month. The manager proposes cutting the price by 10%, which is expected to raise monthly sales by 25%.

parts.label: a

stem: A factory in Karachi makes running shoes, sold at $50 a pair. For each pair: materials $12, labour $8, variable overhead $3, and a sales commission of 5% of the selling price. Fixed costs are $36,000 per month.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by contribution.
parts.answer: Selling price (or revenue) less variable costs; the amount left to pay the fixed costs and then provide profit.
parts.working: 1 mark definition; 1 mark use towards fixed costs and profit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the contribution per pair.
parts.answer: Variable cost = 12 + 8 + 3 + 2.50 commission = 25.50; contribution = 50 − 25.50 = $24.50

Against (max 3): home customers may learn of the lower price and demand the same; uses 9,000 of 12,000 spare units, leaving little room for growth at home; exchange-rate and payment risks; the price is below full cost. stem: Zubair runs a hardware store in Mardan that sells several hundred different products.

A company produced 10,000 units and sold 8,500 units in its first month. Fixed production overhead was $60,000, absorbed on units produced. How will profit under absorption costing compare with profit under marginal costing?

B Marginal profit is $9,000 higher.

D The two profits are the same.
parts.answer: A Absorption profit is $9,000 higher.
parts.working: Fixed overhead per unit = 60,000 ÷ 10,000 = $6. Closing inventory 1,500 units carries 1,500 × 6 = $9,000 of fixed overhead into next month under absorption costing, so absorption profit is $9,000 higher. C wrongly divides the overhead by units sold.

stem: Khyber Foods began making jars of pickle on 1 June. June data: production 5,000 jars, sales 4,200 jars at $30 each. Variable production cost $12 per jar; fixed production overhead $35,000 (absorbed on the normal output of 5,000 jars, so $7 per jar); variable selling cost $1 per jar sold; fixed administration $18,000. There was no opening inventory.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare a statement of profit for June using marginal costing.
parts.answer:
Marginal costing statement
                                                   $         $
Revenue (4,200 × 30)                                   126,000
Variable cost of production (5,000 × 12)      60,000
Less closing inventory (800 × 12)            (9,600)
Variable cost of sales                                (50,400)
Variable selling costs                                 (4,200)
Contribution                                            71,400
Fixed production overhead                             (35,000)
Fixed administration                                  (18,000)
Profit                                                  18,400
parts.working: Closing inventory at 12 (1); contribution 71,400 (1); profit 18,400 (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare a statement of profit for June using absorption costing.
parts.answer:
Absorption costing statement
                                            $         $
Revenue                                         126,000
Cost of production (5,000 × 19)        95,000
Less closing inventory (800 × 19)    (15,200)
Cost of sales                                  (79,800)
Gross profit                                     46,200
Variable selling costs                          (4,200)
Fixed administration                           (18,000)
Profit                                           24,000
parts.working: Full cost 12 + 7 = 19 per unit (1); closing inventory 15,200 (1); profit 24,000 (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the two profit figures are different.
parts.answer: Absorption profit is $5,600 higher because 800 units of closing inventory carry 800 × $7 = $5,600 of fixed production overhead into July, whereas marginal costing charges all the fixed overhead in June.
parts.working: 1 mark figure; 1 mark explanation.

stem:

Production (units)                 6,000    5,500
Sales (units)                      5,000    6,300

parts.label: a

parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.text: Calculate the profit for each month under absorption costing.
parts.answer: Month 1: 42,000 + 1,000 × 9 = $51,000. Month 2: inventory falls by 800 units, so 55,000 − 800 × 9 = $47,800. Month 2 production is 500 units below normal, so 500 × $9 = $4,500 of overhead is under-absorbed and charged as an expense; the difference between the two profits is still fully explained by the change in inventory × $9.
parts.working: M1 inventory change × $9; A1 month 1; M1 decrease deducted; A1 month 2.

parts.answer: Month 1: inventory rises, so some fixed overhead is carried forward in closing inventory. Month 2: inventory falls, so fixed overhead carried forward from month 1 is released into cost of sales, reducing absorption profit.
parts.working: 1 mark each.
