parts.text: Explain how the decision to buy cheaper fabric could cause each of these three variances.
parts.answer: Cheaper fabric lowers the price paid → favourable material price variance (1). Lower quality causes more cutting waste and rejects → adverse material usage variance (1). Workers take longer handling poor fabric and re-cutting → adverse labour efficiency variance (1). The variances are interrelated, so the purchasing decision should be judged on the net effect (1).
parts.working: 1 mark each point.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Three months ago Ahmed Electricals switched to a cheaper supplier of copper wire. Quarterly variances since the change: material price $6,400 favourable; material usage $4,100 adverse; labour efficiency $3,200 adverse. Customer returns of faulty cables have risen from 1% to 4% of sales.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Advise the production director whether the company should continue to buy from the new supplier. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Net effect of the three variances = 6,400 − 4,100 − 3,200 = $900 adverse each quarter, plus higher returns, so the company should probably return to the old supplier or renegotiate quality. Either decision accepted if justified.
parts.working: Calculation (max 2): net variance 6,400 F − 4,100 A − 3,200 A = 900 adverse. Continue (max 3): lower price saves $6,400; waste may fall as workers get used to the material; supplier might improve quality; standards could be revised. Return (max 3): extra waste and labour time outweigh the saving; customer returns up from 1% to 4% damage reputation and future sales; overtime and morale problems. Decision (1).

author: HomiLabs

stem: The owner of a biscuit factory in Lahore is considering introducing standard costing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two benefits to a business of using standard costing.
parts.answer: Any two, explained: it gives targets for planning and budgeting; variances show where performance differs from plan so managers can act (management by exception); it helps control costs and motivate staff; it makes inventory valuation and pricing easier.
parts.working: 1 mark benefit; 1 mark explanation, × 2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two limitations of standard costing.
parts.answer: Any two: standards are costly and time-consuming to set; they quickly become out of date; less suitable for one-off or service work; may demotivate if unrealistic; focus on cost may harm quality.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Siddiqui Tools makes 10,000 drills a year. Skilled workers are paid $18 per hour and take 2 hours per drill. Semi-skilled workers would be paid $14 per hour but would take 2.4 hours per drill, and material waste would rise by 3% of the $30 standard material cost per drill.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Advise the directors whether they should replace the skilled workers with semi-skilled workers. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Relevant cost per drill (labour plus extra material): skilled 2 × 18 = $36.00; semi-skilled 2.4 × 14 = $33.60 plus extra material 3% × 30 = $0.90 = $34.50. Saving $1.50 per drill, $15,000 a year. A justified decision either way.
parts.working: Calculations (max 3): skilled 36.00; semi-skilled 34.50; annual saving 15,000. For (max 2): lower costs improve profit; trained over time the semi-skilled workers may reach the standard time. Against (max 3): 20% more labour hours are needed per drill (2.4 v 2), so the same hours give about 17% less output (an extra 4,000 hours a year for 10,000 drills) – may not meet demand; quality and reputation risk; redundancy costs and staff morale; adverse labour efficiency and material usage variances against the current standards. Decision (1).

author: HomiLabs

stem: The production manager of a shoe factory in Sialkot is setting new labour standards.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between an ideal standard and an attainable standard.
parts.answer: An ideal standard assumes perfect conditions with no waste, idle time or breakdowns; an attainable standard allows for normal waste and inefficiency and can be achieved with reasonable effort.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain which type of standard is more likely to motivate employees.
parts.answer: Attainable: workers can reach it with effort, so it is a realistic target; ideal standards are almost never met, so constant adverse variances demotivate.
parts.working: 1 mark choice; 1 mark reason.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A company selling school shoes in Quetta raised its price from the standard $40 to $45. Its variance report shows a favourable sales price variance of $27,000 and an adverse sales volume variance of $33,600.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the sales price variance and the sales volume variance might be linked.
parts.answer: Raising the price to $45 gives a favourable price variance on each unit sold (1). Customers are price-sensitive, so fewer units are sold than budgeted (1), causing an adverse sales volume variance (1). Other reasons for the volume fall, e.g. a competitor's new product, should also be considered before judging the sales manager (1).
parts.working: 1 mark each point.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A factory in Gujrat makes 12,000 ceramic sinks a year. Each sink currently uses 4 kg of clay at $6.00 per kg and 1.5 labour hours at $15 per hour. A cheaper clay costs $5.20 per kg, but each sink would need 4.5 kg and 1.6 labour hours.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the material and labour cost per unit using (i) the current material and (ii) the cheaper material.
parts.working: M1 current; M1 new; A1 both.

parts.label: b
parts.text: If the standards are not changed, calculate the material price, material usage and labour efficiency variances that the cheaper material would cause for 12,000 units.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State, with a reason, whether the company should change to the cheaper material.
parts.answer: No: the net effect is $10,800 adverse a year (= 12,000 × $0.90), so costs rise despite the lower price.
parts.working: 1 mark decision; 1 mark reason using figures.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A company that makes ceiling fans in Gujrat uses standard costing and wants to hold managers responsible only for costs they control.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each of these variances, state the manager most likely to be responsible and give a reason: material price, material usage, labour rate, sales volume.
parts.answer: Material price – purchasing manager (chooses suppliers and negotiates prices). Material usage – production manager (controls waste in the factory). Labour rate – HR/personnel manager (sets pay and grades of staff). Sales volume – sales/marketing manager (responsible for the number of units sold).
parts.working: 1 mark each (manager with reason).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A manager in a printing company in Lahore is pleased that his department has a large favourable labour rate variance because cheaper trainee staff were used.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a favourable variance is not always good for the business.
parts.answer: A favourable variance may result from poor decisions elsewhere, e.g. cheaper materials (favourable price) causing waste and returns (1); it may mean the standard was set too loosely, hiding inefficiency (1); cost savings such as cutting maintenance or training may harm quality or future performance (1).
parts.working: 1 mark each point, max 3.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Yousaf Plastics investigates any variance greater than 5% of the standard cost to which it relates. Last month's variances:
Variance                      Amount $  F/A  Standard cost $
Material price                   2,300    F           40,000
Material usage                     900    A           40,000
Labour rate                      3,100    A           62,000
Labour efficiency                4,400    A           62,000
Fixed overhead expenditure       1,200    F           30,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Advise the management accountant which variances should be investigated. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Percentages of standard cost: Material price 5.75%; Material usage 2.25%; Labour rate 5.00%; Labour efficiency 7.10%; Fixed overhead expenditure 4.00%. Under the 5% rule investigate material price (5.75%) and labour efficiency (7.10%); labour rate is exactly 5% so borderline.
parts.working: Calculations (max 3): percentages as shown. Points (max 3): material price is favourable but large — may be linked to cheaper material, and to the adverse labour efficiency (poor material slows workers); labour rate at 5% and adverse — check if it is a trend; small variances such as material usage cost more to investigate than they would save; consider trends over several months, controllability and cost of investigation versus benefit. Clear conclusion (1).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A juice factory in Multan had delays in fruit deliveries in August. Its variance report shows an adverse labour efficiency variance and an adverse fixed overhead volume variance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a problem with materials could cause an adverse labour efficiency variance.
parts.answer: Poor-quality or late material (1) means workers waste time waiting, re-working or handling rejects (1), so more hours are worked than the standard allows for the output (1).
parts.working: 1 mark each step.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what an adverse fixed overhead volume variance shows.
parts.answer: Actual output was lower than budgeted output (1), so less fixed overhead was absorbed than budgeted — the fixed costs were spread over fewer units (1).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Malik Packaging installed a new cutting machine seven months ago. Since then the material usage variance has been adverse by about 8% of standard material cost every month. Production staff say the machine design wastes more card than the old one and complain that their bonus, which depends on meeting the standard, is never paid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Advise the directors whether the material usage standard should be revised. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: A justified recommendation, e.g. revise the standard to an attainable level, because the adverse variance is permanent (caused by the new machine) and is demotivating staff, while keeping a target that encourages improvement.
parts.working: Revise (max 4): adverse usage variance of about 8% every month for six months shows the standard is out of date; the cause (new machine design) is outside workers' control; unrealistic standards demotivate and make variance reports useless; budgets and prices based on the old standard understate costs. Do not revise (max 3): the machine may be adjusted or staff trained to reduce waste; revising too easily builds in inefficiency; cost and time of setting new standards; supplier may be responsible. Decision (1).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A textile mill in Karachi had an adverse labour rate variance of $1,800 last month; the standard labour cost of actual output was $45,000. The new manager wants employees to help set next year's standards.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the labour rate variance as a percentage of the standard labour cost.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways in which involving employees in setting standards may affect their behaviour.
parts.answer: Any two, explained: staff feel ownership so are more motivated to meet the standard; standards are more realistic because staff know the work; but staff may build in slack (easy standards) to earn bonuses; discussions take time and may cause conflict.
parts.working: 1 mark point; 1 mark explanation, × 2.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The partners of Hilltop Traders, Quetta, agree to value goodwill at two years' purchase of the average profit of the last three years. Profits were: year 1 $84,000; year 2 $96,000; year 3 $105,000.
What is the value of goodwill?
A $95,000
B $190,000
C $210,000
D $285,000
parts.working: Average profit = (84,000 + 96,000 + 105,000) ÷ 3 = $95,000; × 2 years = $190,000. A is the average only; C uses the latest year; D is the total of three years.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Ali and Bilal share profits 3:2. Chand is admitted and the new ratio is Ali 2, Bilal 2, Chand 1. Goodwill is valued at $60,000 but no goodwill account is to remain in the books.
What is the net effect of the goodwill adjustment on Ali's capital account?
A credit $12,000
B debit $12,000
C credit $36,000
D no change
parts.answer: A credit $12,000
parts.working: Goodwill created in old ratio: Ali credited 3/5 × 60,000 = 36,000. Written off in new ratio: Ali debited 2/5 × 60,000 = 24,000. Net credit $12,000. D is Bilal's position (24,000 − 24,000 = 0), not Ali's.

stem:
Jabbar and Sons, a partnership of opticians in Peshawar, made these profits:
Year  Profit $  Weight

The partners agree to value goodwill at three years' purchase of the weighted average profit.

parts.label: a

parts.label: b

parts.label: c

parts.answer: For example: a good reputation; a loyal customer base.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: reputation; loyal customers; good location; skilled staff; brand name; good supplier relationships.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Usman, Vania and Waleed are partners sharing profits 2:2:1. Waleed retires on 30 June 2026. Goodwill is valued at $45,000. The partners decide that a goodwill account will be opened and kept in the books.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the journal entry to record the goodwill. A narrative is not required.
parts.answer:
Dr $    Cr $
Goodwill          45,000
Capital – Usman           18,000
Capital – Vania           18,000
Capital – Waleed           9,000
parts.working: Dr goodwill 45,000 (B1); Cr capitals in the old ratio 2:2:1 (M1): 18,000, 18,000, 9,000 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why many businesses do not keep a goodwill account in the books after a change of partners.
parts.answer: Goodwill generated inside the business cannot be measured reliably, so IAS 38 does not allow internally generated goodwill to be recognised as an asset; it is written off to the partners' capital accounts.
parts.working: 1 mark: value is subjective / cannot be measured reliably / can change quickly. 1 mark: accounting standards (IAS 38) / prudence do not allow internally generated goodwill to be shown.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Kamran and Laila run a bakery in Islamabad, sharing profits equally. On 1 April 2026 Mehwish is admitted for a one-quarter share of profits; Kamran and Laila will share the remaining three-quarters equally. Goodwill is valued at $72,000 and is not to be recorded in the books.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why an adjustment for goodwill is needed when a new partner is admitted.
parts.answer: The old partners built up the goodwill; without an adjustment the new partner would share in the value they created, so the old partners must be compensated for the share they give up.
parts.working: 1 mark: goodwill was created by the existing partners. 1 mark: new partner gains a share of it / old partners lose part of their share and must be compensated.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the net amount credited or debited to each partner's capital account for goodwill.
parts.answer: Kamran credit $9,000; Laila credit $9,000; Mehwish debit $18,000.

parts.answer:

Capital – Kamran           9,000
Capital – Laila            9,000
parts.working: Dr Mehwish 18,000 (1); Cr Kamran 9,000 and Laila 9,000 (1).

stem: Imran retired from a partnership of engineers in Rawalpindi on 31 December 2025. The amount due to him was $84,000. He received $24,000 in cash on that date. The balance became a loan, repaid in three equal annual instalments starting on 31 December 2026. Interest at 8% per annum on the balance outstanding during each year is paid with each instalment.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount of each loan instalment.

parts.label: b

parts.label: c

parts.answer: Advantage: cash outflow is spread, protecting liquidity. Disadvantage: interest of $9,600 in total is payable and reduces profit.

Jamil and Kiran share residual profits equally. Profit for the year was $96,000. Jamil receives a salary of $12,000. Interest on capital is 6% per annum; capitals are Jamil $50,000 and Kiran $70,000.

A $38,400
B $42,600
C $48,000

stem:

1 March 2025  $6,000
1 September 2025  $9,000
1 December 2025  $12,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the interest on Nabeel's drawings for the year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a partnership agreement may charge interest on drawings.
parts.answer: It discourages partners from withdrawing cash early or excessively, and it is fair to partners who leave their money in the business, because those who draw early benefit from the use of business funds.

stem:
The cash budget of Saeed Packaging Ltd shows a cash deficit of $40,000 for the next three months, after which the balance becomes positive. The directors are considering two options:
Option 1: an overdraft of $40,000 for three months at an interest rate of 12% per annum.
Option 2: offer customers a 2.5% cash discount to pay one month earlier. The directors expect customers owing $64,000 to accept, which would remove the deficit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost of Option 1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the cost of Option 2.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise the directors which option they should choose. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Option 1 is cheaper by $400 and does not depend on customers' behaviour; the bank may withdraw an overdraft at short notice, and it adds to interest costs. Option 2 is more expensive, customers may not all accept, and once offered the discount may be expected permanently, reducing future profit; but it lowers the risk of irrecoverable debts and needs no bank approval. Decision: choose the overdraft because it is cheaper and more certain, provided the bank agrees.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for points for Option 1 (cheaper by 400; certain amount; temporary). Up to 2 marks for points for/against Option 2 (uncertain take-up; permanent expectation; fewer bad debts; no security needed). 1 mark for use of figures. 1 mark for a clear decision consistent with the argument.

stem: Al-Shifa Hospital, Karachi, currently sets departmental budgets centrally. The new finance director suggests participative budgeting.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the term 'participative budgeting'.
parts.answer: Budget holders (department managers) are involved in setting their own budgets with senior management, rather than having budgets imposed.
parts.working: 1 mark: managers take part. 1 mark: contrast with imposed/top-down.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of participative budgeting for the hospital.
parts.answer: Advantages: department heads know their patient numbers and costs, so budgets are more realistic; managers feel ownership and are more motivated to meet them; better communication between departments. Disadvantages: takes longer; managers may build in budgetary slack; targets may not match the hospital's overall goals; senior managers may still override them, causing demotivation.

stem: The directors of Shah Logistics Ltd plan to pay each depot manager a bonus if the depot's actual costs are below its budget.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the term 'budgetary slack'.
parts.answer: Deliberately overstating budgeted costs (or understating revenue) so the target is easier to achieve.
parts.working: 1 mark: deliberate overstatement/understatement. 1 mark: to make the target easy to meet.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise the directors whether they should link the bonus to the budget. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: For: gives managers a clear target and incentive to control costs; aligns their goals with the company's. Against: encourages budgetary slack in the budget-setting stage; managers may cut essential spending (maintenance, training) to earn the bonus; ignores factors outside their control such as fuel prices; may harm service quality. Decision: link bonuses only if budgets are reviewed for slack and include non-financial targets, or use a flexed budget; otherwise do not.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for points for; up to 3 marks for points against (slack, short-termism, uncontrollable costs, quality); 1 mark for a justified decision.

parts.text: State two differences between a joint venture and a partnership.
parts.answer: A joint venture ends when the project is completed, whereas a partnership continues indefinitely; joint venturers usually carry on their own separate businesses and there is usually no firm name or separate continuing set of books.

stem: Two venturers each record their own joint venture transactions in their own books. At the end of the venture a memorandum joint venture account is prepared.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the purpose of the memorandum joint venture account.
parts.answer: It brings together the transactions of all venturers to calculate the profit or loss of the whole venture, so that it can be shared in the agreed ratio.
parts.working: 1 mark: combines all venturers' transactions. 1 mark: to find total profit/loss to be shared.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the memorandum joint venture account is not part of the double-entry system.
parts.answer: Each transaction has already been recorded in a venturer's own 'Joint venture with …' account; the memorandum account is a working statement prepared from copies of those records, so no entries are posted from it.
parts.working: 1 mark: transactions already recorded in venturers' own books. 1 mark: it is only a statement/memorandum, no double entry.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Haider Builders, Lahore, wants to bid for a bridge contract worth $2,400,000.
Option 1: bid alone. Haider would have to hire specialist equipment and engineers; total costs are estimated at $2,280,000.
Option 2: form a joint venture with a foreign engineering company. Total costs of the venture are estimated at $1,950,000 and Haider would receive 40% of the profit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Haider's expected profit under each option.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise Haider Builders which option to choose. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: For the joint venture: higher expected profit ($60,000 more); the foreign partner's expertise lowers the risk of cost overruns and delays; Haider gains experience for future bridge contracts; less finance needed. Against: Haider loses control over decisions; profit depends on the partner's performance; disputes over sharing; Haider builds less of its own reputation. Bidding alone keeps all profit but the margin is only 5% of contract value, so a small overrun would cause a loss. Decision: choose the joint venture, provided a clear written agreement sets out duties, profit sharing and settlement.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for points for the joint venture; up to 2 marks for points against / for bidding alone; 1 mark for use of the calculated figures (e.g. 60,000 difference, 5% margin); 1 mark for a justified decision.

parts.label: b

parts.working: 1 mark: Salma owes Ikram / receivable. 1 mark: cleared by cash received from Salma.

stem: Joint venture transactions may be recorded either in a separate set of books with a joint bank account, or in each venturer's own books.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of keeping a separate set of books with a joint bank account.
parts.answer: Advantage: all receipts and payments pass through one account, so the venture's records are complete and transparent and the profit is easy to calculate. Disadvantage: it costs more time and money to open an account and keep extra books, which may not be worthwhile for a small, short venture.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for an advantage (identify + explain) and up to 2 marks for a disadvantage (identify + explain).

stem: Rashid and Tahir share joint venture profits equally. At the end of their venture in garden furniture, unsold goods that cost $6,000 are taken over by Rashid at an agreed value of $4,000, their net realisable value. Before this item, the memorandum joint venture account showed a profit of $15,000 (all goods counted as sold or taken over at cost).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the revised joint venture profit.
parts.working: Taking over at 4,000 rather than cost 6,000 reduces the credit by 2,000 (M1); 15,000 − 2,000 = 13,000 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate each venturer's share of the revised profit.
parts.answer: $6,500 each

parts.label: c
parts.text: Discuss whether the goods should be taken over at net realisable value rather than cost.
parts.answer: Prudence: goods should not be valued above what they can be sold for, so $4,000 is appropriate if NRV is reliable. However, Rashid benefits if he later sells them for more, so the value must be agreed fairly and independently; Tahir bears half the $2,000 reduction. Conclusion: NRV is acceptable if it is agreed by both venturers or set by an independent valuation.
parts.working: 1 mark: prudence / IAS 2 lower of cost and NRV. 1 mark: conflict of interest – taker benefits from low value. 1 mark: conclusion/agreement needed.

stem: Sialkot Leather sends handbags to an agent in Doha. The agent sells them for a commission and returns the money. A competitor instead works with a Doha trader who shares the profit on the goods equally.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify which arrangement is a consignment and which is a joint venture.
parts.answer: Sialkot Leather and its agent: consignment. The competitor and the Doha trader: joint venture.
parts.working: B1 both correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two differences between a consignment and a joint venture.
parts.answer: In a consignment the consignor owns the goods until they are sold and bears all the profit or loss; the agent earns only commission. In a joint venture the venturers are co-owners for the project and share profit or loss in an agreed ratio. Also, a consignee acts for the consignor as agent, whereas joint venturers are like temporary partners with equal standing.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks per difference: ownership of goods; who bears profit/loss (commission vs share of profit); relationship (principal–agent vs co-venturers).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of the following is a physical security measure for a computerised accounting system?
A a password on each user account
B encryption of the data files
C a locked room for the server
D a firewall on the network
parts.answer: C a locked room for the server
parts.working: A locked room physically prevents access to the hardware. A, B and D are software (logical) controls.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the main purpose of making regular backup copies of accounting data?
A to stop hackers from reading the data
B to allow the data to be restored if it is lost or corrupted
C to check that entries have been input correctly
D to reduce the storage space needed
parts.answer: B to allow the data to be restored if it is lost or corrupted
parts.working: A backup is a copy kept so that lost or damaged data can be recovered. It does not stop unauthorised reading (A, which needs encryption/passwords) or check accuracy (C).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A business's purchase system will not accept a single invoice above $10,000. A clerk keys in an invoice for $85,000 instead of $8,500.
Which validation check will reject the entry?
A format check
B range (limit) check
C presence check
D check digit
parts.answer: B range (limit) check
parts.working: A range or limit check tests that a value lies within set limits. A format check only tests the pattern of characters, which 85,000 still matches; a presence check only tests that a value has been entered.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of the following is a disadvantage of a computerised accounting system compared with a manual system?
A ledger balances are updated automatically
B reports such as the trial balance can be produced quickly
C an input error may be repeated in every record that uses that data
D arithmetic errors in totalling the ledgers are eliminated
parts.answer: C an input error may be repeated in every record that uses that data
parts.working: If wrong data is input, the system processes it faithfully and the error flows through all linked records ('garbage in, garbage out'). A, B and D are advantages.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the purpose of an audit trail in a computerised accounting system?
A to prevent staff from changing their passwords
B to allow each transaction to be traced from its source document through to the financial statements
C to make a copy of all files at the end of each day
D to stop viruses from entering the system
parts.answer: B to allow each transaction to be traced from its source document through to the financial statements
parts.working: An audit trail records who entered or changed each transaction and when, so it can be traced. C describes a backup; D describes antivirus software.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A business uses an integrated computerised accounting system in which every entry must have equal debits and credits.
Which error could still occur?
A a sales ledger total that is added up incorrectly
B a debit entry with no corresponding credit entry
C a trial balance that does not agree
D a sales invoice posted to the account of the wrong customer
parts.answer: D a sales invoice posted to the account of the wrong customer
parts.working: Posting to the wrong customer is an error of commission: debits still equal credits, so the system cannot detect it. The software performs the arithmetic and enforces double entry, so A, B and C cannot occur.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A batch of supplier invoices has a manually calculated batch total of $23,640. After the invoices were keyed in, the computer total was $23,910.
Which single error would explain the difference?
A an invoice for $4,580 was keyed in as $4,850
B an invoice for $270 was not keyed in
C an invoice for $4,850 was keyed in as $4,580
D a credit note for $270 was keyed in as an invoice
parts.answer: A an invoice for $4,580 was keyed in as $4,850
parts.working: The computer total is 270 too high (23,910 − 23,640). Keying 4,850 for 4,580 adds 270. B and C would make the total 270 too low; D would make it 540 too high.

stem: Fatima owns a clothes shop in Hyderabad and keeps her accounts by hand. She is thinking of buying accounting software.

parts.answer: Records and reports (e.g. trial balance, statements to customers) are produced quickly; arithmetic is accurate and ledgers update automatically.

parts.label: b

stem: Ravi Motors, Karachi, keeps its customer and supplier records on a computerised accounting system.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two methods the business could use to prevent unauthorised access to its accounting data.

stem: A trading business in Lahore saves all its accounting data on one office computer.

parts.answer: Make regular backups; store a backup copy off-site or in the cloud.
parts.working: 1 mark each: regular backups; off-site/cloud storage; antivirus software; uninterruptible power supply; fire-proof storage.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a backup copy should be stored away from the office.
parts.answer: If the office suffers a fire, flood or theft, both the computer and an on-site backup could be destroyed; an off-site copy can still be used to restore the records.
parts.working: 1 mark: risk of physical disaster/theft at the office. 1 mark: off-site copy allows restoration.

Range check: tests that the invoice amount is within set limits, e.g. above $0 and below the customer's credit limit. (Also: presence check that no field is left blank.)

stem: Kaghan Supplies gives every customer a four-digit account number followed by a check digit. The check digit is calculated as follows: multiply the four digits by the weights 5, 4, 3 and 2 in order; add the results; divide by 11; the check digit is 11 minus the remainder. When an account number is entered, the computer multiplies the five digits by 5, 4, 3, 2 and 1 and accepts the number only if the total is exactly divisible by 11.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the check digit for account number 3725.
parts.answer: 7 (full number 37257)

parts.label: b
parts.text: A clerk keys in 37527 instead of 37257. Show that the computer will reject it.
parts.answer: Weighted total = 69, which is not divisible by 11, so the number is rejected.
parts.working: 3×5 + 7×4 + 5×3 + 2×2 + 7×1 = 69 (M1); 69 ÷ 11 leaves remainder 3, so rejected (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the type of input error this check is designed to detect.
parts.answer: Transposition errors (digits swapped) and single-digit keying errors.

stem: Zaitoon Traders uses an integrated accounting package in which the sales, purchases, inventory and nominal ledgers are linked.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Margalla Engineering Ltd is replacing its old accounting software with a new system. The finance director must choose between direct changeover (switching completely on one day) and parallel running (running both systems together for three months).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the term 'parallel running'.
parts.answer: Operating the old and new systems at the same time, with the same data, so their results can be compared before the old system is dropped.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise the finance director which method to use. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Parallel running: results from the new system can be checked against the old, and if the new system fails the old one is still available, so the risk of losing accounting records is low; but staff must enter everything twice, which is costly, slow and may cause mistakes. Direct changeover: cheap and quick, and staff concentrate on one system; but if the new system fails there is no fallback and records, payments to suppliers or payroll could be disrupted. Decision: for a company's main accounting records, use parallel running (perhaps for one month-end close only) because the cost of failure is greater than the extra staff time.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for points on parallel running; up to 2 marks for points on direct changeover; 1 mark for applying to the company (size, importance of records, staff time); 1 mark for a justified decision.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A garment exporter in Sialkot has received emails that appear to come from its bank, asking staff to confirm the company's online banking log-in details. Last month another firm in the city had its accounting files locked by ransomware.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by 'phishing' and suggest one way to protect the business against it.
parts.answer: Phishing is a fraudulent message pretending to be from a trusted organisation to trick staff into revealing passwords or bank details. Protection: train staff never to give log-in details by email and to check messages with the bank directly.
parts.working: 1 mark explanation; 1 mark protection (training, spam filters, two-factor authentication).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what is meant by 'ransomware' and suggest one way to protect the business against it.
parts.answer: Ransomware is malicious software that encrypts or locks files and demands payment to release them. Protection: keep regular backups stored separately so files can be restored without paying, and keep antivirus software and updates current.
parts.working: 1 mark explanation; 1 mark protection (separate backups, antivirus, updates, not opening unknown attachments).

author: HomiLabs

stem: The external auditor of Indus Foods Ltd asks whether its accounting software keeps an audit trail.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the term 'audit trail'.
parts.answer: A record kept by the system of every transaction and change, showing who made it and when, so that each entry can be traced from the source document to the financial statements.
parts.working: 1 mark: record of transactions/changes with user and time. 1 mark: allows tracing source to final accounts.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why an audit trail is useful to the auditor.
parts.answer: The auditor can check that recorded figures are supported by source documents and can identify unauthorised or suspicious changes, which helps detect errors and fraud.
parts.working: 1 mark: verify figures to evidence. 1 mark: detect unauthorised changes/fraud.

author: HomiLabs

stem: An online retailer in Karachi stores customers' names, addresses, phone numbers and payment records in its accounting system.

parts.label: a

parts.answer: Keep the data secure: use passwords, encryption and access controls so it cannot be stolen or misused. Use the data only for the purpose it was collected and keep it accurate and up to date, deleting it when no longer needed. (Also: obey data protection law, do not share without consent.)
parts.working: Up to 2 marks per responsibility (1 identify, 1 explain).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A computerised accounting system needs both hardware and software.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between hardware and software, giving one example of each.

stem: The owner of a computerised business says, 'The computer never makes mistakes, so our accounts must be correct.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify and explain two types of error that can still occur in a computerised accounting system.
parts.answer: Error of original entry: a wrong amount is keyed in from the invoice, and the system posts the wrong figure to both accounts. Error of commission: a payment is posted to the wrong supplier's account; debits still equal credits so the system does not detect it. (Also: error of omission, error of principle, compensating errors.)

author: HomiLabs

stem: Sunrise Bakery, Peshawar, is introducing a computerised accounting system.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why staff should be trained before the system is used.
parts.answer: So that they enter transactions correctly and avoid input errors that would make the accounts wrong. So that they can use the system efficiently and obtain the reports needed, getting the expected time savings. (Also: understand security procedures such as passwords and backups; reduce resistance to change.)
parts.working: Up to 2 marks per reason (1 identify, 1 explain).

author: HomiLabs

stem: At Khyber Steel Ltd one purchases clerk can set up new suppliers in the computerised purchase ledger, record invoices and authorise payments. Last year the clerk created a false supplier account and paid $18,000 into his own bank account before the fraud was discovered.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two weaknesses in the control system that allowed the fraud.
parts.answer: There was no segregation of duties: one person could create suppliers, record invoices and approve payments. Access levels were too wide and no one else reviewed new supplier accounts or payments.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Recommend controls to prevent such a fraud happening again. Justify your recommendations.
parts.answer: Separate duties so that different staff create suppliers, record invoices and authorise payments, so fraud needs collusion. Set access levels so the clerk cannot add suppliers; new suppliers approved by a manager with checks on bank details. Review the audit trail and exception reports of new suppliers and payments regularly. Require two authorisations for payments above a set limit.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks per developed recommendation (control + why it works), max 4.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A pharmacy in Rawalpindi uses its accounting software to keep a running record of inventory. author: HomiLabs

stem: Sadia & Co. Ltd introduced a computerised accounting system last year. A director says: 'Now that the software does all the double entry, we no longer need to prepare bank reconciliations or check control accounts.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the director's statement.
parts.answer: Partly true: the software keeps debits equal to credits, posts to ledgers and control accounts automatically and removes arithmetic errors, so some manual checks are no longer needed. However, the bank reconciliation compares the business's records with an independent source (the bank statement); it still finds unpresented cheques, bank charges, direct debits not entered, keying errors and fraud. Errors of commission, omission and original entry are not detected by the software. Control accounts and reconciliations are also internal controls that auditors expect. Conclusion: the statement is not justified; reconciliations should continue, although the software makes them quicker.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for points supporting the statement; up to 3 marks for points against (independent check, errors not detected, fraud, audit expectations); 1 mark for a justified conclusion.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Rehman Electricals, a small business in Multan, is thinking of moving from accounting software on one office computer to a cloud-based accounting package paid for by monthly subscription.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether the business should move to cloud-based accounting.
parts.answer: For: data can be reached from anywhere, e.g. by the owner at home or the accountant; the provider makes automatic backups and updates; no large up-front cost; can link to online banking for automatic bank feeds. Against: depends on a reliable internet connection, which may be a problem in some areas; monthly fees continue for ever; data held by a third party raises security and confidentiality concerns; staff need retraining. Conclusion: move to the cloud if the internet is reliable and the provider has strong security, because backup and access benefits outweigh the subscription cost.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for advantages and up to 2 marks for disadvantages applied to the business; 1 mark for a justified conclusion.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Leila Interiors, Muscat, Oman. At 30 November 2026 the account of Gulf Fabrics in Leila's purchases ledger shows a credit balance of $4,355. The statement received from Gulf Fabrics shows $8,280 owing. These differences were found:
1 an invoice for $1,725 dated 29 November is in the post and has not reached Leila
2 Leila's payment of $2,100 sent on 30 November had not reached Gulf Fabrics
3 goods of $460 returned by Leila have not yet been credited by Gulf Fabrics
4 a cash discount of $90 taken by Leila has been disallowed by Gulf Fabrics because the payment was late
5 an invoice for $1,380 was entered in Leila's books as $1,830.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare a statement reconciling the balance on Gulf Fabrics' account in Leila's purchases ledger with the balance on the supplier's statement.
parts.answer:
$
Balance per purchases ledger                       4,355
Less invoice over-recorded (1,830 − 1,380)          (450)
Corrected ledger balance                           3,905
Add invoice in transit                             1,725
Add payment not yet received by supplier           2,100
Add returns not yet credited by supplier             460
Add discount disallowed by supplier                   90
Balance per supplier's statement                   8,280
parts.working: 1 mark each: correction of 450; invoice in transit; payment in transit; returns and discount; final $8,280 agrees.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which of the differences require an entry in Leila's own books.
parts.answer: Item 5 (reduce the supplier's balance by $450). Item 4 if Leila accepts that the discount was disallowed (Dr discount received, Cr Gulf Fabrics $90). Items 1–3 are timing differences.
parts.working: 1 mark item 5; 1 mark item 4 with reason.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why reconciling suppliers' statements is a useful check on the purchases ledger.
parts.answer: The supplier's statement is independent evidence prepared by an outside party, so it reveals errors in posting to the supplier's account (which a control account may not) and prevents paying the wrong amount.
parts.working: 1 mark independent/external evidence; 1 mark finds posting errors / avoids over- or under-payment.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Haddad Printing, Amman, Jordan. At 31 December 2025 the equipment (cost) account in the ledger had a balance of $186,500. A check against the non-current asset register found:
1 a printer bought for $9,400 was recorded in the ledger but had not been entered in the register
2 a laminator that cost $4,600 was sold during the year; it had been removed from the register but the cost account had not been updated
3 repairs of $2,400 to a printer were debited to the equipment account.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare a statement showing the corrected balance on the equipment (cost) account.
parts.working: 1 mark each adjustment; 1 mark answer (max 3).

parts.label: b
parts.text: The non-current asset register showed total cost of $170,100. Show that, once error 1 is corrected, the register agrees with the corrected ledger balance.
parts.answer: 170,100 + 9,400 = $179,500, the same as the corrected ledger.
parts.working: 1 mark adding 9,400; 1 mark agreement.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two benefits of keeping a non-current asset register in addition to the ledger accounts.
parts.answer: It records each asset's details (location, serial number, cost, depreciation), so assets can be physically checked and losses or theft found; it allows depreciation and disposals to be calculated for each asset; it provides an independent check on the ledger total.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two benefits.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Green Valley Dairy, Abbottabad, has replaced its manual ledgers with accounting software. The owner says that the business no longer needs to check its records because "the computer cannot make mistakes".

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the trial balance produced by the new computerised system will always agree.
parts.answer: Every transaction is entered once and the software automatically posts equal debit and credit entries, so arithmetical and one-sided posting errors cannot happen.
parts.working: 1 mark automatic double entry; 1 mark no casting/single-entry errors.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the business must still verify its accounting records after changing to the computerised system.
parts.answer: Input errors still occur: wrong amounts (original entry), wrong account codes (commission/principle) and omissions are processed faithfully. Bank charges, direct debits and dishonoured cheques are still found only by bank reconciliation. Inventory and non-current assets must still be physically checked. Fraud or unauthorised entries need independent checks.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four relevant points (or 2 points developed).

author: HomiLabs

stem: The trial balance of Zafar Builders' Merchants, Sargodha, at 30 June 2026 has debit totals of $248,615 and credit totals of $249,425.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the balance entered in the suspense account and state whether it is a debit or a credit balance.
parts.answer: 249,425 − 248,615 = $810. The debit side is smaller, so the suspense account has a debit balance of $810.
parts.working: 1 mark amount; 1 mark debit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the business opens a suspense account.
parts.answer: It allows a trial balance (and draft statements) to be prepared on time while the errors are being found; the difference is held temporarily until it can be cleared.
parts.working: 1 mark temporary account; 1 mark allows work to continue while errors are investigated.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why clearing the suspense account does not prove that the accounts are free from errors.
parts.answer: The suspense account only deals with errors that make the totals disagree. Errors of omission, commission, principle, original entry, complete reversal and compensating errors leave the totals equal and are still undetected.
parts.working: 1 mark only errors affecting agreement; 1 mark examples of undetected errors.

author: HomiLabs

stem: At Kibo Builders' Supplies, Arusha, Tanzania, one clerk opens the post, records receipts from customers in the cash book, banks the money, posts the sales ledger and approves irrecoverable debts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the same clerk doing all of these tasks creates a risk of fraud.
parts.answer: The clerk could keep a customer's payment and hide it by delaying the posting, using later receipts from other customers to cover it (teeming and lading), or by writing the debt off as irrecoverable or issuing a false credit note. Nobody independent checks the records.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three points (lack of segregation, example method of concealment, no independent check).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the sales ledger control account and the monthly bank reconciliation, prepared by the owner, would reduce this risk.
parts.answer: The owner prepares the control account from totals of the cash book, sales journal and journal, independent of the clerk; differences with the list of balances must be explained. Unusual write-offs or credit notes appear in the totals. The bank reconciliation checks that receipts recorded were actually banked and in the right amounts.
parts.working: 1 mark independent preparation; 1 mark comparison with list / investigation of write-offs; 1 mark bank reconciliation confirms receipts banked.

author: HomiLabs

stem: The owner of a car-rental business in Dubai makes this statement to her new bookkeeper.

parts.label: a
parts.text: "If my trial balance agrees, my financial statements must be correct." Discuss this statement.
parts.answer:
Agree: a TB that agrees shows debits equal credits, so arithmetical and single-entry errors are unlikely; it is a quick check and the basis for the statements.
Disagree: six types of error do not affect agreement — omission, commission, principle, original entry, complete reversal and compensating errors (examples). Errors of principle and original entry change profit and asset values. The TB says nothing about whether adjustments (accruals, depreciation, irrecoverable debts, inventory valuation) are correct, or whether estimates are reasonable. Fraud can be concealed by balanced entries.
Conclusion: the TB is a necessary but limited check; other verification (control accounts, bank reconciliation, supplier statements, physical counts) and review of adjustments are needed.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for points supporting the statement / purposes of the TB; up to 5 marks for limitations explained with examples (1 per type named with example, 1 per further developed point); 1 mark for a reasoned conclusion within the total. Maximum 8.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Amina owns three shoe shops in Rawalpindi. A clerk spends 20 hours a week on manual sales and purchases ledgers and control accounts and is paid $9 an hour. Accounting software would cost $6,500 a year and would remove this work completely. Assume 52 working weeks a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net annual saving from introducing the software.
parts.answer: Saving in clerk time 20 × 52 × $9 = $9,360; net saving 9,360 − 6,500 = $2,860.
parts.working: 1 mark gross saving; 1 mark net saving.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise Amina whether she should replace her manual control accounts and ledgers with the software. Justify your answer.
parts.answer:
For: net saving of $2,860 a year; automatic posting means control accounts always agree with ledgers and the TB always balances; faster, up-to-date information on customers and suppliers; reports for credit control.
Against: input errors (wrong amount, wrong account) are not detected and a manual control account would no longer act as an independent check; staff training and changeover costs; risk of data loss, viruses or hacking — backups and passwords needed; dependence on one supplier; the clerk's time saved may not be a real saving unless used elsewhere.
Decision: e.g. buy the software because it saves money and gives better information, but keep independent checks such as monthly bank reconciliations and supplier statement reconciliations, with access controls.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for points for (including use of the $2,860); up to 3 marks for points against; 1 mark for a clear decision consistent with the argument.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Zambezi Hardware, Lusaka, Zambia, found two errors at 31 October 2026:
1 a cheque for $1,460 received from R. Banda was entered correctly in the cash book but was not posted to Banda's account in the sales ledger
2 a cheque for $2,750 paid to a supplier was entered in the cash book as $2,570 and posted from there.
Before correction the sales ledger control account showed $46,280 and the list of sales ledger balances totalled $47,740. The cash book showed a debit balance of $5,630.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each error, state which check revealed it, and explain why the other check did not.
parts.answer:
Error 1 is revealed by the sales ledger control account: the cash book total posted to the control account included $1,460 but Banda's account was not credited, so the list exceeds the control account by $1,460. The bank reconciliation does not reveal it because the cash book and bank both show the $1,460 correctly.
Error 2 is revealed by the bank reconciliation: the bank paid $2,750 but the cash book shows $2,570. The purchases ledger control account does not reveal it because the wrong amount was posted from the cash book to both the control account and the supplier's account.
parts.working: 1 mark each: correct check for error 1; why bank rec misses it; correct check for error 2; why control account misses it.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the corrected total of the list of sales ledger balances and the corrected cash book balance.
parts.answer: List: 47,740 − 1,460 = $46,280 (agrees with the control account). Cash book: 5,630 − (2,750 − 2,570) = $5,450.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a business should use more than one method of verification.
parts.answer: Each method checks only certain records and misses certain errors, as shown here; using several methods together covers more types of error and fraud.
parts.working: 1 mark each method has blind spots; 1 mark combination gives wider coverage, with reference to the example.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Ming's Tea House, Kuala Lumpur, recorded sales of $240,000 for the year. After the trial balance had agreed and draft statements were prepared, the auditor found that the sales account had been overcast by $800 and that the wages account had also been overcast by $800.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the trial balance agreed.
parts.answer: The two errors are of equal amount on opposite sides: the sales (credit) total and the wages (debit) total are each $800 too high, so they cancel out — compensating errors.
parts.working: 1 mark compensating errors; 1 mark equal amounts on opposite sides.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the effect of the two errors on (i) gross profit and (ii) profit for the year.
parts.answer: (i) Gross profit is overstated by $800 (sales too high). (ii) Profit for the year is unaffected: sales $800 too high and wages $800 too high cancel.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Assess how far the trial balance can be relied on as a check before the owner uses the gross margin to set next year's prices.
parts.answer: The TB proved only that debits equalled credits; here the gross margin was overstated (sales of $240,000 should have been $239,200), which could lead the owner to think pricing is adequate. Profit for the year is right only by chance. The owner should not rely on the TB alone: control accounts, checking day book casts and analytical review of margins compared with previous years would reveal the error. Conclusion: limited reliance.
parts.working: 1 mark TB checks arithmetic only; 1 mark consequence for gross margin/pricing decisions; 1 mark other checks needed; 1 mark judgement.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which user of a business's financial statements is likely to be most interested in how long the business takes to pay for goods bought on credit?
A a supplier deciding whether to offer credit
B an employee asking for a pay rise
C the tax authority
D a bank deciding on a ten-year mortgage on the premises
parts.answer: A a supplier deciding whether to offer credit
parts.working: The trade payables payment period shows how quickly suppliers are paid, which matters most to a supplier offering credit. A bank lending for ten years is more concerned with long-term profitability, gearing and security.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statements about users of financial statements are correct?
1 A bank considering an overdraft will examine the liquid (acid test) ratio.
2 An employee concerned about job security will be interested in the business's profitability.
3 The tax authority uses the financial statements when assessing tax due on profits.
4 A competitor has a legal right to inspect a sole trader's ledger accounts.
A 1 and 2 only
B 1, 2 and 3 only
C 2 and 4 only
D 1, 2, 3 and 4
parts.answer: B 1, 2 and 3 only
parts.working: Statements 1–3 are correct. A sole trader's records are private; a competitor has no right to inspect them, so statement 4 is wrong and options C and D are wrong.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem: Rahim runs a builders' merchant in Multan as a sole trader. He has a bank loan, buys from 30 suppliers on credit and employs a manager and six staff.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two external users of the financial statements of Rahim Builders' Merchants and explain what information each would want.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. Bank – ability to repay loan and interest (profit, cash, security of assets, gearing). Suppliers – ability to pay on time (liquidity, payables period). Tax authority – profit to calculate tax. Customers – continuity of supply. Potential partner/investor – profitability and return.
parts.working: 1 mark each user; 1 mark each for relevant information linked to that user's purpose.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify one internal user and explain one way in which this user would use the financial statements.
parts.answer: The owner (Rahim) – to measure profit and decide whether to expand, cut costs or change prices; or the manager – to control costs against budgets.
parts.working: 1 mark user; 1 mark use.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem: Lyallpur Spinning Ltd is a private limited company in Faisalabad with 450 employees.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the employees of Lyallpur Spinning Ltd are interested in the company's financial statements.
parts.answer: To judge job security (is the company profitable and able to pay its debts?) and to judge whether the company can afford pay rises or bonuses.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two reasons.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the government (tax authority) is interested in the company's financial statements.
parts.answer: To calculate the corporation tax due on the company's profits and to check that the tax returns are accurate; also for national statistics.
parts.working: 1 mark for tax assessment; 1 mark for check/statistics.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a potential investor would find the latest statement of financial position on its own insufficient.
parts.answer: It shows the position at one date only and historical values; the investor also needs profit trends, cash flows, dividends and future prospects.
parts.working: 1 mark one date/historical; 1 mark needs other information.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem: Maria owns a café in Lima, Peru, employs a manager and rents the premises.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between internal users and external users of financial statements.
parts.answer: Internal users work within the business and run it (owners who manage it, managers); external users are outside the business (lenders, suppliers, customers, government, investors).
parts.working: 1 mark each definition.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two examples of each type of user for a café owned by a sole trader.
parts.answer: Internal: the owner, the café manager. External: the bank, suppliers of food and drink, the tax authority, the landlord, customers.
parts.working: 1 mark each, two internal and two external.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem: A large hospital in Kampala, Uganda, is choosing a supplier of surgical gloves for a five-year contract. One possible supplier is Delta Medical Supplies Ltd.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the hospital is interested in the financial statements of Delta Medical Supplies.
parts.answer: A five-year contract relies on Delta continuing to trade; if Delta fails, supplies of essential items stop and the hospital must find a new supplier at short notice.
parts.working: 1 mark continuity of supply; 1 mark consequence for the hospital.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify two ratios the hospital should examine and explain why each is relevant.
parts.answer: Current/liquid ratio – can Delta pay its debts and keep trading? Profit margin/ROCE – is Delta profitable enough to survive? Gearing – is it at risk from high borrowing? Trade payables days – is Delta paying its own suppliers late (sign of cash problems)?
parts.working: 1 mark each ratio; 1 mark each explanation (two ratios).

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem: Indus Ceramics plc is a public limited company with 12,000 shareholders, most of whom take no part in running the business.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare the information needs of the shareholders and the directors of Indus Ceramics plc.
parts.answer: Shareholders want returns: dividends, EPS, share price, and evidence that directors are managing the company well (stewardship). Directors need detailed information for planning and control: costs by product, budgets, cash forecasts, performance of departments, to make decisions.
parts.working: 2 marks shareholders' needs explained; 2 marks directors' needs explained.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the directors have access to more detailed information than the shareholders.
parts.answer: Directors run the company and receive internal management accounts; published accounts are summarised and some information is commercially sensitive, so it is not released to outsiders (including competitors).
parts.working: 1 mark internal management information; 1 mark summarised/confidential published accounts.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem: Users of financial statements need information that is useful to them.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the meaning of relevance, reliability (faithful representation), comparability and understandability as qualities of useful financial information.
parts.answer: Relevance: information that can affect users' decisions (timely, helps predict/confirm). Reliability: free from material error and bias, complete, a faithful picture. Comparability: prepared consistently so it can be compared over time and with other businesses. Understandability: presented clearly so that a user with reasonable knowledge can understand it.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how relevance and reliability may conflict when a business prepares its financial statements.
parts.answer: Information is most relevant when it is up to date, but producing it quickly may mean using estimates that are less reliable; waiting to check figures improves reliability but makes them less timely.
parts.working: 1 mark timeliness vs accuracy; 1 mark example/explanation.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem: Thar Coal Mining Ltd operates a large open-cast mine in Sindh and is the main employer in the area.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the local community is interested in the financial statements of Thar Coal Mining Ltd.
parts.answer: Employment and income in the area depend on the mine continuing; the community also wants to know whether the company can pay for land restoration and environmental damage (provisions).
parts.working: 1 mark jobs/local economy; 1 mark environmental obligations.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the government is interested in the financial statements of Thar Coal Mining Ltd, other than for taxation.
parts.answer: To monitor a strategically important industry (energy supply), to decide on grants or subsidies, to check compliance with regulations and licence conditions, for national statistics.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two reasons.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two limitations of the published financial statements for these users.
parts.answer: They show financial information only, not environmental or social effects; they are historical and summarised; they do not show the company's future plans in detail.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem: Ravi Foods, a supermarket chain in Lahore, has asked a supplier, Sunflower Oils Ltd, to increase its credit period from 30 to 60 days and to double its credit limit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why Sunflower Oils Ltd would want to see the financial statements of Ravi Foods before agreeing to the request.
parts.answer: Sunflower Oils will be owed money for 60 days; it needs evidence that Ravi Foods can pay (liquidity, cash) and is profitable enough to continue trading, otherwise it risks an irrecoverable debt.
parts.working: 1 mark risk of non-payment; 1 mark need to judge ability to pay.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two other sources of information Sunflower Oils could use before deciding.
parts.answer: Trade references from other suppliers; bank reference; credit rating agency report; Ravi's payment record with Sunflower so far; visits to the premises.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one limitation of using Ravi Foods' financial statements for this decision.
parts.answer: They may be out of date (prepared months after the year end) and show the position on one day, which may have been window dressed; they do not show what will happen in the next 60 days.
parts.working: 1 mark limitation; 1 mark explanation.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem: Atlas Shipping plc is financed by equity of $120 million and 7% loan notes of $60 million. The directors plan to borrow a further $40 million to buy two new ships, which are expected to earn a return of 11% a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss why the shareholders and the loan note holders of Atlas Shipping plc may take different views of the company's plan to borrow a further $40 million.
parts.answer:
Shareholders: higher gearing can raise EPS and returns if the return on the new investment exceeds the interest rate; no dilution of control. But more risk: interest must be paid before dividends, profits become more volatile.
Loan note holders: their security falls as more debt ranks alongside or ahead of them; interest cover falls; higher risk of default; they may want covenants or higher interest. They do not share in extra profits.
Conclusion: shareholders may welcome it if expected returns are high; lenders are likely to oppose it.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for shareholders' view (both sides); up to 3 marks for lenders' view; maximum 6. A conclusion or comparison is needed for full marks.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem:
The workers' union at Kohinoor Footwear Ltd, Sialkot, is studying the company's published statements:
                                  2024        2025
Revenue ($)                  4,200,000   4,800,000
Wages ($)                    1,020,000   1,080,000
Number of employees                125         120
Profit for the year ($)        504,000     640,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate for each year: (i) profit for the year per employee (ii) wages as a percentage of revenue, to two decimal places (iii) average wage per employee.
parts.working: 1 mark each figure.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The union asks for an 8% pay rise for all employees for 2026. Evaluate whether the financial statements support this claim.
parts.answer:
For: profit up 27% (504,000 → 640,000) and profit per employee up from $4,032 to $5,333; wages fell from 24.29% to 22.50% of revenue. Cost of an 8% rise = 1,080,000 × 8% = $86,400, well within the profit increase of $136,000.
Against: average wage already rose 10.3%; past profit does not guarantee future profit; the company may need profit for investment, loan repayment or dividends; liquidity not shown.
Judgement: the figures broadly support a rise, perhaps linked to productivity.
parts.working: 1 mark use of figures for; 1 mark cost of rise calculated ($86,400); 1 mark point against; 1 mark judgement.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem: A finance student in Singapore is preparing for a debate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: "Published financial statements meet the needs of all users." Discuss this statement.
parts.answer:
Support: statements follow IFRS, are audited, consistent and comparable; they give useful common information — profit, assets, liabilities, cash flows — that most users need; notes add detail.
Against: they are general-purpose and cannot meet every user's specific need; historical, published months after the year end; summarised (no product or branch detail for managers); based on historical cost so may not show current values; ignore non-financial factors (staff skills, customer loyalty, environmental impact); some users (e.g. employees, local community) want information not given; complex to understand for non-specialists; may be window dressed.
Conclusion: they meet the basic needs of investors and lenders reasonably well, but other users need extra information (management accounts, forecasts, reports).
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for points in support; up to 4 marks for limitations linked to particular users; 1 mark for reasoned conclusion. Maximum 8.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A business has a current ratio of 1.5 : 1 and a liquid (acid test) ratio of 1.0 : 1. It buys inventory on credit. What is the effect on the two ratios?
A current ratio increases; liquid ratio no change
B current ratio decreases; liquid ratio decreases
C current ratio no change; liquid ratio decreases
D current ratio decreases; liquid ratio no change
parts.answer: B current ratio decreases; liquid ratio decreases
parts.working: Current assets and current liabilities rise by the same amount; because the current ratio is above 1 it moves towards 1, so it falls. Liquid assets are unchanged but current liabilities rise, so the liquid ratio falls. D forgets that current liabilities rise in the liquid ratio.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A business has a current ratio of 2.4 : 1 and a liquid (acid test) ratio of 1.5 : 1. Its current liabilities are $36,000. What is the value of its inventory?
A $32,400
B $54,000
C $86,400
D $18,000
parts.working: Current assets = 2.4 × 36,000 = 86,400; liquid assets = 1.5 × 36,000 = 54,000; inventory = 86,400 − 54,000 = $32,400. B is the liquid assets and C the total current assets.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem:
Kandy Spice Traders, Sri Lanka, provides the following at 31 March 2026:
                                           $
Inventory                             38,600
Trade receivables                     24,150
Other receivables (prepayments)        1,250
Cash in hand                             830
Trade payables                        29,400
Other payables (accruals)              2,100
Bank overdraft                         6,500

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate, to two decimal places: (i) the current ratio (ii) the liquid (acid test) ratio.
parts.working: Each ratio: 1 mark correct totals/method, 1 mark answer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Comment on the liquidity of the business.
parts.answer: The current ratio is below the commonly quoted 2 : 1 and the liquid ratio is well below 1 : 1, so the business could not pay its current liabilities from liquid assets if they fell due now; it relies on selling inventory and on the overdraft.
parts.working: 1 mark comment on each ratio with figure.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem: Hassan is studying two liquidity ratios for his clothing business in Bahawalpur.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between the current ratio and the liquid (acid test) ratio.
parts.answer: The current ratio compares all current assets with current liabilities. The liquid ratio leaves out inventory, comparing only assets that are cash or quickly turned into cash with current liabilities.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why inventory is excluded from the liquid ratio.
parts.answer: Inventory must first be sold (often on credit) and the money collected before it can pay debts; this takes time and its value may be uncertain (obsolete or slow-moving goods).
parts.working: 1 mark not immediately convertible; 1 mark uncertainty of value/time.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a liquid ratio well above 1 : 1 is not necessarily a good sign.
parts.answer: Too much money is tied up in cash and receivables that earn little return; large receivables may mean poor credit control and risk of irrecoverable debts.
parts.working: 1 mark idle funds/low return; 1 mark poor credit control.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem: Al-Hamra Furniture, Muscat, Oman, has these current assets and liabilities at 31 December 2025: inventory $84,000; trade receivables $61,500; bank $22,500; trade payables $41,000; other payables $3,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the working capital and the current ratio (to two decimal places).
parts.working: 1 mark current assets total; 1 mark working capital; 1 mark ratio.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two disadvantages to the business of holding this level of working capital.
parts.answer: Money tied up in inventory and receivables earns no return and could be invested or used to repay borrowing; large inventory risks obsolescence, damage and storage costs; high receivables increase the risk of irrecoverable debts; cash held idle loses value through inflation.
parts.working: 2 marks per disadvantage explained (identify + consequence).

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem: Zarina Pharmacy, Tashkent, Uzbekistan, sells mainly for cash. At 30 September 2026: inventory $52,000; trade receivables $9,800; bank $3,400; trade payables $31,600; other payables $1,400.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the liquid (acid test) ratio, to two decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark method; 1 mark answer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what this ratio shows and whether the pharmacy is necessarily at risk.
parts.answer: For every $1 of current liabilities there is only $0.40 of liquid assets, so the pharmacy cannot meet its short-term debts without selling inventory. Not necessarily at risk: most of its sales are for cash and its inventory sells quickly, so cash comes in daily before suppliers must be paid.
parts.working: 1 mark interpretation with figure; 1 mark risk; 1 mark cash sales / fast-moving inventory.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem:
Fietsen van Dijk, a bicycle retailer in Utrecht, Netherlands:
At 31 December                2024 $      2025 $
Inventory                     40,000      62,000
Trade receivables             35,000      41,000
Bank                           8,000           –
Trade payables                30,000      44,000
Other payables                 2,000       3,000
Bank overdraft                     –       7,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the current ratio and the liquid (acid test) ratio for each year, to two decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark each ratio.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Comment on the change in liquidity between 2024 and 2025.
parts.answer: Both ratios have fallen. The liquid ratio has dropped below 1 : 1, so liquid assets no longer cover current liabilities. The bank balance has turned into an overdraft and trade payables have risen by $14,000, while inventory has risen by $22,000 — money is tied up in inventory. The business may struggle to pay suppliers on time.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three relevant points using figures.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem:
Nile Office Supplies, Cairo, Egypt, has current assets of $60,000 (including inventory of $25,000) and current liabilities of $30,000. Four possible transactions are:
(i) inventory costing $4,000 is sold for $6,000 cash
(ii) $5,000 is paid to trade payables
(iii) a computer is bought for $8,000, paid from the bank
(iv) a five-year bank loan of $10,000 is received.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the current ratio and the liquid (acid test) ratio before any of the transactions, to two decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate both ratios, to two decimal places, after transaction (i) and after transaction (ii). Treat each transaction separately.
parts.working: (i) CA 60,000 − 4,000 + 6,000 = 62,000, inventory 21,000; (ii) CA and CL both fall by 5,000. 1 mark each ratio.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate both ratios, to two decimal places, after transaction (iii) and after transaction (iv). Treat each transaction separately.
parts.working: (iii) CA falls by 8,000 (the computer is a non-current asset); (iv) CA rises by 10,000, CL unchanged (the loan is non-current). 1 mark each ratio.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem:
Extracts from the statements of financial position of two companies ($000):
                           FreshMart     Karakoram
                        supermarkets   Engineering
Inventory                      1,800           900
Trade receivables                100         1,600
Cash and bank                    400           200
Trade payables                 3,100         1,200

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the current ratio and the liquid (acid test) ratio for each business, to two decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why FreshMart can operate safely with much lower liquidity ratios than Karakoram Engineering.
parts.answer: FreshMart sells for cash, so it has almost no receivables and cash comes in every day. Its inventory sells within days. It buys on credit and pays suppliers after it has sold the goods.
