Karakoram sells on credit, holds raw materials and work in progress for long periods and must wait for customers to pay, so it needs a larger cushion.
parts.working: 1 mark each for four points; must compare the two businesses for full marks.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem:
Kwame's printing business in Accra has current assets of $48,000 (including inventory $30,000) and current liabilities of $40,000 (including a bank overdraft of $15,000). He is considering:
A converting the overdraft into a five-year bank loan
B selling a spare delivery van for $9,000 cash.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the current ratio and the liquid (acid test) ratio at present, to two decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate both ratios, to two decimal places, under each proposal.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise Kwame which proposal will do more to improve liquidity. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Proposal A improves both ratios more, and removes the risk of the bank demanding repayment of the overdraft; but it adds a long-term commitment with interest. Proposal B brings in real cash but is a one-off and the van may be needed. Decision with reason, e.g. A.
parts.working: 1 mark comparison using figures; 1 mark justified decision.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem: Lotus Garden Centre, Hanoi, Vietnam, has a current ratio of 1.8 : 1 and a liquid (acid test) ratio of 0.9 : 1. Its inventory is $45,000. Its only liquid assets are trade receivables and cash, and trade receivables are four times the cash balance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the current liabilities and the total current assets.
parts.answer: Inventory = (1.8 − 0.9) × current liabilities, so current liabilities = 45,000 ÷ 0.9 = $50,000. Current assets = 1.8 × 50,000 = $90,000.
parts.working: 1 mark method; 1 mark each figure.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the cash balance and the trade receivables.
parts.answer: Liquid assets = 0.9 × 50,000 = 45,000 = receivables + cash = 5 × cash, so cash = $9,000 and trade receivables = $36,000.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Credit sales for the year were $292,000. Calculate the trade receivables turnover in days.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: d
parts.text: The owner plans to use all the cash to pay trade payables. Calculate both ratios after the payment and comment on the result.
parts.answer: Current 81,000 : 41,000 = 1.98 : 1; liquid 36,000 : 41,000 = 0.88 : 1. The current ratio improves but the liquid ratio falls and there is no cash left to pay day-to-day expenses.
parts.working: 1 mark each ratio; 1 mark comment.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem:
Hilal Steel Ltd has been asked by a new customer, Orion Hardware, Ankara, Turkey, for 60 days' credit. Orion's ratios for the last two years were:
                                2023        2024
Current ratio               2.10 : 1    1.60 : 1
Liquid ratio                1.20 : 1    0.80 : 1
Trade payables (days)             34          48
Orion's statement of financial position at 31 December 2025 showed: inventory $96,000; trade receivables $41,000; cash $2,000; trade payables $112,000; bank overdraft $14,000. Credit purchases for 2025 were $576,000. Revenue has grown each year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate for 2025: (i) the current ratio (ii) the liquid (acid test) ratio, both to two decimal places (iii) the trade payables turnover, to the nearest whole day.
parts.working: 1 mark each for (i) and (ii); 2 marks for (iii) (method, answer).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise Hilal Steel whether to give Orion Hardware a 60-day credit period. Justify your answer.
parts.answer:
Against: both ratios have fallen every year (current 2.10 → 1.10, liquid 1.20 → 0.34); Orion now has an overdraft and very little cash; it is taking 71 days to pay suppliers compared with 34 days in 2023, so it already pays late — a 60-day term may become 90+ days; risk of irrecoverable debt.
For: revenue is growing, so it may become a valuable customer; inventory is high and could be sold; new sales for Hilal Steel.
Other: obtain trade references, set a low credit limit, ask for security, offer shorter terms or cash on delivery.
Decision: do not give 60 days' credit at present, or give a small credit limit on 30 days with close monitoring.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for points against using figures; up to 2 marks for points for; 1 mark for other factors/conditions; 1 mark for clear decision.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem:
Sadia's online kitchenware business in Islamabad has grown quickly:
                            2024 $      2025 $
Revenue                    400,000     640,000
Inventory                   50,000      98,000
Trade receivables           40,000      92,000
Bank (overdraft)            12,000    (38,000)
Trade payables              35,000      71,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the current ratio and the liquid (acid test) ratio for each year, to two decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what is meant by overtrading and why Sadia's business shows signs of it.
parts.answer: Overtrading is expanding sales faster than the working capital available can support. Revenue rose by 60% but inventory almost doubled and receivables more than doubled, the bank balance became an overdraft and payables doubled; liquidity ratios have fallen sharply.
parts.working: 1 mark definition; 2 marks evidence from figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two actions Sadia could take to improve liquidity without stopping growth.
parts.answer: Introduce long-term finance (bank loan or new capital) to fund working capital; tighten credit control or offer cash discounts; reduce inventory levels; use factoring.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A business made credit purchases of $365,000 and cash purchases of $73,000 in the year. Trade payables at the year end were $42,000. What is the trade payables turnover?
A 9 days
B 35 days
C 42 days
D 50 days
parts.answer: C 42 days
parts.working: Use credit purchases only: 42,000 ÷ 365,000 × 365 = 42 days. B (35 days) wrongly uses total purchases of $438,000; A is the number of times (8.69) misread as days.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A trader's revenue for the year was $365,000. All goods are sold at a mark-up of 25% on cost. Opening inventory was $28,000 and closing inventory was $36,000. What is the rate of inventory turnover in days, based on average inventory?
A 32 days
B 40 days
C 43 days
D 45 days
parts.answer: B 40 days
parts.working: Cost of sales = 365,000 × 100/125 = 292,000. Average inventory = (28,000 + 36,000) ÷ 2 = 32,000; 32,000 ÷ 292,000 × 365 = 40 days. A divides by revenue instead of cost of sales; C treats 25% as a margin (cost of sales 273,750, giving 42.7 days); D uses closing inventory only.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem: Chenab Textiles, Faisalabad, had revenue of $960,000 for the year, of which $240,000 was cash sales. Credit purchases were $540,000. At the year end trade receivables were $88,000 and trade payables were $51,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate, to the nearest whole day: (i) the trade receivables turnover (ii) the trade payables turnover.
parts.working: (i) 1 mark credit sales, 1 mark answer; (ii) 1 mark method, 1 mark answer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Comment on the relationship between the two results.
parts.answer: Customers take about 45 days to pay but suppliers are paid in about 34 days, so cash leaves the business 11 days before it comes in; the business must finance the gap (overdraft) and may have cash flow problems.
parts.working: 1 mark comparison with figures; 1 mark consequence for cash.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem: Sahara Tiles, Marrakech, Morocco. For the year ended 31 December 2025: inventory at 1 January $46,500; purchases $371,000; inventory at 31 December $53,500.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of inventory turnover for 2025 (i) in times, to two decimal places (ii) in days, to the nearest whole day.
parts.working: 1 mark cost of sales; 1 mark average inventory; 1 mark each answer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In 2024 inventory turned over 9.10 times. Suggest two reasons for the change and one consequence for the business.
parts.answer: Reasons: buying in larger quantities (bulk discounts); slower sales or a fall in demand; holding a wider range; obsolete items not cleared. Consequence: more cash tied up, higher storage and insurance costs, risk of damage or obsolescence.
parts.working: 1 mark each reason (two); 1 mark consequence.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem: Eduardo's building supplies business in Manila, Philippines, has annual credit sales of $730,000 and customers take on average 60 days to pay. He is considering offering a 2% cash discount for payment within 10 days. He expects customers accounting for half of credit sales to take the discount; the rest would still pay in 60 days. The business has a bank overdraft costing 12% a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the trade receivables at present and the expected trade receivables if the discount is offered.
parts.working: 1 mark present; 1 mark 35 days; 1 mark $70,000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the annual cost of the discount and the annual saving in overdraft interest.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise Eduardo whether to offer the discount. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: On these figures the discount costs $1,300 a year more than it saves. But faster collection may reduce irrecoverable debts and administration, and improve liquidity. Decision, e.g. do not offer 2% — try 1% or tighter credit control instead.
parts.working: 1 mark net cost $1,300; 1 mark non-financial/other point; 1 mark decision.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem: Green Thumb Garden Centre, York, England, has a 31 December year end. Cost of sales was $512,000. Inventory was $22,000 on 1 January and $18,000 on 31 December. The average of the inventory figures at the end of each month was $64,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of inventory turnover in times using (i) the average of opening and closing inventory (ii) the average of the monthly inventory figures. Give answers to one decimal place.
parts.working: 1 mark average 20,000; 1 mark each answer (max 3).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the two results are so different and which is more useful to the owner.
parts.answer: A garden centre is seasonal: inventory is low in December (winter) and high in spring and summer. Year-end figures are not typical, so (i) overstates how fast inventory sells. The monthly average (8 times) better reflects the real position and is more useful.
parts.working: 1 mark seasonal business; 1 mark year-end not representative; 1 mark choice with reason.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem:
Baobab Traders, Dar es Salaam, makes all sales and purchases on credit. For the year ended 30 June 2026:
- trade receivables at 30 June 2026 were $54,000 and the trade receivables turnover was 45 days
- the gross margin was 30%
- the rate of inventory turnover was 8 times, based on average inventory; opening inventory was $36,000
- trade payables at 30 June 2026 were $42,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the credit sales for the year.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the cost of sales.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the closing inventory.
parts.working: 1 mark average; 1 mark closing.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the credit purchases.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Calculate the trade payables turnover, to the nearest whole day.
parts.working: 1 mark method; 1 mark answer.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem: Saffron Motors Components, Pune, India, uses raw materials costing $1,440,000 a year and holds average raw materials inventory of $180,000. A supplier offers a just-in-time (JIT) service that would reduce average inventory to 5 days' usage, but would charge 2% more for all materials. Holding inventory costs 15% of its value a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the present raw materials inventory turnover in days, to one decimal place.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the average inventory under JIT and the annual saving in holding costs, to the nearest $.
parts.working: 1 mark average inventory; 1 mark reduction; 1 mark saving.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the extra annual cost of materials under JIT and the net financial effect.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Advise the directors whether to introduce JIT. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Financially JIT costs about $4,759 more each year, and there is a risk of production stopping if a delivery is late. But there may be other savings (less space, less waste, obsolescence) and a better inventory turnover. Decision, e.g. do not adopt unless the supplier lowers the price or other savings are proven.
parts.working: 1 mark financial/non-financial point; 1 mark justified decision.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem:
Two hotels in Zanzibar, Tanzania, report for 2025:
                              Palm Court  Harbour View
Revenue ($)                    2,400,000     1,950,000
Non-current assets ($)         6,000,000     3,900,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the non-current asset turnover for each hotel, to two decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what the results show.
parts.answer: Harbour View generates $0.50 of revenue for every $1 of non-current assets compared with $0.40 at Palm Court, so it uses its non-current assets more efficiently.
parts.working: 1 mark interpretation; 1 mark comparison.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why Palm Court's non-current asset turnover is lower.
parts.answer: Its buildings may have been revalued recently or are newer (higher carrying amount); lower occupancy; expensive facilities (pool, spa) that add assets but little revenue; it may have bought land for future expansion.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A sole trader's profit for the year was $36,000 after charging loan interest of $4,000. At the year end her capital was $180,000 and she had a long-term loan of $50,000. What is the return on capital employed?
A 15.65%
B 17.39%
C 20.00%
D 22.22%
parts.working: ROCE = (profit for the year + loan interest) ÷ (capital + non-current liabilities) × 100 = 40,000 ÷ 230,000 × 100 = 17.39%. C uses profit ÷ capital only; A forgets to add back the interest.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A business sells all its goods at a mark-up of 25% on cost. Its operating expenses are 12% of revenue and it has no other income. What is its profit margin?
A 8%
B 10.67%
C 13%
D 20%
parts.working: A mark-up of 25% gives a gross margin of 25 ÷ 125 = 20%. Profit margin = 20% − 12% = 8%. C (13%) wrongly subtracts 12% from the mark-up; D is the gross margin.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem: Mwangi Shoes, Nakuru, Kenya, had revenue of $248,000, cost of sales of $161,200 and operating expenses of $59,520 for the year ended 31 December 2025.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate: (i) the gross margin (ii) the profit margin (iii) operating expenses as a percentage of revenue.
parts.working: 1 mark each (gross profit 248,000 − 161,200 = 86,800).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the profit margin is lower than the gross margin.
parts.answer: Gross profit is before operating expenses; the profit margin is after deducting expenses (rent, wages, etc.), which take 24% of revenue.
parts.working: 1 mark expenses deducted; 1 mark link to 24%.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem: Lin's gift shop in Ipoh, Malaysia, adds a mark-up of 40% to the cost of all goods.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between mark-up and gross margin.
parts.answer: Mark-up is gross profit as a percentage of cost of sales; gross margin is gross profit as a percentage of revenue (selling price).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the gross margin, to two decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark method; 1 mark answer.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Cost of sales for the year was $140,000. Calculate the revenue and gross profit.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem: Extract from the financial statements of Galle Fort Hotels Ltd for 2025: profit from operations $456,000; finance costs $48,000; equity $2,400,000; 8% loan notes $600,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the return on capital employed, to two decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark capital employed 3,000,000; 1 mark answer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why profit from operations, rather than profit for the year, is used to calculate the return on capital employed.
parts.answer: Capital employed includes the loan notes; profit before interest (and tax) is the return earned for all providers of that capital, lenders as well as shareholders.
parts.working: 1 mark profit before interest; 1 mark matches capital including loans.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem:
Kestrel Packaging Ltd, Durban, South Africa:
                                2024 $      2025 $
Revenue                      1,500,000   2,100,000
Profit from operations         180,000     210,000
Capital employed             1,200,000   1,750,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate for each year: (i) the profit from operations margin (ii) the asset turnover (revenue ÷ capital employed), to two decimal places (iii) the return on capital employed.
parts.working: 1 mark each figure.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show how the margin and asset turnover combine to give the return on capital employed, and explain why ROCE fell although profit rose.
parts.answer: ROCE = margin × asset turnover: 12% × 1.25 = 15%; 10% × 1.20 = 12%. Profit rose by $30,000 but capital employed rose by $550,000 and each $ of revenue earned less profit, so the return on the extra capital was low.
parts.working: 1 mark relationship shown; 1 mark explanation.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem:
Farhan sells mobile phone accessories in Rawalpindi.
                          2024 $      2025 $
Revenue                  820,000     910,000
Gross profit             295,200     291,200

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the gross margin for each year.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the gross profit Farhan would have made in 2025 if the 2024 gross margin had been maintained, and the shortfall.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest three possible reasons for the fall in gross margin.
parts.answer: Higher purchase prices not passed on; price cuts or discounts to increase sales (revenue rose 11%); change in sales mix towards lower-margin goods; loss or theft of inventory; loss of bulk discounts; closing inventory written down.
parts.working: 1 mark each for three reasons.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem:
Café Saigon, Ho Chi Minh City:
                            2024 $      2025 $
Revenue                    600,000     640,000
Gross profit               210,000     224,000
Wages                       90,000     115,200
Rent                        36,000      38,400
Advertising                 12,000      25,600
Other expenses              30,000      32,000
Profit for the year         42,000      12,800

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the gross margin, each expense as a percentage of revenue and the profit margin for both years.
parts.answer:
Gross margin: 35% both years.
Wages: 15% → 18%
Rent: 6% → 6%
Advertising: 2% → 4%
Other expenses: 5% → 5%
Profit margin: 42,000 ÷ 600,000 = 7% → 12,800 ÷ 640,000 = 2%
parts.working: 1 mark gross margin; 1 mark each expense ratio pair; 1 mark profit margins.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the main causes of the fall in the profit margin and comment on whether the extra advertising was worthwhile.
parts.answer: Gross margin is unchanged, so the fall is in expenses: wages up from 15% to 18% and advertising doubled from 2% to 4% of revenue. Revenue rose only $40,000, adding $14,000 of gross profit, but advertising rose by $13,600 — it barely paid for itself.
parts.working: 1 mark identifies wages and advertising; 1 mark judgement on advertising with figures.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem: Sapphire Glass plc, for the year ended 31 March 2026: revenue $3,200,000; gross profit $1,120,000; distribution costs $310,000; administrative expenses $266,000; finance costs $96,000; tax $112,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate: (i) the gross margin (ii) the profit from operations margin (iii) the margin based on profit for the year.
parts.working: 1 mark (i); 1 mark profit from operations and (ii); 1 mark profit for the year; 1 mark (iii).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a potential lender would focus on the profit from operations margin rather than the profit for the year margin.
parts.answer: Profit from operations is before interest and tax, so it shows the profit available to pay interest; the profit for the year depends on how the company is financed (existing interest) and on tax.
parts.working: 1 mark before interest; 1 mark independent of financing/ability to pay interest.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem: Ruta Furniture, Vilnius, Lithuania, has capital employed of $850,000. The owner wants a return on capital employed of 18% next year. Operating expenses are fixed at $197,000 and the gross margin is 35%. This year's revenue was $880,000. The business has no loans.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit from operations needed to achieve the target return.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the revenue needed to achieve this profit.
parts.working: 1 mark adding expenses; 1 mark dividing by 35%; 1 mark answer.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in revenue needed, to two decimal places, and comment on whether the target is realistic.
parts.answer: (1,000,000 − 880,000) ÷ 880,000 × 100 = 13.64%. A 13.64% rise in one year needs strong demand or price rises; price rises may reduce the margin; costs are unlikely to stay fixed. Possible only with a clear sales plan.
parts.working: 1 mark method; 1 mark answer; 1 mark comment.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem:
Hira makes and sells handmade notebooks in Lahore at $15 each; each costs $9 to make. She sells 24,000 a year and her operating expenses are $96,000.
Option A: cut the price to $13.50; sales would rise to 34,000; delivery costs would add $6,000 to expenses.
Option B: keep the price; spend an extra $18,000 on advertising; sales would rise to 28,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the revenue, gross profit, gross margin, profit and profit margin (to two decimal places) at present and under each option.
parts.answer:
Current: revenue 360,000; gross profit 144,000 (40.00%); profit 48,000 (13.33%)
A: revenue 459,000; gross profit 153,000 (33.33%); profit 51,000 (11.11%)
B: revenue 420,000; gross profit 168,000 (40.00%); profit 54,000 (12.86%)
parts.working: 2 marks for each column (deduct 1 per error).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise Hira which option to choose. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Option B gives the highest profit ($54,000) and keeps the 40% gross margin; Option A raises revenue most but the price cut lowers gross margin to 33.33% and profit to $51,000. Both beat the present $48,000. Risks: B depends on advertising working; A may start a price war. Decision: B.
parts.working: 1 mark comparison of profits; 1 mark risk/other factor; 1 mark decision.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem:
Two similar companies run warehouses near Jebel Ali, Dubai.
Alpha Logistics Ltd: profit from operations $420,000; capital employed $3,500,000. During the year Alpha revalued its property upwards by $1,000,000, which increased the year's depreciation by $25,000.
Beta Storage Ltd: profit from operations $380,000; capital employed $2,000,000. Its property is at historical cost.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the return on capital employed for each company, to two decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Recalculate Alpha's return on capital employed as if the property had not been revalued.
parts.working: 1 mark capital employed; 1 mark profit; 1 mark answer.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain whether Beta is really more profitable than Alpha.
parts.answer: Most of the gap is caused by the revaluation, which raises capital employed and depreciation. On a like-for-like basis Alpha earns 17.80% against Beta's 19.00%, so Beta is still slightly better, but the difference is small. Beta's assets at old historical cost may also flatter its ratio.
parts.working: 1 mark revaluation distorts; 1 mark comparison of adjusted figures; 1 mark conclusion.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A company has issued ordinary shares of $500,000, reserves of $400,000 and 6% loan notes of $300,000. It has no preference shares. What is its gearing ratio?
A 20.00%
B 25.00%
C 33.33%
D 75.00%
parts.working: Gearing = non-current liabilities ÷ (equity + non-current liabilities) × 100 = 300,000 ÷ 1,200,000 = 25.00%. C compares the loan notes with equity only (300 ÷ 900).

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A company's earnings per share are 48 cents and its dividend cover is 3 times. Its share price is $6.00. What is the dividend yield?
A 0.89%
B 2.67%
C 8.00%
D 37.50%
parts.working: Dividend per share = 48 ÷ 3 = 16 cents; yield = 0.16 ÷ 6.00 × 100 = 2.67%. C (8.00%) is the earnings yield (48 ÷ 600).

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem: Mehran Cables plc has 2,500,000 ordinary shares and 5% preference shares. For 2025: profit for the year $860,000; preference dividend paid $60,000; ordinary dividend paid 10 cents per share. The market price of an ordinary share is $4.80.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the earnings per share.
parts.working: 1 mark deducting preference dividend; 1 mark answer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the dividend cover.
parts.working: 1 mark dividend total; 1 mark answer.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the price earnings ratio and the dividend yield (to two decimal places).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the preference dividend is deducted when calculating earnings per share.
parts.answer: Preference dividends must be paid before ordinary shareholders receive anything, so they are not part of the earnings available to ordinary shareholders.
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem: Kalahari Freight Ltd, Gaborone, Botswana, had profit from operations of $285,000 for 2025. Interest on its long-term bank loan was $38,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the interest cover, to two decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark method; 1 mark answer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what interest cover shows to the providers of the company's loan.
parts.answer: How many times the profit before interest could pay the interest due; a high cover means interest is safe even if profits fall.
parts.working: 1 mark meaning; 1 mark safety/risk.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one reason why ordinary shareholders would be concerned if the interest cover fell sharply.
parts.answer: Interest is paid before dividends, so less profit is left for dividends / risk of default could threaten the company.
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem: Taurus Engineering plc has 8% loan notes of $2,000,000 and profit from operations of $720,000. It plans to borrow a further $1,500,000 at 9% a year, which is expected to increase profit from operations by $150,000 a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the present interest cover and income gearing (interest as a percentage of profit from operations), to two decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate both ratios, to two decimal places, if the new loan is taken.
parts.working: 1 mark interest; 1 mark each ratio.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Comment on the change from the point of view of the existing lenders.
parts.answer: Their interest is covered fewer times (4.50 → 2.95) and a third of operating profit now goes on interest, so the risk of default rises if profits fall; they may ask for security or covenants.
parts.working: 1 mark using figures; 1 mark risk.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem:
Xenon Software plc: earnings per share 42 cents; share price $8.40.
Yarrow Brick plc: earnings per share 65 cents; share price $5.85.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the price earnings ratio for each company.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what the difference in the price earnings ratios suggests about how investors view the two companies.
parts.answer: Investors pay $20 for each $1 of Xenon's earnings but only $9 for Yarrow's, so they expect Xenon's earnings to grow faster or consider it lower risk; Yarrow may be seen as having poor prospects or high risk, or may be undervalued.
parts.working: 1 mark meaning of P/E; 1 mark Xenon expectations; 1 mark Yarrow.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one limitation of using the price earnings ratio to choose between the two companies.
parts.answer: Share prices change daily / EPS is based on past profit / the companies are in different industries with different typical P/E ratios.
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem: Orchid Pharma plc has 6,000,000 ordinary shares of $1 each. Profit attributable to ordinary shareholders is $1,500,000 a year and is expected to stay the same. The share price is $3.50. The directors make a bonus issue of 1 new share for every 4 held.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the earnings per share before and after the bonus issue.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the expected share price after the bonus issue and show that the price earnings ratio is unchanged.
parts.working: 1 mark price; 1 mark P/E both.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The directors intend to keep the dividend at 10 cents per share. Calculate the dividend cover before and after the bonus issue and comment.
parts.answer: Before: dividends 600,000; cover 1,500,000 ÷ 600,000 = 2.50. After: dividends 750,000; cover 2.00. Shareholders receive 25% more dividend in total, but less profit is retained and cover falls, so the dividend is less safe if profits fall.
parts.working: 1 mark each cover; 1 mark comment.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem: Cedar Bay Resorts plc has 4,000,000 ordinary shares; equity of $3,200,000; 10% loan notes of $1,200,000; and surplus cash of $1,500,000 that earns no interest. Profit from operations is $640,000 a year. Tax is 25% of profit after interest. The directors propose to use $1,200,000 of the cash to repay the loan notes now. Capital employed = equity + loan notes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate, before and after the repayment: (i) the gearing ratio (ii) the interest cover (iii) the return on capital employed (iv) the earnings per share (in cents). Give answers to two decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark each pair; 2 marks for EPS (1 each).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise the directors whether to repay the loan notes now. Justify your answer.
parts.answer:
For: EPS rises by 2.25 cents, ROCE rises, no gearing so lower financial risk, saves $120,000 interest a year.
Against: uses $1.2m of the $1.5m cash, leaving little for emergencies or investment; cheaper to keep the loan if the cash could earn more than 10% in the business; may need to borrow again later at a higher rate.
Decision, e.g. repay because the cash is idle and the loan costs 10%.
parts.working: 1 mark each for points for and against (max 3); 1 mark for decision.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem:
Mehwish owns a bakery in Quetta. Her ratios and the industry averages for 2025 are:
                             Mehwish  Industry
Gross margin                     42%       38%
Profit margin                     9%       12%
Current ratio                1.4 : 1   1.8 : 1
Trade receivables (days)          12        10
Inventory turnover (days)          3         4

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two ratios in which Mehwish's bakery performs better than the industry average and two in which it performs worse.
parts.answer:
Better: gross margin (42% compared with 38%); inventory turnover (3 days compared with 4 days — inventory sells faster, important for fresh bread).
Worse: profit margin (9% compared with 12%); current ratio (1.4 : 1 compared with 1.8 : 1, weaker liquidity); trade receivables (12 days compared with 10 days, customers pay more slowly).
parts.working: 1 mark each for two better and two worse ratios, with figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the profit margin is below the industry average even though the gross margin is above it.
parts.answer: Expenses are a larger share of revenue (42 − 9 = 33% compared with 38 − 12 = 26%), e.g. higher rent, wages or energy costs.
parts.working: 1 mark expenses higher; 1 mark figures.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem: Ibrahim's grocery shop in Jhelum has capital employed of $250,000 and made a profit of $32,000 last year. He works full time in the shop and takes no salary. A supermarket has offered him a job as a manager at $24,000 a year. He could sell the shop for $250,000 and invest the money at 6% a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the return on capital employed for Ibrahim's shop, to two decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total annual income Ibrahim would receive if he sold the shop for $250,000, invested the money and took the job.
parts.working: 1 mark interest; 1 mark total.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise Ibrahim whether to sell the shop. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Financially, selling gives $39,000 compared with $32,000 profit — $7,000 more, with less risk and fixed hours. But he would lose independence; the shop's profit could grow; the price may not be achieved; the bank rate could fall; job security is not certain. Decision with reason.
parts.working: 1 mark comparison using figures; 2 marks non-financial / other factors; 1 mark decision.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem:
Amara wants to buy a pharmacy in Lagos, Nigeria. Two are for sale:
                                Shop P      Shop Q
Asking price ($)               300,000     220,000
Profit 2023 ($)                 52,000      24,600
Profit 2024 ($)                 49,000      27,500
Profit 2025 ($)                 45,000      30,800
Current assets ($)              58,000      51,000
Current liabilities ($)         40,000      25,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate for each shop: (i) the return on the asking price (profit ÷ price × 100) (ii) the current ratio, to two decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise Amara which shop she should buy. Justify your answer.
parts.answer:
Shop P: higher return now (15% vs 14%) and higher absolute profit, but profits have fallen for three years and liquidity is weaker; costs $80,000 more.
Shop Q: slightly lower return, but profits are rising and liquidity is stronger; cheaper, leaving her $80,000 for other uses; if the trend continues Q's return will soon exceed P's.
Decision, e.g. Shop Q because its trend and liquidity are better and it is cheaper.
parts.working: 2 marks points for P; 2 marks points for Q; 1 mark decision.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem: Blue Mosque Carpets Ltd, Istanbul, has profit from operations of $360,000 and capital employed of $2,000,000. It is considering a new branch that would cost $250,000, financed by a bank loan at 10% a year. The branch is expected to have revenue of $400,000 a year at a gross margin of 30%, and operating expenses of $85,000 a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the expected annual profit from operations of the new branch.
parts.working: 1 mark gross profit; 1 mark answer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the return on capital employed of the branch, and of the whole company after the expansion, to two decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark branch; 1 mark each for company figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise the directors whether to open the branch. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: The branch returns 14% — above the 10% loan interest, so it adds $10,000 to profit after interest, but below the present 18%, so company ROCE falls. Gearing rises. First-year forecasts may be optimistic, but a new branch may grow and build the brand. Decision with reason.
parts.working: 1 mark financial comparison; 1 mark other factor; 1 mark decision.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem:
Andean Textiles, Arequipa, Peru, asks its bank to increase its overdraft limit. The bank has these ratios:
                                      2023        2024
Return on capital employed          18.50%      15.20%
Current ratio                     1.90 : 1    1.50 : 1
Trade receivables (days)                38          46
For 2025: profit from operations $84,000; capital employed $700,000; current assets $210,000; current liabilities $175,000; trade receivables $79,000; credit sales $497,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate for 2025: (i) the return on capital employed (ii) the current ratio, to two decimal places (iii) the trade receivables turnover, to the nearest whole day.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise the bank whether to increase the overdraft limit from $40,000 to $90,000. Justify your answer.
parts.answer:
Against: ROCE has fallen each year (18.5% → 15.2% → 12.0%); the current ratio has fallen from 1.90 to 1.20; customers now take 58 days instead of 38, suggesting weak credit control or customers in difficulty; the request may be to cover poor cash management rather than growth; risk of non-repayment.
For: the business is still profitable; ROCE of 12% is above typical overdraft rates; a larger overdraft may help it through a temporary problem; assets may give security.
Conditions: ask for a cash budget, security over property, a plan to collect receivables faster, a lower increase.
Decision: e.g. refuse the full increase; offer a smaller increase with security and conditions.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks against, up to 2 marks for, 1 mark conditions/other information, 1 mark decision.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem:
Faisal holds shares in Golden Crescent plc, which has 10,000,000 ordinary shares in issue.
                                      2024        2025
Profit for the year ($)          4,200,000   3,600,000
Ordinary dividends paid ($)      2,000,000   2,400,000
Share price at year end ($)           5.04        4.20
Gearing                                22%         41%

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate for each year: (i) earnings per share (ii) dividend per share (iii) dividend cover (iv) dividend yield, to two decimal places (v) price earnings ratio, to two decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark for each ratio for both years.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise Faisal whether to buy more shares in Golden Crescent plc. Justify your answer.
parts.answer:
For: higher dividend (24c) and yield (5.71%) — attractive for income; share price has fallen, so shares are cheaper.
Against: EPS has fallen 14%; dividend was raised while profit fell, so it is now covered only 1.5 times and two-thirds of profit is paid out; it may not be sustainable; gearing has nearly doubled to 41%, increasing risk; falling share price shows the market's concern; P/E fell slightly.
Other: compare with other companies, find reasons for falling profit, Faisal's attitude to risk.
Decision, e.g. do not buy more until profits recover and gearing falls.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for, up to 3 marks against, 1 mark other information, 1 mark decision.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem: Grace is using ratio analysis to review her grocery business in Kingston, Jamaica.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three limitations of ratio analysis.
parts.answer: Any three of: based on historical information; ignores inflation; different accounting policies between businesses; year-end figures may not be typical (seasonal, window dressing); ignores non-financial factors; ratios show symptoms not causes; different definitions of ratios; businesses of different size or industry are hard to compare.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one of the limitations you have stated.
parts.answer: e.g. Ratios use past figures; conditions such as competition or costs may change, so past ratios may not predict future performance.
parts.working: 1 mark statement; 1 mark consequence for users.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem: A student is comparing the financial statements of businesses in Doha, Qatar.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why comparing the ratios of a jeweller with those of a supermarket is of limited use.
parts.answer: Businesses in different industries have very different typical ratios: a jeweller has a high gross margin and slow inventory turnover, a supermarket a low margin and fast turnover; differences reflect the industry, not efficiency.
parts.working: 1 mark different industries have different norms; 1 mark example.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the use of historical cost can make ratios misleading.
parts.answer: Assets bought long ago are shown at old cost less depreciation, so capital employed is understated and ROCE overstated compared with a business with new assets; values do not reflect current prices.
parts.working: 1 mark old values; 1 mark effect on ratio.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why ratios on their own do not explain why performance has changed.
parts.answer: Ratios show what has changed (e.g. margin fell) but not the cause; further investigation of the underlying records and business events is needed.
parts.working: 1 mark symptoms not causes; 1 mark need for further investigation.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem: On 30 June 2026 Diaz Auto Parts, Santiago, Chile, had current assets of $90,000 (including bank $34,000) and current liabilities of $60,000. On 30 June, the last day of its financial year, it paid $30,000 to suppliers from the bank.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by window dressing.
parts.answer: Arranging transactions just before the year end so that the financial statements look better than the normal position, e.g. paying suppliers or delaying purchases to improve ratios.
parts.working: 1 mark meaning; 1 mark example.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the current ratio before and after the payment.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the ratio after the payment may mislead a lender.
parts.answer: The improvement is temporary; the business has the same net working capital ($30,000) and less cash; in the new year it will buy on credit again and the ratio will fall back.
parts.working: 1 mark same working capital/less cash; 1 mark temporary.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem: Tomasz calculates that his bakery in Kraków, Poland, had a gross margin of 46% in 2025.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a single year's ratio is of limited use on its own.
parts.answer: A ratio has no meaning unless it is compared with something: one figure cannot show whether performance is good or bad, improving or getting worse.
parts.working: 1 mark need comparison; 1 mark cannot judge trend/standard.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State three bases with which Tomasz could compare his ratios.
parts.answer: Previous years of the same business (trends); other businesses in the same industry; industry averages; budgeted or target ratios.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem: Ali & Sons, Peshawar, had profit from operations of $96,000 for 2025. Capital employed was $520,000 at the start of the year and $680,000 at the end.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the return on capital employed using (i) closing capital employed (ii) average capital employed. Give answers to two decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark (i); 1 mark average; 1 mark (ii).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why ratios must be calculated in the same way when businesses or years are compared.
parts.answer: Different definitions give different results (here 14.12% vs 16.00%), so differences could come from the method rather than real performance.
parts.working: 1 mark different results; 1 mark misleading comparison.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem: Mint Ltd and Sage Ltd, two identical courier companies in Kuala Lumpur, each bought delivery equipment costing $200,000 at the start of the year. Each made a profit before depreciation of $150,000 and has other net assets of $300,000. Mint uses straight-line depreciation at 20% a year; Sage uses reducing balance at 30% a year. Capital employed = other net assets + carrying amount of the equipment.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the depreciation charge, profit from operations and return on capital employed (to two decimal places) for each business for the first year.
parts.working: 1 mark each depreciation; 1 mark each profit; 1 mark each ROCE.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what this shows about comparing ratios of different businesses.
parts.answer: The businesses are identical but Mint appears more profitable only because of its depreciation policy; differences in accounting policies distort comparisons, so users must read the notes.
parts.working: 1 mark difference caused by policy; 1 mark need to check policies.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem: The owner of a shoe shop in Colombo says sales are growing: revenue was $500,000 in 2024 and $540,000 in 2025. General prices rose by 10% over the year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in revenue in money terms.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the 2025 revenue in 2024 prices, to the nearest $, and the real percentage change, to two decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark method; 1 mark revenue in 2024 prices; 1 mark real change (a fall).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the owner's claim may be misleading.
parts.answer: Prices rose by 10%, so the 8% rise in money revenue is a real fall of about 1.82% — fewer goods were sold. Financial statements and ratios are not adjusted for inflation.
parts.working: 1 mark real fall; 1 mark statements not adjusted for inflation.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem:
Rana Opticians, Lahore, has two branches. For 2025:
                          Mall $  Old Town $
Revenue                  600,000     400,000
Gross profit             240,000      60,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the gross margin of each branch and of the business as a whole.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how ratios calculated from the totals for the whole business could mislead the owner.
parts.answer: The overall 30% looks acceptable but hides a very weak Old Town branch earning only 15%; totals combine different activities, so the owner may not see where the problem is and fail to act (e.g. investigate pricing or theft at Old Town).
parts.working: 1 mark averages hide differences; 1 mark using figures; 1 mark consequence for decisions.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem: An investor in Mauritius is considering buying a beach hotel. The hotel's ratios for the last three years are strong.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify four non-financial factors that ratio analysis would not reveal about the hotel.
parts.answer: Any four: customer satisfaction and online reviews; quality and morale of staff; location and access; reputation/brand; condition of the building beyond its carrying amount; environmental and safety record; new competitors opening nearby; quality of management.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why these factors are important to the buyer.
parts.answer: They affect future revenue and costs; for example poor reviews or a new competitor could reduce future occupancy and profit even though current ratios look good.
parts.working: 1 mark link to future performance; 1 mark example.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem: Ocean Fresh Seafoods, Gwadar, had revenue of $1,250,000 in 2025 and a profit for the year of $145,000. This profit included a profit of $60,000 on the sale of a plot of land.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit margin for 2025 (i) as reported (ii) excluding the profit on disposal. Give answers to two decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Comment on the trend in the profit margin, given that it was 7.50% in 2024.
parts.answer: The reported margin suggests a rise from 7.50% to 11.60%, but the underlying margin fell to 6.80%; the improvement comes from a one-off gain that will not be repeated.
parts.working: 1 mark underlying fall; 1 mark one-off item explanation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why one-off items limit the usefulness of ratio analysis.
parts.answer: They distort the year's figures, so trends and comparisons are misleading unless the item is identified and removed; users may not find them if the statements are summarised.
parts.working: 1 mark distort trends; 1 mark need adjustment.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem: An investor in Johannesburg is reading the published financial statements of a company listed on the stock exchange.

parts.label: a
parts.text: "Ratio analysis tells a potential investor everything she needs to know before buying shares in a company." Discuss this statement.
parts.answer:
Usefulness: ratios summarise large amounts of data; allow comparison over time and with other companies; investment ratios (EPS, P/E, dividend yield and cover) and gearing give direct information about returns and risk; profitability and liquidity show strength.
Limitations: historical; affected by accounting policies, window dressing and one-off items; ignore inflation; year-end may be unrepresentative; differences in size and industry; ignore non-financial factors (management quality, market position, innovation, economic and political conditions); share price reflects expectations not in the statements; ratios show symptoms not causes.
Conclusion: useful starting point, but the investor also needs forecasts, directors' reports, market information and non-financial factors.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for uses; up to 4 marks for limitations explained; 1 mark for conclusion. Maximum 8.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem:
Two supermarket companies in Nairobi each have revenue of $1,500,000 and profit of $300,000 before premises costs.
Leaseway Ltd rents its premises for $90,000 a year; its capital employed is $800,000.
Ownhome Ltd owns its premises (carrying amount $1,200,000, depreciation $30,000 a year); its capital employed is $2,000,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit from operations, the profit from operations margin and the return on capital employed for each company, to two decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark each profit; 1 mark each pair of ratios.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the ratios give a misleading picture of which company is better managed.
parts.answer: The trading performance is identical; the difference arises only because Leaseway rents premises (rent expense, no asset) while Ownhome owns them (depreciation, large asset in capital employed). Leaseway looks better on ROCE, Ownhome on margin. Different ways of financing and holding assets distort comparisons; Ownhome also gains from any rise in property value, which the ratios ignore.
parts.working: 1 mark identical trading; 1 mark explanation of rent vs ownership; 1 mark each ratio affected differently; 1 mark further point.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem: Bilal runs an electrical shop in Sukkur as a sole trader. Revenue $900,000; profit for the year $108,000. He takes no salary. A competitor, Zest Electricals Ltd, had revenue of $950,000 and profit from operations of $76,000 after paying its managing director a salary of $40,000. Bilal says his business is more profitable.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit margin of each business, to two decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Recalculate Bilal's profit margin after charging a notional salary equal to that paid to Zest's director.
parts.working: 1 mark adjusted profit; 1 mark answer.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Evaluate Bilal's claim that his business is more profitable than Zest Ltd.
parts.answer: On reported figures Bilal's margin is 4 points higher, but a sole trader's profit includes the reward for the owner's work; after a $40,000 salary his margin falls to 7.56%, below Zest's 8.00%. His claim is not supported; other differences (rent, size, accounting policies) should also be checked.
parts.working: 1 mark reported comparison; 1 mark adjusted comparison; 1 mark judgement.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Analysis and communication of accounting information
stem: Pearl River Bakeries Ltd, Guangzhou, China, had revenue of $2,000,000 in 2025 and a profit from operations margin of 12%. Capital employed is $1,500,000. A large competitor has opened nearby; the directors forecast that in 2026 revenue will fall by 15% and the margin will fall to 10%. Capital employed will not change.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit from operations and the return on capital employed for 2025 and for the 2026 forecast, to two decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark each figure.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss the limitations of using last year's ratios to judge the company's future performance.
parts.answer: Ratios are based on past results; the new competitor will change revenue and margins (forecast ROCE falls by 4.67 points). External factors (economy, exchange rates, costs) change; the forecast itself is an estimate. Ratios ignore management plans to respond. Use with forecasts and market information.
parts.working: 1 mark historical; 1 mark use of figures; 1 mark external changes; 1 mark conclusion.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Partnership or sole trader acquired by a company
stem:
On 1 May 2025 Quail Ltd bought the business of Nadia and Omar, partners trading in Islamabad. Quail Ltd took over these assets and liabilities at the agreed values shown:
                                  $
Premises                    140,000
Fixtures and fittings        22,000
Inventory                    18,600
Trade receivables            12,400
Trade payables               (9,800)
Bank loan                   (25,000)
The purchase consideration was settled by: $30,000 paid from Quail Ltd's bank account; 80,000 ordinary shares of $1 each issued at $1.25 per share; and $40,000 of 6% debentures issued to the partners.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the business purchase account in the books of Quail Ltd.
parts.answer:
Business purchase account
Dr: Premises 140,000; Fixtures and fittings 22,000; Inventory 18,600; Trade receivables 12,400; Goodwill 11,800 = 204,800
Cr: Trade payables 9,800; Bank loan 25,000; Vendors – Nadia and Omar 170,000 = 204,800
parts.working: Purchase consideration = 30,000 + (80,000 × 1.25) 100,000 + 40,000 = 170,000 (B1). Net assets = 158,200 (M1). Goodwill = 170,000 − 158,200 = 11,800 (A1). Assets debited (B1), liabilities and vendors credited (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare the vendors' account in the books of Quail Ltd to show how the consideration was settled.
parts.answer:
Vendors (Nadia and Omar) account
Dr: Bank 30,000; Ordinary share capital 80,000; Share premium 20,000; 6% debentures 40,000 = 170,000
Cr: Business purchase 170,000
parts.working: B1 bank; B1 share capital 80,000 and share premium 20,000 shown separately; B1 debentures and totals agree.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the annual debenture interest Quail Ltd must now pay, and explain one effect of the debenture issue on Quail Ltd's gearing.
parts.answer: 40,000 × 6% = $2,400 a year. Gearing rises because long-term borrowing (debentures) increases relative to equity, so fixed interest must be paid before any dividend.
parts.working: B1 interest 2,400; B1 explanation of higher gearing.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A pharmacy in Hyderabad, Sindh, is for sale. Its average annual profit is $72,000 and its net assets have a fair value of $520,000. A normal rate of return for a pharmacy business is 10% of net assets. The buyer agrees to value goodwill at three years' purchase of the super profit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the normal profit expected on the net assets.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the super profit.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the value of goodwill and the total price for the pharmacy.
parts.answer: Goodwill $60,000; price $580,000

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why goodwill is based on super profit rather than total profit in this method.
parts.answer: The buyer could earn the normal return just by investing the same amount in similar net assets; only profit above that normal return is due to the business's reputation, location and customers, so only that excess is paid for as goodwill.
parts.working: 1 mark normal return available anyway; 1 mark goodwill = earnings above normal.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Lotus Ltd, Dubai, bought the business of a sole trader. The fair value of the net assets taken over was $160,000. Lotus Ltd paid: $45,000 in cash; 120,000 ordinary shares of $0.50 each, issued at $0.80 per share; and $30,000 of 8% debentures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total purchase consideration.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the increase in Lotus Ltd's ordinary share capital and in its share premium account.
parts.answer: Share capital $60,000; share premium $36,000

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the goodwill arising on the purchase.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Mango Ltd, Multan, bought the business of a sole trader who wished to retire quickly. Mango Ltd paid $210,000 in cash. The fair value of the identifiable net assets taken over was $224,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the difference between the purchase consideration and the fair value of the net assets, and state what this difference is called.
parts.answer: $14,000; negative goodwill (a gain on a bargain purchase)
parts.working: 224,000 − 210,000 = 14,000 (B1); named as negative goodwill / bargain purchase (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how Mango Ltd should treat this amount in its financial statements.
parts.answer: Mango Ltd first re-checks that the fair values of the assets and liabilities are correct; any remaining amount is recognised immediately as a gain in the statement of profit or loss.
parts.working: 1 mark reassess fair values; 1 mark gain in profit or loss immediately (not shown as an asset).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why the sole trader accepted less than the fair value of the net assets.
parts.answer: Any two: wanted a quick sale to retire; saves time and cost of selling assets one by one; poor recent profits; ill health; no family member to take over; needs cash now.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Neem Ltd is buying a garment business in Sialkot. The directors list the following things that make the business valuable:
1 a registered trademark for the business's school uniforms
2 a loyal group of regular customers who return every year
3 a highly skilled and experienced workforce
4 a patent for a stain-resistant fabric treatment
5 a convenient location close to several large schools

parts.label: a
parts.text: State, for each item 1 to 5, whether Neem Ltd would record it as a separate identifiable asset or whether it forms part of goodwill.
parts.answer: 1 separate identifiable (intangible) asset; 2 part of goodwill; 3 part of goodwill; 4 separate identifiable (intangible) asset; 5 part of goodwill
parts.working: 1 mark each. Trademarks and patents are legal rights that can be separately identified and valued; customer loyalty, the workforce and location cannot be separated from the business, so they are part of goodwill.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define goodwill.
parts.answer: The amount by which the value of a business as a whole exceeds the fair value of its identifiable net assets.

author: HomiLabs

stem: On 1 January 2023 Olive Ltd recorded purchased goodwill of $60,000 when it bought a bakery in Lahore. Annual impairment reviews found impairment losses of $7,500 at 31 December 2023 and $4,000 at 31 December 2024. At 31 December 2025 the recoverable amount of the bakery had risen and was well above its carrying amount.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the carrying amount of goodwill at 31 December 2024.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the effect of the 2024 impairment loss on the profit for 2024.
parts.answer: Profit for the year is reduced by $4,000 (an expense in the statement of profit or loss).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State, with a reason, whether Olive Ltd may reverse the earlier impairment losses at 31 December 2025.
parts.answer: No. An impairment loss on goodwill can never be reversed, because any rise in value would be internally generated goodwill, which may not be recognised.
parts.working: B1 no; B1 reason (internally generated goodwill not recognised).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Rehana runs a hardware business in Quetta. Her statement of financial position at 31 August 2025 showed:
                                  $
Premises                    110,000
Equipment                    26,000
Inventory                    19,500
Trade receivables            16,000
Bank                          7,200
Trade payables              (11,400)
Bank loan                   (30,000)
On that date Saffron Ltd bought the business. Rehana kept the bank balance and repaid the bank loan herself. The remaining assets and liabilities were taken over, with these adjustments:
• premises revalued at $134,000 and equipment at $21,500
• inventory costing $2,300 was found to be damaged and worthless
• an allowance for irrecoverable debts of 5% is to be made on trade receivables
Saffron Ltd paid by issuing 150,000 ordinary shares of $1 each at $1.40 per share.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the value of the net assets taken over by Saffron Ltd.
parts.working: Premises 134,000 + equipment 21,500 (B1) + inventory 17,200 (B1) + receivables 16,000 × 95% = 15,200 (B1) − payables 11,400 = 176,500 (A1). Bank and loan excluded.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the goodwill on the purchase.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the increase in Saffron Ltd's share capital and share premium.
parts.answer: Share capital $150,000; share premium $60,000
parts.working: B1 each.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Daniyal is selling his printing business in Karachi. He has two offers:
Offer A: $250,000 in cash. Daniyal would deposit the cash in a bank account paying 5% interest a year.
Offer B: from Falcon Ltd, 160,000 ordinary shares of $1 each valued at $1.50 per share, plus $40,000 of 9% debentures. Falcon Ltd has paid a dividend of $0.12 per share for each of the last three years.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total value of Offer B.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate Daniyal's expected annual income from each offer.
parts.answer: Offer A $12,500; Offer B $22,800

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise Daniyal which offer he should accept. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: For B: higher value ($30,000 more) and higher income ($10,300 more); shares may rise in value; debenture interest is secure. Against B: dividends are not guaranteed and share price may fall; shares may be hard to sell if Falcon is a private company; risk concentrated in one company; cash gives certainty and flexibility. Decision with reason, e.g. accept B if he can accept the risk and does not need cash now.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for points for B, up to 2 for points against/for A (using figures), 1 mark for a justified decision.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Ivy Ltd plans to buy a sole trader's café in Kuala Lumpur. The café's average annual profit is $66,000, but the owner has never charged a salary for his own work. Ivy Ltd would have to employ a manager at $18,000 a year. Ivy Ltd expects a return of 12% a year on businesses of this kind. The fair value of the café's net assets is $345,000. Goodwill is to be valued by capitalising the maintainable profit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the maintainable profit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the value of the whole business by capitalising the maintainable profit at 12%.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the value of goodwill.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the manager's salary is deducted before valuing the business.
parts.answer: Ivy Ltd will have to pay a manager, so the profit it will actually earn is lower; using the owner's profit without a salary would overstate the profit and the price.
parts.working: 1 mark cost the buyer will bear; 1 mark otherwise value overstated.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Hazel Ltd agreed a purchase consideration of $288,000 for a partnership business in Peshawar. $48,000 was paid by cheque and the rest by issuing ordinary shares of $0.50 each at $1.60 per share.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of shares issued.
parts.answer: 150,000 shares

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the amounts credited to the share capital and share premium accounts.
parts.answer: Share capital $75,000; share premium $165,000

parts.label: c
parts.text: Prepare the journal entry in Hazel Ltd's books to record the settlement of the consideration. A narrative is not required.
parts.answer: Dr Vendors (partnership) 288,000; Cr Bank 48,000; Cr Ordinary share capital 75,000; Cr Share premium 165,000
parts.working: B1 debit vendors; B1 credit bank; B1 credits to share capital and share premium.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Jasmine Ltd's profit from operations is $180,000 a year on capital employed of $1,200,000. It is considering buying a sole trader's business for $300,000 (net assets $240,000 and goodwill $60,000), paid by issuing shares. The business is expected to add $39,000 a year to Jasmine Ltd's profit from operations.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Jasmine Ltd's return on capital employed before the purchase.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the expected return on capital employed after the purchase, and the return on the purchase price of the new business.
parts.answer: After: 14.60%; on the new business: 13.00%

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise the directors whether they should buy the business. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Against: return on the purchase (13%) is below the existing 15%, so overall ROCE falls to 14.60%; goodwill of $60,000 may be impaired; new shares dilute control. For: profit rises by $39,000; possible synergies or cost savings not in forecast; removes a competitor; growth and market share. Decision justified.
parts.working: 1 mark each side using figures, 1 mark non-financial point, 1 mark justified decision.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Larkspur Ltd is negotiating to buy the business of Waleed, a sole trader in Rawalpindi. Waleed's reported profits were:
Year ended 30 June      Profit $
2023                      61,000
2024                      54,500
2025                      70,000
Further information:
1 Waleed has never charged himself a salary. Larkspur Ltd will employ a manager at $20,000 a year.
2 The 2024 profit is after a one-off loss of $7,500 caused by a flood; this will not happen again.
3 The 2025 profit includes rent received of $4,000 from sub-letting part of the premises; the sub-letting ends when the business is sold.
Goodwill is to be valued at 2.5 years' purchase of the average adjusted profit. The agreed value of the net assets is $292,500. The consideration is to be paid 25% in cash and the rest in ordinary shares of $1 each issued at $2.50 per share.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the adjusted profit for each year and the average adjusted profit.
parts.working: Deduct 20,000 each year (B1); add back 7,500 in 2024 (B1); deduct 4,000 in 2025 (B1); average 129,000 ÷ 3 = 43,000 (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the goodwill and the total purchase consideration.
parts.answer: Goodwill $107,500; consideration $400,000

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the number of shares issued and the share premium created.
parts.answer: 120,000 shares; share premium $180,000

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the rent received is removed from the 2025 profit.
parts.answer: Goodwill should reflect profits the buyer can expect to keep earning (maintainable profit). The rent will stop, so including it would overstate future profit and the price.
parts.working: 1 mark maintainable/future profit; 1 mark overstatement.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
On 1 March 2025 Banyan Ltd, Colombo, bought a partnership business. It paid $34,000 in cash and issued 90,000 ordinary shares of $1 each; the market price of a Banyan Ltd share on that date was $2.40. The fair value of the identifiable net assets acquired was $228,500.
Banyan Ltd also paid legal and due-diligence fees of $6,500 for the purchase, and $2,800 of costs for issuing the new shares. Before the purchase the share premium account had a balance of $40,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the goodwill arising on the purchase.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the balance on the share premium account after the purchase.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State how the legal and due-diligence fees are treated, and their effect on profit for the year.
parts.answer: They are acquisition costs, charged as an expense in the statement of profit or loss (not added to goodwill); profit for the year falls by $6,500.
parts.working: B1 expense, not goodwill; B1 profit reduced by 6,500.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the directors might have preferred to add the fees to goodwill.
parts.answer: Adding them to goodwill would avoid reducing this year's profit (and EPS); the cost would only reach profit later if goodwill were impaired. This is not allowed because the fees are not part of the value of the business acquired.
parts.working: 1 mark higher reported profit; 1 mark reason not allowed.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Cypress Ltd expects a return of at least 12% a year on the price it pays for any business. It is choosing between two businesses for sale in Faisalabad:
                                 Business X    Business Y
                                          $             $
Asking price                       380,000       300,000
Fair value of net assets           320,000       290,000
Expected annual profit              52,000        33,000
Business X has a well-known brand and a long-term supply contract with a supermarket chain. Business Y owns modern machinery but its two largest customers are reviewing their contracts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the goodwill included in each asking price.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the expected return on the asking price for each business, to two decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise the directors which business, if either, they should buy. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: X: return 13.68% exceeds the 12% target; brand and supermarket contract support future profit; but goodwill of $60,000 is high and may be impaired. Y: return 11.00% is below target; goodwill is low and price is mostly backed by tangible assets (lower risk of loss); but risk of losing key customers could cut profit further. Other factors: finance available, fit with existing business, reliability of forecasts. Decision: buy X (meets target, stronger future prospects) – or a justified alternative.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks on X, up to 2 marks on Y using figures, 1 mark other factor, 1 mark justified decision.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
The owner of a private school in Abbottabad is selling the business to Elm Education Ltd. The school's profits, after charging a fair salary for the head teacher, were:
Year      Profit $   Weight
2023        50,000        1
2024        56,000        2
2025        62,000        3
The agreed value of the net assets is $400,000. A normal return for this kind of business is 11% a year. Elm Education Ltd proposes to value goodwill at 2.5 years' purchase of the super profit, based on the weighted average profit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the weighted average profit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the super profit and the goodwill proposed by Elm Education Ltd.
parts.answer: Super profit $14,000; goodwill $35,000

parts.label: c
parts.text: The owner is asking $460,000 for the school. Calculate how many years' purchase of super profit this price implies, to two decimal places.
parts.answer: 4.29 years
parts.working: Goodwill in asking price 460,000 − 400,000 = 60,000 (M1); ÷ 14,000 = 4.29 years (A1).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why a weighted average is used, and one reason why the owner may argue for a higher number of years' purchase.
parts.answer: Weighting gives more importance to recent profits, which better predict future profit when profits are rising. Owner's argument: e.g. strong reputation and waiting list mean super profits are likely to last longer than 2.5 years.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Kamran, a sole trader in Hyderabad, India, is merging his business with that of Lakshmi to form a partnership. His statement of financial position before the merger showed: premises $85,000; vehicle $14,000; inventory $12,600; trade receivables $9,000; bank $3,400; trade payables $6,800.
For the merger it was agreed that: premises are valued at $98,000; the vehicle at $11,500; inventory at $11,900; and an allowance for irrecoverable debts of 4% is made on trade receivables. Other items are taken over at book value.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Kamran's capital according to his statement of financial position before the merger.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate Kamran's opening capital in the partnership.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the net gain on revaluation.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why an allowance for irrecoverable debts is made before the receivables are transferred.
parts.answer: Prudence: some customers may not pay, so receivables should not be overstated; otherwise Kamran would be credited with capital for amounts the partnership may never collect, which would be unfair to Lakshmi.
parts.working: 1 mark prudence/not overstated; 1 mark fairness between partners.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Lina and Musa, two sole traders selling mobile phone accessories in Amman, merged their businesses on 1 January 2025. Lina brought in net assets of $90,000 and Musa $60,000. Their partnership agreement says profits and losses are shared in the ratio of their opening capitals. The profit for the first year was $72,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit-sharing ratio in its simplest form.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate each partner's share of the profit for the first year.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State how profits would be shared if the partners had no partnership agreement, and give one reason why sharing in the capital ratio may be unfair to Musa.
parts.answer: Equally (Partnership Act 1890). Musa may work longer hours or bring more skill/customers, but receives a smaller share because he brought less capital.
parts.working: B1 equally; B1 reason.

author: HomiLabs

stem: On 1 April 2025 Nida brought the following into a new partnership formed by merging her business with that of Parveen: premises $120,000; equipment $15,000; inventory $8,000; and her trade payables of $5,000, which the partnership took over.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Nida's opening capital.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare the journal entry in the partnership's books to record the assets and liabilities brought in by Nida. A narrative is required.
parts.answer: Dr Premises 120,000; Dr Equipment 15,000; Dr Inventory 8,000; Cr Trade payables 5,000; Cr Capital – Nida 138,000. Narrative: assets and liabilities introduced by Nida on the merger of her business into the partnership.
parts.working: B1 assets debited; B1 payables credited; B1 capital credited 138,000; B1 narrative.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Two sole traders who run neighbouring shoe shops in Mardan are planning to merge their businesses into a partnership.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three matters that their partnership agreement should cover because of the merger.
parts.answer: Any three: agreed values of each trader's assets and liabilities; value and treatment of goodwill (kept or written off); which liabilities the partnership takes over; profit-sharing ratio; interest on capital and drawings; partners' salaries; amount of capital each must keep in the business.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the agreed values of the assets may differ from their book values.
