parts.answer: Book values are based on historical cost less depreciation, which may not reflect current market values (e.g. property prices rise, inventory becomes obsolete); fair values are needed so each trader's capital is fair.
parts.working: 1 mark historical cost; 1 mark fairness/current value.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Owais and Pervez merged their tailoring businesses in Lahore on 1 July 2025. Goodwill of each business is valued at 1.5 times the average profit of its last two years, and goodwill is to be kept in the partnership books.
                       Owais $    Pervez $
Profit 2023/24          28,000      21,000
Profit 2024/25          32,000      25,000
Agreed net assets       70,000      58,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the goodwill of each business.
parts.answer: Owais $45,000; Pervez $34,500
parts.working: Averages 30,000 and 23,000; × 1.5 (B1 each).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate each partner's opening capital.
parts.answer: Owais $115,000; Pervez $92,500
parts.working: Net assets + goodwill (B1 each).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the total of the partnership's opening statement of financial position (net assets including goodwill).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Qadir, Rubina and Sana each ran a small courier business in Karachi. On 1 October 2025 they merged to form a partnership sharing profits equally. Agreed values were:
                       Qadir $   Rubina $    Sana $
Net assets              64,000     51,000    47,000
Goodwill                30,000     18,000    12,000
Goodwill is to be credited to each partner and then written off in the profit-sharing ratio; it is not kept in the books.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate each partner's opening capital after goodwill has been written off.
parts.working: Total goodwill 60,000 written off 20,000 each (B1); Qadir 94,000 − 20,000 (B1); Rubina 69,000 − 20,000 (B1); Sana 59,000 − 20,000 (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: For each partner, calculate the gain or loss caused by this treatment of goodwill compared with their net assets brought in.
parts.answer: Qadir gains $10,000; Rubina loses $2,000; Sana loses $8,000

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why Qadir gains even though goodwill is not shown in the books.
parts.answer: He brought in the most goodwill but bears only one third of the write-off, so his capital is credited with the excess.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Tariq, a sole trader in Riyadh, is about to merge his business with that of Umar. Before the merger he adjusts his own books to the agreed values. His capital balance before any adjustment is $88,000. Agreed changes:
• premises: book value $60,000, agreed value $75,000
• machinery: book value $22,000, agreed value $17,500
• inventory: book value $9,800, agreed value $9,100
• goodwill of $12,000 is to be recognised

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the revaluation account in Tariq's books.
parts.answer:
Revaluation account
Dr: Machinery 4,500; Inventory 700; Capital – Tariq (gain) 21,800 = 27,000
Cr: Premises 15,000; Goodwill 12,000 = 27,000
parts.working: B1 premises 15,000 credit; B1 goodwill 12,000 credit; B1 machinery and inventory debits; B1 gain 21,800 to capital.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the capital Tariq will transfer to the partnership.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a decrease in the value of machinery is debited to the revaluation account.
parts.answer: A fall in an asset's value is a loss, which reduces the owner's capital; the asset account is credited and the loss debited.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Uzair and Vania merged their businesses in Nairobi on 1 June 2025, taking over all assets and liabilities at book value. On that date:
                              Uzair $     Vania $
Premises                            –      75,000
Equipment                      30,000           –
Inventory                      14,000       9,500
Trade receivables              11,500       7,800
Bank                            6,000     (2,600) overdraft
Trade payables                 (8,200)    (10,400)
Uzair's trade receivables include $3,000 owed by Vania's business, and Vania's trade payables include the same $3,000 owed to Uzair. The partnership will keep one bank account and the overdraft is cleared from Uzair's bank balance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate each partner's opening capital.
parts.answer: Uzair $53,300; Vania $79,300
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare the opening statement of financial position of the partnership at 1 June 2025.
parts.answer:
Non-current assets: premises 75,000; equipment 30,000 = 105,000
Current assets: inventory 23,500; trade receivables 16,300; bank 3,400 = 43,200
Current liabilities: trade payables 15,600
Net assets 132,600
Capital: Uzair 53,300; Vania 79,300 = 132,600
parts.working: B1 non-current assets; B1 receivables 16,300 (inter-business debt removed); B1 payables 15,600; B1 bank 3,400; B1 capitals and balancing totals.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the $3,000 is removed from both receivables and payables.
parts.answer: After the merger it is a debt the partnership owes to itself, so it is no longer an asset or a liability.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Wasim and Yasmin, sole traders in Islamabad, agreed to merge their businesses into a new private limited company, WY Foods Ltd. Agreed values: Wasim – net assets $140,000 and goodwill $20,000; Yasmin – net assets $96,000 and goodwill $4,000. Each receives ordinary shares of $1 each, issued at par, equal to the total value of the business brought in.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of shares issued to each owner.
parts.answer: Wasim 160,000; Yasmin 100,000
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the voting shares held by each owner, to two decimal places.
parts.answer: Wasim 61.54%; Yasmin 38.46%

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for Yasmin of merging into a limited company rather than a partnership.
parts.answer: Advantage: limited liability – she can lose only her investment. Disadvantage: as a minority shareholder Wasim can outvote her on ordinary resolutions; or more regulation and published accounts.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Zain owns a software repair business in Lahore that earns a profit of $40,000 a year. Ahsan, who runs a similar business, suggests merging into a partnership. The forecast profit of the merged business is $115,000 a year. The proposed agreement is:
• capitals: Zain $120,000, Ahsan $80,000
• interest on capital at 5% a year
• salaries: Zain $15,000, Ahsan $10,000
• remaining profit shared equally

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the residual profit to be shared equally.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate Zain's total expected income from the partnership.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise Zain whether he should agree to the merger. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: For: income rises from $40,000 to $61,000 (+$21,000); shared workload, skills and customers; more capital for growth. Against: forecast may be optimistic; profits must be shared and decisions agreed with Ahsan; unlimited liability for Ahsan's actions (joint and several); he puts in more capital but residual profit is shared equally; disputes may arise. Decision justified.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for points for, up to 2 against, 1 mark use of figures, 1 mark justified decision.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Akbar and Bano are partners in a printing business in Gujranwala, sharing profits 3 : 2. Their capitals are Akbar $80,000 and Bano $60,000. On 1 January 2025 their partnership merged with the business of Chen, a sole trader, who brought in net assets of $45,000. Goodwill was valued at $40,000 for the partnership and $15,000 for Chen's business. In the new partnership Akbar, Bano and Chen will share profits 2 : 2 : 1. Goodwill is not to be kept in the books.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount of goodwill credited to and debited to each partner's capital account.
parts.answer: Credited: Akbar $24,000; Bano $16,000; Chen $15,000. Debited (written off 2 : 2 : 1): Akbar $22,000; Bano $22,000; Chen $11,000
parts.working: B1 partnership goodwill 3 : 2; B1 Chen 15,000; B1 total 55,000; B1 write-off 2 : 2 : 1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate each partner's capital after the merger.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why Bano's capital falls even though her business had goodwill of $40,000.
parts.answer: She is credited with $16,000 (2/5 of her old firm's goodwill) but debited with $22,000 (2/5 of the total goodwill of $55,000). The extra $6,000 is her payment for a 2/5 share of Chen's goodwill ($15,000 × 2/5), which she now shares in.
parts.working: 1 mark debit 22,000 exceeds credit 16,000; 1 mark she is paying for a share of the goodwill owned by others.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Daud and Erum, sole traders in Peshawar, merged their businesses on 1 September 2025 to form Dera Supplies Ltd.
• Daud's business: assets less current liabilities $150,000, but it also has a $30,000 loan from a relative. The company takes over the loan by issuing $30,000 of 7% debentures to the relative. Daud's goodwill is valued at $25,000.
• Erum's business: net assets $95,000; goodwill $5,000.
Each owner receives ordinary shares of $1 each, issued at $1.25 per share, equal to the value of his or her net assets plus goodwill.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the value of the business brought in by each owner.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of shares issued to each owner.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the company's ordinary share capital, share premium and total equity on 1 September 2025.
parts.answer: Share capital $196,000; share premium $49,000; total equity $245,000
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the ordinary shares held by Daud, to two decimal places, and explain one reason why Erum may be concerned.
parts.answer: 59.18%; Daud holds a majority so can control ordinary resolutions and the board.
parts.working: B1 percentage; B1 explanation.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Two partnerships of architects in Karachi merged on 1 March 2025.
• Faraz and Gohar shared profits 3 : 2; capitals Faraz $70,000, Gohar $50,000; goodwill of their firm valued at $50,000.
• Hania and Irfan shared profits equally; capitals Hania $65,000, Irfan $45,000; goodwill of their firm valued at $30,000.
In the merged partnership Faraz, Gohar, Hania and Irfan will share profits 3 : 2 : 3 : 2. Goodwill is to be credited to the old partners in their old ratios and written off in the new ratio; it is not kept in the books.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net adjustment to each partner's capital for goodwill, stating whether it is an increase or a decrease.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate each partner's capital in the merged partnership.
parts.working: B2 all four correct; B1 two correct.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why Hania and Irfan might still agree to these terms.
parts.answer: Their share of a larger firm's profit (50% in total, the same as Faraz and Gohar) may give them a higher income than before, even though their firm had less goodwill; access to bigger clients, shared costs.
parts.working: 1 mark profit share/higher income; 1 mark other benefit.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Jamal and Kiran merged their sole-trader businesses on 1 January 2025 to form a partnership. Their opening capitals, based on the agreed values of the net assets they brought in, were Jamal $84,000 and Kiran $56,000. The partnership agreement provides for:
• interest on capital at 6% a year
• a salary for Kiran of $12,000 a year
• interest on drawings: Jamal $500, Kiran $375
• remaining profit shared in the ratio of opening capitals
Profit for the year ended 31 December 2025 was $68,000. Before the merger Kiran's own business made a profit of $30,000 a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the appropriation account for the year ended 31 December 2025.
parts.answer: Profit for the year 68,000; add interest on drawings Jamal 500, Kiran 375 = 68,875; less interest on capital Jamal 5,040, Kiran 3,360; salary Kiran 12,000; residual profit 48,475 shared Jamal 29,085 (3/5), Kiran 19,390 (2/5).
parts.working: B1 interest on drawings added; B1 interest on capital; B1 salary; B1 residual 48,475; B1 shares in 3 : 2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate Kiran's total income from the partnership for the year, net of interest on drawings, and compare it with her profit before the merger.
parts.answer: $34,375; $4,375 more than the $30,000 she earned alone

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the partners chose to share residual profit in the ratio of opening capitals and how Kiran's salary balances this.
parts.answer: Capital ratio rewards Jamal for bringing more net assets (3 : 2). Kiran's salary rewards her for the extra work she does, so the agreement rewards both capital and effort.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Laila and Moin are merging their stationery businesses in Lahore into a partnership that will share profits equally. Laila's draft statement of financial position shows net assets of $92,000. Before the merger the following are discovered in Laila's books:
1 electricity of $1,400 owing has not been recorded
2 inventory is overstated by $2,600 because damaged items were valued at cost
3 a customer owing $1,800 has become bankrupt and will pay nothing
Moin's net assets are agreed at $70,000. Goodwill is valued at $18,000 for Laila's business and $12,000 for Moin's. Goodwill is to be credited to each partner and then written off equally.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Laila's agreed net assets.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate each partner's opening capital.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Laila argues that the goodwill should be kept in the books rather than written off. Discuss whether this would be better for her.
parts.answer: If goodwill were kept, capitals would be Laila $104,200 and Moin $82,000. The difference between them is $22,200 either way (89,200 − 67,000 = 104,200 − 82,000), so her position relative to Moin is the same. Keeping it would only help if interest on capital is paid (higher capital, more interest – but Moin gains too). Kept goodwill may later be impaired, and any loss would be shared equally. Conclusion: not clearly better for her; writing it off is more prudent.
parts.working: 1 mark figures/same difference; 1 mark impairment or interest point; 1 mark reasoned conclusion.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A detergent maker in Dhaka uses a standard of 3 kg of powder base per carton at a standard price of $2.20 per kg. It calculates the material price variance when material is purchased. In September it bought 12,000 kg of powder base for $25,800 and used 11,200 kg to make 3,700 cartons.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the actual price paid per kg.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the material price variance, stating whether it is favourable or adverse.
parts.answer: $600 favourable

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the material usage variance, stating whether it is favourable or adverse.
parts.answer: $220 adverse

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the price variance is based on the 12,000 kg bought, not the 11,200 kg used.
parts.answer: The variance is identified when the purchase is made, so the buyer is held responsible at once and inventory can be held at standard price.

stem: A hospital laundry in Kuala Lumpur sets a standard of 12 minutes of labour per load washed, at $15 per hour. In March it washed 9,000 loads. Staff worked and were paid for 1,850 hours at a total cost of $28,490.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the standard hours allowed for the loads washed.
parts.answer: 1,800 hours

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the labour rate variance.
parts.answer: $740 adverse
parts.working: Actual hours at standard rate 1,850 × 15 = 27,750 (M1); 27,750 − 28,490 = 740 A (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the labour efficiency variance.
parts.answer: $750 adverse

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the total labour variance and show that it equals the sum of the rate and efficiency variances.
parts.answer: $1,490 adverse

author: HomiLabs

stem: A shoe-polish maker in Lagos has a standard material cost of $18 per tin (6 kg at $3 per kg). In July it made 2,400 tins, using 15,000 kg of material that cost $43,500.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total material cost variance.
parts.answer: $300 adverse

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the material price variance and the material usage variance.
parts.answer: Price $1,500 favourable; usage $1,800 adverse

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason why a favourable price variance might be linked to an adverse usage variance.
parts.answer: Cheaper, lower-quality material may cause more waste.

stem: A print shop in Nairobi produces packs of printed leaflets. Standard variable cost per pack: materials $7.50; labour $12.00; variable overhead $3.00. In May it produced 5,200 packs. Actual costs were: materials $38,900; labour $63,100; variable overhead $15,950.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the standard cost of the actual output for each element of cost.
parts.answer: Materials $39,000; labour $62,400; variable overhead $15,600
parts.working: 5,200 × each standard (B1 each).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the variance for each element and the total variable cost variance, stating whether each is favourable or adverse.
parts.answer: Materials $100 F; labour $700 A; variable overhead $350 A; total $950 A
parts.working: B1 each element; B1 total.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State which manager is most likely to be asked to explain the labour variance.
parts.answer: The production (print room) supervisor/manager responsible for staff.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A manufacturer of steel kettles in Gujranwala budgeted to sell 6,000 kettles in a quarter at $50 each. Standard variable cost is $30 per kettle and standard fixed overhead is $8 per kettle. It actually sold 5,700 kettles at $51.50 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the sales price variance.
parts.answer: $8,550 favourable

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the sales volume variance using (i) standard profit (absorption costing) and (ii) standard contribution (marginal costing).
parts.answer: (i) $3,600 adverse; (ii) $6,000 adverse
parts.working: Standard profit 50 − 38 = 12 (B1); 300 × 12 = 3,600 A (B1). Standard contribution 20 (B1); 300 × 20 = 6,000 A (B1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the two sales volume variances are different.
parts.answer: Under marginal costing fixed overhead is not charged per unit, so each lost sale loses the full contribution of $20 rather than the profit of $12.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Marigold Ltd, Chennai, uses standard absorption costing. Its budgeted profit for April was $84,000. The variances for April were:
Variance                             $
Sales price                      6,200 F
Sales volume                     9,600 A
Material price                   2,150 A
Material usage                   1,300 F
Labour rate                        900 F
Labour efficiency                3,400 A
Variable overhead expenditure      450 A
Variable overhead efficiency       680 A
Fixed overhead expenditure       1,500 F
Fixed overhead volume            2,400 A

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare a statement reconciling the budgeted profit with the actual profit for April.
parts.answer: Budgeted profit 84,000; total favourable variances 9,900; total adverse variances 18,680; net adverse 8,780; actual profit 75,220
parts.working: B1 budgeted profit; B1 favourable total 9,900; B1 adverse total 18,680; M1 adjust; A1 actual profit 75,220.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify two variances in the list that may have the same cause, and explain the link.
parts.answer: E.g. labour efficiency adverse and variable overhead efficiency adverse – both depend on hours worked, so slow working raises both; or sales price favourable and sales volume adverse – higher price reduced demand.
parts.working: 1 mark pair; 1 mark explanation.

stem: A paint factory in Lahore has a standard of 2.5 kg of pigment per drum at $5.15 per kg. In June it made 3,000 drums. All pigment bought was used. The material price variance was $1,240 adverse and the actual price paid was $5.31 per kg.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the quantity of pigment used.

parts.answer: $1,287.50 adverse

stem: An air-cooler assembler in Multan uses two grades of labour. Standard per cooler: skilled 2 hours at $20 per hour; semi-skilled 3 hours at $12 per hour. In August 1,500 coolers were made. Actual labour: skilled 3,100 hours costing $63,550; semi-skilled 4,350 hours costing $50,460.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the labour rate and efficiency variances for skilled labour.
parts.answer: Rate $1,550 adverse; efficiency $2,000 adverse

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the labour rate and efficiency variances for semi-skilled labour.
parts.answer: Rate $1,740 favourable; efficiency $1,800 favourable

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the total labour variance and comment on what the four variances suggest.
parts.answer: $10 adverse in total. Almost nil overall, but skilled staff were paid more and took longer, while semi-skilled staff were cheaper and quicker – possibly semi-skilled work was done by skilled staff, or overtime was paid to skilled staff.
parts.working: B1 total; B1 comment.

stem: A candle maker in Colombo uses two materials. Standard per candle: wax 0.4 kg at $3.50 per kg; fragrance oil 0.02 litres at $40 per litre. In November 25,000 candles were made. Actual usage: wax 10,300 kg costing $35,535; fragrance oil 480 litres costing $20,160.

stem:
Penang Solar Frames Sdn Bhd makes aluminium frames for solar panels and uses standard absorption costing. Standard cost card per frame:
                                          $
Materials       3 kg × $6.00           18.00
Labour          1.5 hours × $16.00     24.00
Variable o/h    1.5 hours × $4.00       6.00
Fixed o/h       1.5 hours × $12.00     18.00
Standard cost                          66.00
Selling price                          95.00
Budgeted output and sales were 4,000 frames.
Actual results for the month: 4,200 frames were made and sold at $93 each. Materials: 12,900 kg costing $76,110. Labour: 6,150 hours costing $100,860. Variable overhead $25,830. Fixed overhead $74,500.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the budgeted profit and the actual profit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the sales price and sales volume variances.

parts.text: Calculate the material, labour and variable overhead variances (price/rate/expenditure and usage/efficiency).

stem: A furniture workshop in Chiniot pays a standard labour rate of $14 per hour. In October it made 4,120 chairs. Labour worked 12,600 hours. The total labour variance was $2,100 adverse and the labour rate variance was $1,260 favourable.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the actual rate paid per hour and the actual labour cost.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the labour efficiency variance.
parts.answer: $3,360 adverse
parts.working: Total = rate + efficiency, so efficiency = 2,100 A + 1,260 = 3,360 A (B1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the standard hours allowed for actual output, and the standard hours per chair.
parts.answer: 12,360 hours; 3 hours per chair

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the standard labour cost per chair.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A company in Ipoh makes one product. Budgeted production and sales were 10,000 units at a standard price of $30. Standard variable cost is $18 per unit and budgeted fixed overhead is $50,000, absorbed per unit of budgeted output. Actual production and sales were 9,200 units. All actual prices, costs and fixed overhead were exactly as standard.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the budgeted profit under absorption costing and under marginal costing.
parts.answer: $70,000 under both

parts.label: b
parts.text: Under absorption costing, calculate the sales volume variance and the fixed overhead volume variance.
parts.answer: Sales volume $5,600 A; fixed overhead volume $4,000 A

parts.label: c
parts.text: Under marginal costing, calculate the sales volume variance.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the actual profit and explain why both systems give the same actual profit in this case.
parts.answer: $60,400. Production equals sales, so no fixed overhead is carried forward in inventory; the absorption sales volume variance plus the fixed overhead volume variance (5,600 + 4,000) equals the marginal sales volume variance (9,600).
parts.working: B1 profit 9,200 × 12 − 50,000; B1 no inventory change; B1 variances reconcile.

stem: A courier company in Nairobi uses standard costing for each delivery. Standard per delivery: fuel 0.6 litres at $1.80 per litre; driver time 0.25 hours at $10 per hour. In January it made 48,000 deliveries. Fuel used was 30,400 litres costing $53,200. Drivers worked 12,500 hours and were paid $122,500.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the fuel price and fuel usage variances.
parts.answer: Price $1,520 F; usage $2,880 A

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the driver rate and driver efficiency variances.
parts.answer: Rate $2,500 F; efficiency $5,000 A

parts.label: c
parts.text: Prepare a statement reconciling the standard cost of the actual deliveries with the actual cost.
parts.answer: Standard cost of 48,000 deliveries 171,840; add adverse: fuel usage 2,880, driver efficiency 5,000; less favourable: fuel price 1,520, driver rate 2,500; actual cost 175,700
parts.working: B1 standard cost 171,840; B1 variances correctly signed; B1 actual 175,700.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one cause that could explain both adverse usage/efficiency variances.
parts.answer: Heavy traffic or road works: longer journeys use more fuel and take more driver time.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A furniture maker in Peshawar reports a favourable labour rate variance and an adverse labour efficiency variance for the same month.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how one decision could have caused both variances.
parts.answer: Using less-skilled or trainee workers paid a lower rate gives a favourable rate variance (B1), but they work more slowly or need supervision (B1), so more hours are taken than standard, giving an adverse efficiency variance (B1).
parts.working: B1 cheaper labour; B1 slower working; B1 link to each variance.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one other possible cause of an adverse labour efficiency variance that is not linked to the rate paid.
parts.answer: Any one: machine breakdowns; poor-quality material; poor supervision; low morale; new product/learning time.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A company selling solar lanterns in Karachi reports a favourable sales volume variance and an adverse sales price variance for the quarter.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two possible reasons for the adverse sales price variance.
parts.answer: Any two: price cut to win market share; discounts for bulk orders; competitors lowered prices; seasonal promotion.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two possible reasons for the favourable sales volume variance, other than a price change.
parts.answer: Any two: successful advertising; competitor left the market; higher demand due to power cuts; new retailer/distribution channel; better product quality.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A garment factory in Faisalabad has an adverse fixed overhead expenditure variance for the year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two possible reasons for an adverse fixed overhead expenditure variance.
parts.answer: Any two: rent or rates increased; higher insurance premium; unexpected repairs; electricity standing charges rose; extra supervisory salaries.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the production manager may not be responsible for this variance.
parts.answer: Many fixed costs (rent, insurance, rates) are set by contracts or outside bodies and decided by senior management, so they are outside the production manager's control.
parts.working: 1 mark costs set externally/by others; 1 mark not controllable.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Hassan is setting up standard costing in his bicycle-parts workshop in Lahore.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'standard cost'.
parts.answer: A predetermined (planned) cost of producing one unit under expected efficient conditions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two sources of information Hassan could use to set the standard price of materials.
parts.answer: Any two: suppliers' price lists or quotations; past purchase invoices adjusted for inflation; trade discounts negotiated; forecasts of market prices.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two sources of information he could use to set the standard labour time per part.
parts.answer: Any two: time-and-motion (work) studies; past production records; trial runs; engineers' estimates; industry benchmarks.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: The finance director of a soft-drinks bottler in Lahore says the business uses 'management by exception' with its monthly variance reports.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by management by exception.
parts.answer: Managers compare actual results with standards and spend their time only on significant variances (exceptions), not on items that are close to standard.
parts.working: 1 mark compare with standard; 1 mark focus on significant variances.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two benefits of management by exception.
parts.answer: Any two: saves managers' time; focuses attention on problems; quicker corrective action; reduces information overload.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A packaging factory in Dubai has a favourable labour efficiency variance and an adverse labour rate variance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two possible reasons for the favourable labour efficiency variance.
parts.answer: Any two: more skilled/experienced workers; better machinery; good-quality materials; bonus scheme motivating faster work; better supervision.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two possible reasons for the adverse labour rate variance.
parts.answer: Any two: pay rise not built into the standard; overtime premium paid; higher-grade workers used; shortage of labour forcing higher wages.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A shoe factory in Kasur introduced a bonus for production workers: every worker who makes more pairs than the standard in a week receives a bonus of 10% of their weekly wage.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the likely effect of the bonus scheme on (i) the labour rate variance, (ii) the labour efficiency variance and (iii) the material usage variance.
parts.answer: (i) Adverse: bonus payments increase the actual rate per hour above standard (B1) unless the bonus is in the standard (B1). (ii) Favourable: workers work faster to earn the bonus, fewer hours per pair (B1 B1). (iii) Possibly adverse: rushing causes more mistakes and wasted leather (B1), so more material is used per pair (B1).
parts.working: 2 marks for each of (i), (ii), (iii): direction + reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one way the factory could stop the bonus scheme from harming quality.
parts.answer: Pay the bonus only on pairs that pass quality inspection (or deduct for rejects).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Rose Textiles, Karachi, investigates a variance when it is more than 5% of the related standard cost. The material usage variance for dyed cotton over four months was:
Month       Variance $   Standard material cost $
January        900 A                    30,000
February     1,240 A                    31,000
March        1,680 A                    32,000
April        2,170 A                    31,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the variance as a percentage of standard material cost for each month, to two decimal places.
parts.answer: January 3.00%; February 4.00%; March 5.25%; April 7.00%
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The policy would first investigate the variance in March. Advise the management accountant whether it should have been investigated earlier. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: The variance is adverse every month and rising steadily (3% → 7%), which shows a persistent trend rather than random fluctuation; small adverse variances that grow suggest a developing problem (e.g. machine wear, poor material). It should have been investigated in February when the trend became clear, even though below 5%; the cost of investigating early is small compared with continued losses. A rule based only on size ignores trends.
parts.working: 1 mark trend; 1 mark persistent vs random; 1 mark cost/benefit; 1 mark justified advice.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
The management accountant of a dairy in Multan must decide whether to investigate two adverse variances. Each investigation costs $1,200.
Variance            Chance the cause can be corrected   Saving if corrected
Material usage                    40%                        $4,500
Labour efficiency                 25%                        $3,600

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the expected benefit of investigating each variance and the expected net benefit after the cost of investigation.
parts.answer: Material usage: expected saving $1,800, net benefit $600. Labour efficiency: expected saving $900, net cost $300.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise the management accountant which variance(s) to investigate. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Investigate material usage: expected net benefit $600. On these figures do not investigate labour efficiency (expected net cost $300), unless the probability or savings are underestimated, the variance is recurring (savings in future months too) or it links to quality/safety problems.
parts.working: 1 mark each decision with figures; 1 mark qualification (recurring savings/non-financial).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A soap manufacturer in Lahore set a standard price of $8.00 per kg for palm oil 18 months ago. Since then the market price of palm oil has risen by 8%. Last month the purchasing manager bought 21,000 kg at $8.75 per kg. The directors want to reduce the purchasing manager's bonus because of the large adverse price variance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the material price variance using the original standard.
parts.answer: $15,750 adverse

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the standard price updated for the 8% market rise, and the price variance against this updated standard.
parts.answer: $8.64 per kg; $2,310 adverse

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise the directors whether they should reduce the purchasing manager's bonus. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Most of the variance ($13,440 of $15,750) is caused by the out-of-date standard and market prices outside the manager's control, so it would be unfair to penalise for it; only $2,310 is controllable, which is about 1.3% of cost and may reflect urgent purchases or quality. Standards should be revised. A small reduction might be justified only if the $2,310 was due to poor buying. Decision with reason.
parts.working: 1 mark uncontrollable portion with figure; 1 mark controllable portion; 1 mark need to revise standards/motivation; 1 mark justified decision.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Atlas Engineering, Rawalpindi, pays a bonus to the department manager whose controllable variances are best. Material prices are the responsibility of the central purchasing department. Last month's variances:
Variance              Machining dept $   Assembly dept $
Material price             3,000 A             1,100 A
Material usage             1,800 F             1,500 A
Labour rate                  400 A             2,600 F
Labour efficiency          2,400 F             3,900 A
Labour rates are set by each department manager, who chooses which grade of worker to use.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net total variance for each department, and the net controllable variance for each department manager.
parts.answer: Totals: Machining $800 F; Assembly $3,900 A. Controllable (excluding material price): Machining $3,800 F; Assembly $2,800 A.
parts.working: B1 each figure.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise the directors which manager should receive the bonus. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Machining: its controllable variances are $3,800 F, and the adverse price variance is the purchasing department's responsibility. Assembly saved on wages by using cheaper staff (2,600 F) but lost more through slower work and waste (5,400 A). The machining manager should receive the bonus; check that favourable variances were not achieved by cutting quality.
parts.working: 1 mark controllability; 1 mark analysis of assembly trade-off; 1 mark decision.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A kitchenware factory in Gujrat received a rush order for 800 cooking pots at $70 each. Standard variable cost per pot: materials $20; labour 2 hours × $12 = $24; variable overhead $4. To finish on time all 1,600 labour hours had to be worked as overtime, paid at time-and-a-half. All other costs were at standard. The production manager is now being criticised for a large adverse labour rate variance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the labour rate variance caused by the order.
parts.answer: $9,600 adverse

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the standard contribution from the order and the actual contribution after the overtime premium.
parts.answer: Standard contribution $17,600; actual contribution $8,000

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise the directors whether the production manager should be blamed for the variance. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: The order still added $8,000 of contribution, so accepting it was profitable; the overtime was a planned consequence of the sales decision, not inefficiency. The variance should be reported separately or charged to the sales department that accepted the deadline. However, if overtime could have been avoided by better scheduling, part of the cost is controllable. Possible goodwill with the customer. Decision: do not blame the production manager.
parts.working: 1 mark contribution still positive; 1 mark controllability/responsibility; 1 mark other factor; 1 mark decision.

author: HomiLabs

stem: To reduce costs, the managers of a bottling plant in Karachi cut the machine maintenance budget for the quarter, which gave a favourable fixed overhead expenditure variance of $6,000. During the quarter machine breakdowns caused 420 extra labour hours (standard rate $15 per hour; variable overhead absorbed at $5 per labour hour) and 650 kg of extra material scrap (standard price $4 per kg).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the adverse variances caused by the breakdowns, naming each variance.
parts.answer: Labour efficiency $6,300 A; variable overhead efficiency $2,100 A; material usage $2,600 A
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the net effect on profit of the decision to cut maintenance.
parts.answer: $5,000 worse (adverse)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise the managers whether they should keep the reduced maintenance budget. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: No: the $6,000 saving is outweighed by $11,000 of extra costs, giving a net loss of $5,000; further risks include late deliveries, lost customers, safety hazards and shorter machine life. Variances should be read together, not individually; a favourable variance is not always good. Possibly reinstate planned preventive maintenance.
parts.working: 1 mark net figure; 1 mark interrelated variances; 1 mark non-financial; 1 mark decision.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A maker of electric fans in Gujrat uses standard marginal costing. The budget is 6,000 fans a quarter at $80, with a standard variable cost of $50 per fan. The sales director proposes cutting the price to $74 and expects sales to rise to 7,200 fans. Fixed costs would not change.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the sales price variance and the sales volume variance that would arise if the forecast is achieved.
parts.answer: Sales price $43,200 adverse; sales volume $36,000 favourable

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the change in total contribution, and the number of fans that must be sold at $74 to earn the same contribution as the budget.
parts.answer: Contribution falls by $7,200; 7,500 fans needed

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise the sales director whether to cut the price. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: On the forecast, contribution falls by $7,200, so the cut should not go ahead unless at least 7,500 fans can be sold; higher volume also needs more production capacity, working capital and labour. For: may gain market share long-term and win repeat customers; competitors may also cut prices. Decision justified.
parts.working: 1 mark use of figures; 1 mark break-even volume; 1 mark other factor; 1 mark decision.

author: HomiLabs

stem: TechCase Ltd, Shenzhen, makes phone cases. Most production is done by automated machines, labour is a small part of cost, and each design is sold for only about six months before being replaced. The company uses total quality management and buys materials just in time. A director suggests stopping standard costing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Advise the directors whether TechCase Ltd should continue to use standard costing. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Against: standards take time to set and quickly go out of date with short product lives; labour variances matter little when machines do the work; TQM aims at continuous improvement, not just meeting a standard; JIT means price variances from bulk buying are less relevant; variance reports may come too late. For: still useful for material cost control, pricing new designs, budgeting and spotting problems; standards can be updated more often or combined with non-financial measures (defect rates, delivery times). Decision justified, e.g. keep a simplified, regularly updated system.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks against, up to 2 for, 1 mark justified decision.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A tile factory in Gujranwala is choosing between two labour standards for laying a batch of tiles: an ideal standard of 2.0 hours per batch (no breaks, no machine stoppages) and an attainable standard of 2.2 hours per batch. Last month 10,000 batches took 22,500 hours, paid at the standard rate of $15 per hour.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the labour efficiency variance using each standard.
parts.answer: Ideal $37,500 adverse; attainable $7,500 adverse

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise the factory which standard it should use. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Attainable: a variance of $7,500 A (about 2.3%) shows workers were close to a realistic target, so it is useful for control and motivation. Ideal: permanent large adverse variances ($37,500) may demotivate staff and make it hard to see real problems; but it shows the maximum possible improvement. Decision: attainable standard, perhaps reviewing it regularly towards the ideal.
parts.working: 1 mark each standard with figure; 1 mark motivation; 1 mark decision.

parts.text:

At the year end a trader forgot to record electricity of $620 that had been used but not yet billed. What is the effect of this omission on the financial statements?

B profit understated by $620 and current liabilities overstated by $620
C profit overstated by $620 and current assets overstated by $620
D profit understated by $620 and current assets understated by $620
parts.answer: A profit overstated by $620 and current liabilities understated by $620

stem:
Mariam runs an online tutoring business in Lahore; her year ends on 31 December. Her internet and telephone account has two parts:
• line rental of $210 per quarter, paid in advance on 1 March, 1 June, 1 September and 1 December, each payment covering the following three months;
• call and data charges, billed every quarter in arrears.
At 1 January 2026 line rental for January and February 2026 ($140) had been prepaid and call charges of $95 were owing.
Payments in 2026: line rental 4 × $210; call and data charges $1,180.
On 2 February 2027 she received a bill of $315 for call and data charges for November 2026 to January 2027.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the line rental prepaid at 31 December 2026.
parts.working: Payment on 1 December covers Dec–Feb; January and February = 2/3 × 210 = $140 B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the call and data charges accrued at 31 December 2026.
parts.working: November and December = 2/3 × 315 = $210 B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Prepare the internet and telephone account for the year ended 31 December 2026, showing the balances brought down on 1 January 2027.
parts.answer:
Dr: balance b/d (prepaid) 140; bank (rental) 840; bank (calls) 1,180; balance c/d (accrued) 210 = 2,370.
Cr: balance b/d (accrued) 95; statement of profit or loss 2,135; balance c/d (prepaid) 140 = 2,370.
1 Jan 2027: Dr balance b/d 140; Cr balance b/d 210.
parts.working: B1 opening balances both sides; B1 payments; B1 closing prepayment c/d on credit; B1 closing accrual c/d on debit; B1 transfer to SOPL $2,135 (OF); B1 balances b/d on correct sides

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why two balances can be carried down on the same expense account.
parts.answer: Two different parts of the expense are at different stages: rental has been paid for a future period (asset) while calls have been used but not yet paid (liability). Each must be shown separately in the SOFP rather than netted off.
parts.working: 1 mark: one part is prepaid/asset and one accrued/liability; 1 mark: they are shown separately (current asset and current liability), not offset

author: HomiLabs

stem: Owais owns a car-wash business in Karachi. He says: 'My profit is just the cash I received during the year minus the cash I paid out.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why Owais's method may not give the correct profit for the year.
parts.answer: Cash paid or received in the year may relate to other periods (e.g. rent paid in advance, bills owing at the year end), so profit must match income and expenses to the period in which they were earned or incurred.
parts.working: 1 mark: cash timing differs from period of the expense/income; 1 mark: the accruals (matching) concept requires income and expenses of the period

stem:
Leila runs a dental practice in Dubai. Her draft profit for the year ended 30 June 2026 is $62,450. Her draft statement of financial position shows current assets of $18,900 and current liabilities of $11,300. The following have not been taken into account:
1 Cleaning contract: $300 per month; the June 2026 invoice has not been paid or recorded.
2 Professional indemnity insurance of $2,880 was paid on 1 March 2026 for the twelve months to 28 February 2027 and was all charged as an expense.
3 A patient prepaid $1,500 on 25 June 2026 for treatment to be carried out in July 2026; it was included in fee income.
4 Rent receivable from a pharmacy sub-letting part of the building, $650 for June 2026, has not been received or recorded.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare a statement of corrected profit for the year ended 30 June 2026.

At the start of the year a business had a provision for doubtful debts of $2,600. At the end of the year trade receivables were $40,000 and the provision is to be 5% of trade receivables. How does the change in the provision affect the financial statements?

stem:
Saima's draft profit for the year ended 31 December 2026 is $37,820. Her draft statement of financial position shows trade receivables of $46,500 less a provision for doubtful debts of $1,200 (the provision brought forward from 2025, unchanged). The following were then discovered:
1 A debt of $900 owed by T. Hussain is irrecoverable and has not been written off.
2 $420 received from J. Ahmed, whose debt was written off in 2024, was credited to sales.
3 A debt of $350 owed by P. Khan, written off in June 2026, was paid in full in December 2026; the receipt was credited to P. Khan's account and is included in trade receivables as a credit balance, reducing the total.
4 The provision for doubtful debts is to be 4% of trade receivables at 31 December 2026.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the corrected trade receivables (before the provision) at 31 December 2026.

parts.working: − 900 B1; item 2: reclassify sales to irrecoverable debts recovered, no effect on profit B1; + 350 recovered income B1; provision 1,838 − 1,200 = 638 increase deducted; corrected $36,632 B1 (OF)

stem: Nasreen's draft profit for the year ended 31 December 2026 is $44,600. On 1 October 2026 she bought a delivery van for $24,000 by cheque. The bookkeeper debited the payment to motor repairs. Nasreen depreciates vehicles at 20% per annum using the straight-line method, with a full month's charge in the month of purchase. No depreciation has been charged on the new van.

parts.label: a

parts.answer: Capital expenditure buys or improves a non-current asset that benefits several years (the van) and goes to the SOFP; revenue expenditure is the day-to-day running cost consumed within the year (e.g. repairs) and goes to the SOPL. Treating the van as repairs understated profit and non-current assets.

stem: Before preparing final financial statements, a trader makes year-end adjustments to the figures in the trial balance.

parts.label: a

A trader has a damaged bicycle helmet that cost $40. It can be sold for $55 if repaired at a cost of $10. The salesperson receives commission of 10% of the selling price. At what value should the helmet be included in closing inventory?
A $39.50
B $40.00
C $45.00

parts.working: NRV = 55 − 10 − 5.50 = $39.50, which is below cost $40, so the lower figure is used. B ignores the selling costs.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
At 31 December 2025 a trader valued a line of inventory at its cost of $6,000, although its net realisable value was only $4,500. The goods were sold in 2026 for $4,500. What is the effect of this error?
A profit for 2025 overstated by $1,500 and profit for 2026 understated by $1,500
B profit for 2025 understated by $1,500 and profit for 2026 overstated by $1,500
C profit for 2025 overstated by $1,500 and no effect on profit for 2026
D no effect on profit for 2025 and profit for 2026 understated by $1,500
parts.answer: A profit for 2025 overstated by $1,500 and profit for 2026 understated by $1,500
parts.working: Closing inventory 2025 too high → 2025 profit too high by $1,500. It becomes opening inventory 2026, so 2026 cost of sales is too high and 2026 profit too low. C forgets the effect carried into the next year.

stem: Sana owns a gift shop in Lahore. Her assistant suggests that closing inventory should be valued at its selling price, 'because that is what the goods are worth'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why inventory is not normally valued at selling price.
parts.answer: Valuing at selling price would include profit before the goods are sold; profit is only recognised when it is realised (realisation concept), and prudence means assets should not be overstated.
parts.working: 1 mark: includes unrealised profit; 1 mark: realisation/prudence

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why inventory is reduced to net realisable value when this is below cost.
parts.answer: If goods will be sold for less than they cost, the loss is foreseeable; prudence requires the loss to be recognised now and the asset not to be overstated.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A business increases its output from 1,000 units to 2,000 units in a month. Which statement is correct, assuming there is no change in capacity?
A total fixed cost doubles
B variable cost per unit halves
C fixed cost per unit halves
D total variable cost stays the same
parts.answer: C fixed cost per unit halves
parts.working: Total fixed cost is unchanged, so it is spread over twice as many units and fixed cost per unit halves. B is wrong: variable cost per unit stays constant; it is total variable cost that doubles.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Total costs of a business were $52,000 when 4,000 units were made and $79,000 when 7,000 units were made. Fixed costs increase by $6,000 when output exceeds 5,000 units. What is the total cost of making 6,000 units?

B $70,000
C $72,000
D $76,000
parts.working: Remove the step: (79,000 − 6,000 − 52,000) ÷ 3,000 = $7 variable cost per unit; fixed cost below 5,000 units = 52,000 − 28,000 = 24,000. At 6,000 units: 24,000 + 6,000 + 42,000 = $72,000. B ($70,000) uses a high–low rate of $9 that ignores the step in fixed cost.

parts.label: a

parts.label: b

parts.label: c

parts.label: d

parts.answer: Uses only two observations, which may be unusual; assumes a straight-line cost relationship; ignores step changes in fixed cost; the relationship may not hold outside the observed range.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A business uses the AVCO method. It held 100 kg of material costing $4.00 per kg and then received 300 kg at $4.80 per kg. What is the average cost per kg after the receipt?
A $4.20
B $4.40
C $4.60
D $4.80
parts.working: (400 + 1,440) ÷ 400 = $4.60. B ($4.40) is the simple average of the two prices and ignores the quantities.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Purchase prices have fallen steadily throughout the year. Which statement is correct?
A FIFO gives a higher profit than AVCO
B AVCO gives a higher closing inventory value than FIFO
C under FIFO, closing inventory is valued at the oldest prices
D FIFO and AVCO give the same cost of sales
parts.answer: B AVCO gives a higher closing inventory value than FIFO
parts.working: With falling prices FIFO leaves the newest (cheapest) items in closing inventory, while AVCO includes some older, dearer costs, so AVCO's closing inventory is higher and its profit is higher. A is the result when prices are rising, not falling.

stem:
Nile Print Supplies, Cairo, uses FIFO for printer cartridges. Movements in March 2026:

author: HomiLabs

stem: Darzi Uniforms, Karachi, prices each job at total cost plus 25%. Job J47, 120 school blazers, needs 250 metres of fabric. Inventory of the fabric before the job: 180 metres bought at $9.00 per metre, then 300 metres bought at $9.60 per metre. The job also needs 40 direct labour hours at $15 per hour, and production overhead is absorbed at $12 per direct labour hour.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost of fabric charged to Job J47 using (i) FIFO and (ii) AVCO.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the price of Job J47 under each method.
parts.working: Add labour 600 and overhead 480, then × 1.25: B1 each

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the choice of method affects the price quoted to the customer.
parts.answer: Material cost is part of total cost and price is cost plus a mark-up; with rising prices AVCO charges a higher cost than FIFO, so the price is higher.
parts.working: 1 mark: cost-plus link; 1 mark: rising prices → AVCO higher

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Gulf Tyres, a trader in Muscat, is deciding whether to use FIFO or perpetual AVCO for one type of tyre. January 2026:
Date     Details
1 Jan    Opening inventory 400 tyres at $20.00
3 Jan    Bought 600 tyres at $22.00
10 Jan   Sold 700 tyres at $35.00
18 Jan   Bought 500 tyres at $25.00
25 Jan   Sold 600 tyres at $36.00

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the value of closing inventory at 31 January using (i) FIFO and (ii) AVCO.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the gross profit for January under each method.
parts.working: Revenue 46,100 B1; cost of sales FIFO 28,700 M1, AVCO 28,985 M1; both gross profits A1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise the owner which method to adopt. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Points for FIFO: higher profit and closing inventory when prices rise; inventory close to current prices in SOFP; matches the physical flow of tyres; simple. Points for AVCO: smooths price changes; lower profit may mean lower tax; cost of sales nearer to current costs. Both are allowed by IAS 2; whichever is chosen must be used consistently. Decision with reason.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for each side, 1 mark for a justified decision (max 5)

stem:
Kandy Tea Packers records the following for packaging film in June 2026:

parts.label: a

parts.answer: The periodic method includes the later, dearer 20 June receipt in the cost of the 12 June issue; the perpetual method prices each issue only from goods held at the time, so more of the higher cost stays in closing inventory.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of the following is a disadvantage of a just-in-time inventory system?
A production may stop if a supplier delivers late
B more warehouse space is needed
C more working capital is tied up in inventory
D inventory is more likely to become obsolete
parts.answer: A production may stop if a supplier delivers late
parts.working: With little or no buffer inventory, any late or faulty delivery can halt production. B, C and D are disadvantages of holding large inventories, which JIT reduces.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A company's average inventory is expected to fall from $250,000 to $70,000 if it adopts JIT. Holding costs are 14% of average inventory each year. More frequent deliveries will cost an extra $9,500 a year. What is the net annual saving?
A $15,700
B $25,200
C $25,500
D $34,700
parts.working: (250,000 − 70,000) × 14% = 25,200; less 9,500 = $15,700. B ignores the extra delivery cost; D adds it instead of deducting it.

stem: Amna Pharma Distributors, Lahore, keeps a large buffer inventory of every product so that it never runs out.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three costs of holding inventory.
parts.answer: e.g. storage/warehouse rent; insurance; security; interest on capital tied up (opportunity cost); deterioration, expiry and obsolescence; handling staff.
parts.working: 1 mark each, any three

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a just-in-time system differs from holding a buffer inventory.
parts.answer: Under JIT materials or goods are delivered only when they are needed, in small frequent deliveries, so little or no inventory is held; a buffer inventory is a safety stock kept in case of delays or high demand.
parts.working: 1 mark JIT description; 1 mark buffer contrast

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net annual financial effect of adopting JIT.
parts.answer: Net saving $10,500
parts.working: Interest saved 13,500 B1; rent 14,000 B1; obsolescence 9,000 B1; extra component cost 18,000 B1; delivery admin 8,000 and net $10,500 B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise the directors whether to adopt JIT. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Financial benefit of $10,500 a year. Against: reliance on one supplier; risk of stoppages from late deliveries or road disruption; price premium may rise; quality must be right first time. For: less space, less obsolescence, better cash flow, supplier relationship. Decision.
parts.working: 1 mark uses figure; up to 2 marks non-financial points for, up to 2 against (max 4 points); 1 mark justified decision (max 5)

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the expected net annual saving from JIT.
parts.working: Holding saving 45,000 B1; expiry saving 22,000 B1; stock-out cost 21,000 B1; net $46,000 B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise the hospital's managers whether to adopt JIT for its pharmacy. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: For: saving of $46,000; less expired medicine; space freed for clinical use; capital released. Against: a stock-out of a critical medicine could put patients' lives at risk, which is not captured by $3,500; emergencies and outbreaks cause sudden demand; dependence on one wholesaler and on Karachi traffic; reputation and legal risk. Possible compromise: JIT for routine items while keeping safety stocks of critical/life-saving medicines. Clear decision.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for points in favour, up to 3 against (non-financial points needed for full marks), 1 mark for a justified decision

stem: Coastal Furniture, Mombasa, is introducing a just-in-time system for timber.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the effect of JIT on the working capital of the business.

parts.working: 1 mark lower inventory; 1 mark effect on cash/working capital

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the choice between FIFO and AVCO has less effect on profit after JIT is introduced.

parts.working: 1 mark small inventory; 1 mark difference lies in inventory valuation

parts.label: c

parts.answer: Reliable, punctual deliveries; consistent quality; located close by / able to make small frequent deliveries; willing to agree long-term contracts.

stem:

stem: Rehan Products sells 10,000 kettles a year at $80 each. Variable costs per kettle are: materials $30, labour $15, variable overheads $5. Next year materials will cost 10% more and labour 6% more; variable overheads will not change.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the current contribution to sales ratio.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the new variable cost per kettle.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the selling price needed to keep the contribution to sales ratio unchanged.

parts.label: d
parts.text: If the price stays at $80, calculate the number of kettles that must be sold to keep total contribution at its current level. Give a whole number.
parts.answer: 11,495 kettles
