author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A product sells for $45 and has variable costs of $27 per unit. Fixed costs are $63,000. What is the break-even point in units?
A 1,400
B 2,333
C 3,500
D 5,250
parts.working: 63,000 ÷ (45 − 27) = 3,500. B divides by the variable cost instead of the contribution.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Budgeted sales are 6,000 leaflet packs at $9 each. Variable cost is $5 per pack and fixed costs are $12,000. What is the margin of safety in packs?
A 1,333
B 3,000
C 4,667
D 6,000
parts.working: Contribution 9 − 5 = $4 per pack; break-even 12,000 ÷ 4 = 3,000 packs; margin of safety 6,000 − 3,000 = 3,000 packs. A divides fixed costs by the selling price; C uses the wrong break-even point.

stem: Nimra's Bakery, Karachi, sells birthday cakes at $30 each. Ingredients and packaging cost $18 per cake. Rent and other fixed costs are $36,000 a year. Budgeted sales are 4,000 cakes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the break-even point in cakes and in revenue.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the margin of safety in cakes and as a percentage of budgeted sales.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the budgeted profit for the year.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Jamal, who runs a small bakery in Peshawar, has been told that his business 'has a margin of safety of 25%'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the break-even point.
parts.answer: The level of sales at which total revenue equals total costs, so there is neither profit nor loss (total contribution equals fixed costs).
parts.working: B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what a margin of safety of 25% means for Jamal.
parts.answer: Budgeted (or actual) sales are 25% above break-even sales: sales could fall by a quarter before the bakery starts to make a loss.
parts.working: 1 mark sales above break-even; 1 mark interpretation

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two ways Jamal could increase his margin of safety.
parts.answer: Increase sales volume; raise selling price; reduce variable cost per unit; reduce fixed costs (any change that lowers break-even or raises budgeted sales).
parts.working: 1 mark each

author: HomiLabs

stem: A business sells a product at $20 per unit. Variable cost is $12 per unit and fixed costs are $40,000. A break-even chart is drawn with units sold on the horizontal axis (0 to 10,000 units) and $ on the vertical axis. Budgeted sales are 8,000 units.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the coordinates of the points where (i) the total cost line meets the vertical axis and (ii) the total revenue line and total cost line cross.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the vertical distance between the total revenue line and the total cost line at 9,000 units, and state what it represents.
parts.answer: $32,000; the profit at 9,000 units

parts.label: c
parts.text: State how the margin of safety at budgeted sales would be shown on the chart and calculate it.
parts.answer: The horizontal distance between the break-even point and budgeted sales: 3,000 units
parts.working: B1 description; B1 3,000 units

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Desert Rose Café, Muscat, does not calculate costs per unit. Its selling prices and cost structure were the same in two months:
Month      Revenue $    Profit $
March       200,000      10,000
April       260,000      31,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the contribution to sales ratio.
parts.working: Change in profit 21,000 ÷ change in revenue 60,000 M1 A1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the monthly fixed costs.
parts.working: 200,000 × 35% = 70,000 contribution M1; − 10,000 profit A1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the break-even revenue, to the nearest cent.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the margin of safety in April as a percentage of revenue, to two decimal places.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A garment maker in Karachi sells a jacket for $25. Variable cost is $15 per jacket and fixed costs are $90,000 a year. Budgeted sales are 14,000 jackets. The landlord has announced a rent increase of $12,000 a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the break-even point and the margin of safety (in units and as a percentage of budgeted sales) before the rent increase.
parts.answer: Break-even 9,000 jackets; margin of safety 5,000 jackets, 35.71%
parts.working: B1 each

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the break-even point and the margin of safety after the rent increase.
parts.answer: Break-even 10,200 jackets; margin of safety 3,800 jackets, 27.14%
parts.working: B1 each

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the effect of the rent increase on the risk faced by the business.
parts.answer: Higher fixed costs raise the break-even point and reduce the margin of safety, so a smaller fall in sales would cause a loss: the business is riskier.
parts.working: 1 mark effect on BE/MOS; 1 mark risk

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Indus Valves sells one product at $50. Expected demand is 12,000 units a year. The directors are choosing between two methods of production:
Method        Variable cost per unit $   Fixed costs per year $
Manual                   30                     120,000
Automated                22                     200,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the break-even point in units for each method. Round up to whole units.
parts.answer: Manual 6,000; automated 7,143
parts.working: B1 each

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the margin of safety as a percentage of expected demand for each method. Give each answer to one decimal place.
parts.answer: Manual 50.0%; automated 40.5%
parts.working: B1 each

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the profit at expected demand under each method.
parts.answer: Manual $120,000; automated $136,000
parts.working: B1 each

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the level of sales at which both methods give the same profit.
parts.answer: 10,000 units

parts.label: e
parts.text: Advise the directors which method to choose. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Automated gives $16,000 more profit at 12,000 units and is better above 10,000 units, but it has a higher break-even point and lower margin of safety, so it is riskier if demand falls below 10,000. Consider reliability of the demand forecast, cost of finance for the machinery, effect on workers and quality. Decision.
parts.working: 1 mark uses figures; up to 2 marks each side; 1 mark decision (max 5)

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Mughal Tiles sells two products, X and Y. Fixed costs are $72,000 a month.
Product   Selling price $   Variable cost $
X               40                25
Y               30                20
Currently X and Y are sold in the ratio 2 : 3 (by units).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the break-even point in units of each product and the break-even revenue.
parts.working: Batch contribution 2 × 15 + 3 × 10 = 60 M1; 1,200 batches A1; 2,400 X and 3,600 Y A1; revenue 204,000 A1

parts.label: b
parts.text: The sales mix changes to 1 : 1. Calculate the new break-even revenue.
parts.working: Batch contribution 25 M1; 2,880 batches A1; × 70 = 201,600 A1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the break-even revenue changes when the sales mix changes.
parts.answer: X has a higher contribution to sales ratio (37.5%) than Y (33.3%); selling relatively more X raises the average C/S ratio, so less revenue is needed to cover fixed costs.
parts.working: 1 mark different C/S ratios; 1 mark effect of mix

author: HomiLabs

stem: Pine View Hotel, Murree, has 60 rooms and is open 365 nights a year. The average room rate is $80 per night. Variable costs (cleaning, laundry, breakfast and toiletries) are $20 per occupied room-night. Fixed costs are $788,400 a year. Budgeted occupancy is 75%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the break-even number of room-nights and the break-even occupancy percentage.
parts.answer: 13,140 room-nights; 60%

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the margin of safety in room-nights and the budgeted profit.
parts.answer: 3,285 room-nights; profit $197,100

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the average room rate needed to break even if occupancy is only 50%.
parts.working: Room-nights 10,950; contribution needed 72 per night M1; + 20 = 92 A1

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one reason why CVP analysis may be less reliable for a hotel than for a manufacturer.
parts.answer: Room rates vary by season and by booking channel, so a single selling price is unrealistic (or many costs such as staff are stepped/semi-variable).
parts.working: B1

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A manufacturer of school bags in Multan sells each bag for $18. Total costs in two recent months were:
Month     Output (bags)   Total cost $
August        3,000          52,000
October       5,000          72,000
Budgeted sales for next month are 4,000 bags.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the high–low method to find the variable cost per bag and the monthly fixed costs.
parts.answer: Variable $10; fixed $22,000

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the break-even point in bags.
parts.answer: 2,750 bags

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the margin of safety as a percentage of budgeted sales.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
On a break-even chart, what does the area between the total revenue line and the total cost line, to the right of the break-even point, represent?
A contribution
B fixed costs
C profit
D margin of safety
parts.answer: C profit
parts.working: Beyond break-even, revenue exceeds total cost and the gap is profit. A is wrong: contribution is the gap between revenue and variable cost. D is a horizontal distance, not an area.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statements about cost–volume–profit analysis are correct?
1 Fixed costs are assumed to be constant within the relevant range.
2 It is assumed that all units produced are sold.
3 It is assumed that the selling price falls as more units are sold.
4 It can be used for several products if the sales mix is constant.
A 1, 2 and 3
B 1, 2 and 4
C 2, 3 and 4
D 1, 3 and 4
parts.answer: B 1, 2 and 4
parts.working: CVP assumes a constant selling price per unit, so statement 3 is false; the other three are standard assumptions or uses. Options A, C and D all include statement 3.

stem: The owner of a flour mill in Okara is using CVP analysis. Her accountant tells her that 'fixed costs are only fixed within the relevant range'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by the relevant range.
parts.answer: The range of output over which the assumed cost behaviour (fixed costs constant, variable cost per unit constant) holds true.
parts.working: 1 mark range of activity; 1 mark cost behaviour assumptions valid

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one example of how fixed costs at the mill might change outside the relevant range.
parts.answer: e.g. output above capacity needs a second milling machine, extra rented storage or another supervisor, so fixed costs step up.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two uses of CVP analysis for the owner.
parts.answer: Find break-even output; set sales targets for a target profit; measure margin of safety/risk; assess effect of changes in price, costs or volume; compare alternatives.
parts.working: 1 mark each

author: HomiLabs

stem: Afzal sells mobile phone covers from a stall in Rawalpindi. He has worked out his break-even point but does not understand why his accountant says it 'depends on several assumptions'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three assumptions of CVP analysis.
parts.answer: Selling price per unit is constant; variable cost per unit is constant; fixed costs are constant; costs can be split into fixed and variable; production equals sales (no inventory changes); constant sales mix.
parts.working: 1 mark each, any three

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why one of these assumptions may not hold for Afzal's business.
parts.answer: e.g. he may give discounts for bulk buyers or reduce prices to clear old designs, so the selling price is not constant; or suppliers give quantity discounts so variable cost per cover falls.
parts.working: 1 mark identifies assumption; 1 mark applied reason

author: HomiLabs

stem: A business sells a product with a contribution of $15 per unit. Fixed costs are $45,000. A profit–volume chart is drawn, with units sold on the horizontal axis and profit or loss on the vertical axis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the value where the profit line meets the vertical axis.
parts.answer: −$45,000 (a loss equal to fixed costs)
parts.working: B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the number of units where the profit line crosses the horizontal axis.
parts.answer: 3,000 units (break-even)
parts.working: B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the profit shown on the chart at 5,000 units.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State one advantage of a profit–volume chart compared with a break-even chart.
parts.answer: It shows profit or loss at any level of activity directly, without reading the gap between two lines.
parts.working: B1

author: HomiLabs

stem: Lahore Garments sells a uniform at $30. Variable cost is $12 per unit for output up to 10,000 units. If output exceeds 10,000 units, a bulk discount on cloth reduces variable cost to $11 per unit on all units. Fixed costs are $150,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit at 12,000 units assuming variable cost is $12 per unit, as basic CVP analysis would.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the actual profit at 12,000 units.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain which assumption of CVP analysis is shown to be unrealistic, and why this matters to the managers.
parts.answer: The assumption that variable cost per unit is constant at all levels of output (linear cost line). Bulk discounts make the cost line non-linear, so CVP forecasts become inaccurate outside the relevant range: here profit is understated by $12,000, which could lead to a wrong decision.
parts.working: 1 mark assumption; 1 mark non-linearity/relevant range; 1 mark consequence with figure

author: HomiLabs

stem: Sohni Shoes sells 9,000 pairs of sandals a month at $40 a pair. Variable cost is $24 a pair and fixed costs are $96,000 a month. The sales manager proposes cutting the price by 10%, which she expects to increase sales volume by 20%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the current monthly profit and the monthly profit under the proposal.
parts.answer: Current $48,000; proposal $33,600

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how CVP analysis helps the managers decide on this proposal.
parts.answer: It shows quickly that although volume rises, contribution per pair falls from $16 to $12, so profit falls by $14,400; managers can test 'what if' changes in price, cost and volume before acting.
parts.working: 1 mark what-if/sensitivity; 1 mark applied to the figures

author: HomiLabs

stem: The bursar of a private school in Islamabad wants to use break-even analysis to find how many pupils the school needs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two difficulties in applying CVP analysis to the school.
parts.answer: e.g. fees differ by class and some pupils receive scholarships, so there is no single selling price; teacher costs are stepped (a new teacher for every extra class), not fixed or variable; some costs are semi-variable and hard to split; pupil numbers are fixed for the year so 'volume' changes only once a year.
parts.working: 1 mark each difficulty identified (×2), 1 mark each applied explanation (×2)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the bursar could still make use of the analysis.
parts.answer: Use an average fee and average variable cost per pupil, and calculate break-even for each range of class sizes (relevant range); review the results as numbers change.
parts.working: 1 mark each sensible suggestion

author: HomiLabs

stem: A business sells two products. Product A has a contribution to sales ratio of 50% and product B of 25%. Fixed costs are $90,000 a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the break-even revenue if revenue is earned 60% from A and 40% from B.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the break-even revenue if revenue is earned 40% from A and 60% from B.
parts.working: Weighted C/S 35% M1; 90,000 ÷ 0.35 A1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a single break-even figure for this business can be misleading.
parts.answer: Break-even depends on the sales mix; if customers buy relatively more of the low-margin product B than planned, the business needs more revenue to break even than the single figure suggests.
parts.working: 1 mark depends on mix; 1 mark consequence

author: HomiLabs

stem: Indus Mats sells mats at $20 each. Variable production cost is $12.50 per mat and fixed production overheads are $30,000 a month. There are no other costs. In March it produced 5,000 mats but sold only 4,000. There was no opening inventory. The company values inventory using absorption costing, with overheads absorbed on actual production.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the break-even point in mats using CVP analysis.
parts.answer: 4,000 mats

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit for March using (i) marginal costing and (ii) absorption costing.
parts.working: Marginal: contribution 30,000 − fixed 30,000 = 0 M1 A1; absorption: overhead $6 per mat M1; 1,000 × 6 carried forward = 6,000 A1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the absorption costing statement shows a profit at the break-even level of sales, and what this shows about the assumptions of CVP analysis.
parts.answer: Under absorption costing $6,000 of the fixed overhead is carried forward in closing inventory, so not all fixed costs are charged in March. CVP assumes production equals sales (no change in inventory) and treats all fixed costs as period costs, so the break-even point is only consistent with marginal costing.
parts.working: 1 mark overhead deferred in inventory; 1 mark CVP assumes production = sales; 1 mark CVP matches marginal costing

author: HomiLabs

stem: Pearl Water Pumps budgets to sell 10,000 pumps at $60 each. Variable cost is $35 per pump and fixed costs are $200,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the budgeted profit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by which each of the following could change, on its own, before the business makes a loss: (i) selling price; (ii) variable cost per unit; (iii) fixed costs; (iv) sales volume. Give answers to two decimal places.
parts.answer: (i) 8.33% fall; (ii) 14.29% rise; (iii) 25.00% rise; (iv) 20.00% fall
parts.working: Each: profit ÷ the relevant total. (i) 50,000 ÷ 600,000 M1 A1; (ii) 50,000 ÷ 350,000 M1 A1; (iii) 50,000 ÷ 200,000 B1; (iv) margin of safety 2,000 ÷ 10,000 B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise the managers which factor they should monitor most closely. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Selling price: a fall of only 8.33% eliminates profit, the smallest margin of the four. They should monitor competitors' prices and avoid discounting; variable cost (14.29%) is next most sensitive.
parts.working: 1 mark identifies selling price; 1 mark uses figure; 1 mark sensible action/comparison

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Sabz Organic Foods is launching a new jar of honey priced at $45. Variable cost is $27 a jar and annual fixed costs are $180,000. The marketing team gives three sales forecasts for the first year:
Forecast       Jars
Pessimistic    8,000
Most likely   12,000
Optimistic    15,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit or loss for each forecast.
parts.answer: Pessimistic loss $36,000; most likely profit $36,000; optimistic profit $90,000
parts.working: B1 each

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the break-even point and the margin of safety at the most likely forecast as a percentage.
parts.working: B1 each

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise the directors whether to launch the product, discussing the usefulness and limitations of CVP analysis in this decision.
parts.answer: CVP shows the product is profitable at the most likely level but the margin of safety is small (16.67%) and the pessimistic case gives a $36,000 loss. Limitations: forecasts are estimates; price may need to change; costs may not be linear (bulk buying, step costs); single-product assumption ignores effect on existing products; non-financial factors (brand, customer demand for organic food). Decision justified.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks use of results; up to 3 marks limitations/other factors; 1 mark justified decision

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Under marginal costing, how is closing inventory of finished goods valued?
A at prime cost
B at variable production cost
C at variable production cost plus variable selling cost
D at full production cost including fixed overheads
parts.answer: B at variable production cost
parts.working: Marginal costing includes only variable production costs in inventory; fixed production overheads are period costs. C is wrong because selling costs are never part of inventory value; D describes absorption costing.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
During a period, a company's inventory of finished goods fell by 600 units. Fixed production overhead is absorbed at $8 per unit. Which statement is correct?
A absorption costing profit is $4,800 higher than marginal costing profit
B marginal costing profit is $4,800 higher than absorption costing profit
C both methods give the same profit
D marginal costing profit is $600 higher than absorption costing profit
parts.answer: B marginal costing profit is $4,800 higher than absorption costing profit
parts.working: When inventory falls, absorption costing releases fixed overhead carried forward from the previous period into this period's costs, so absorption profit is lower by 600 × 8 = $4,800. A applies when inventory rises.

stem:
The cost card for one unit of a product made by Al-Hamd Industries shows:
                                     $
Direct materials                      9
Direct labour                         6
Variable production overhead          3
Fixed production overhead absorbed    5
Variable selling cost                 2
At the end of the month there are 1,200 units in closing inventory.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the value of closing inventory using (i) marginal costing and (ii) absorption costing.
parts.working: Marginal 18 per unit M1 A1; absorption 23 per unit M1 A1

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the difference between the two values and explain why it arises.
parts.answer: $6,000: absorption costing includes $5 of fixed production overhead in each unit of inventory, which marginal costing charges as a period cost.
parts.working: 1 mark figure; 1 mark explanation

author: HomiLabs

stem: The managers of Swat Woollens produce internal reports using marginal costing, but the published financial statements use absorption costing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the two methods can give different profits for the same period.
parts.answer: They value inventory differently: absorption includes fixed production overhead in inventory, so part of the period's fixed overhead is carried forward (or brought forward) when inventory levels change; marginal costing charges all fixed overhead in the period.
parts.working: 1 mark inventory valuation; 1 mark change in inventory levels

parts.label: b
parts.text: State when the two methods give the same profit.
parts.answer: When there is no change in inventory levels (production equals sales, and the overhead rate per unit is the same).
parts.working: B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why absorption costing must be used for the published financial statements.
parts.answer: IAS 2 requires inventory to include all production costs, including a share of fixed production overheads, so that costs are matched with the revenue when the goods are sold (accruals concept).
parts.working: 1 mark IAS 2 requirement; 1 mark matching

author: HomiLabs

stem: Thar Coal Briquettes uses marginal costing for internal reports. For June the marginal costing profit was $46,500. Inventory of finished briquettes was 800 tonnes at 1 June and 2,300 tonnes at 30 June. Fixed production overhead is absorbed at $7 per tonne (the same rate as in May).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit for June using absorption costing.
parts.working: Increase in inventory 1,500 tonnes M1; × 7 = 10,500 M1; 46,500 + 10,500 A1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare a statement reconciling the two profits.
parts.answer: Marginal costing profit 46,500; add fixed overhead in closing inventory 16,100; less fixed overhead in opening inventory 5,600; absorption costing profit 57,000
parts.working: 1 mark each adjustment with correct sign

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the absorption costing profit is higher.
parts.answer: Inventory rose, so some of June's fixed overhead is carried forward to July in closing inventory instead of being charged in June.
parts.working: B1

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit for each year using marginal costing.
parts.working: B1 each

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit for each year using absorption costing.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the total profit for the two years under each method and explain the difference.
parts.answer: Marginal $258,000; absorption $266,000; difference $8,000 = 2,000 cartons in closing inventory at 31 December 2026 × $4
parts.working: 1 mark totals; 1 mark explanation

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the overhead absorption rate and the under- or over-absorption of fixed production overhead.
parts.answer: $5 per pair; under-absorbed $8,000

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare a statement of profit for the year using absorption costing.
parts.answer: Revenue 600,000; production cost 22,000 × 19 = 418,000 less closing inventory 2,000 × 19 = 38,000; cost of sales 380,000; add under-absorption 8,000; gross profit 212,000; less variable selling 20,000 and administration 40,000; profit $152,000
parts.working: B1 revenue; B1 production at $19; B1 closing inventory; B1 under-absorption added; B1 non-production costs; B1 profit

parts.label: c
parts.text: Prepare a statement of profit using marginal costing.
parts.answer: Revenue 600,000; variable cost of sales 280,000; variable selling 20,000; contribution 300,000; fixed production 118,000; administration 40,000; profit $142,000
parts.working: B1 variable costs; B1 contribution; B1 fixed costs; B1 profit

parts.label: d
parts.text: Reconcile the two profits.
parts.answer: Difference $10,000 = 2,000 pairs × $5 fixed overhead in closing inventory
parts.working: M1 A1

author: HomiLabs

stem: Ravi Engineering reported a marginal costing profit of $60,000 for the year. Opening inventory was 1,500 units, valued under absorption costing with fixed production overhead of $6.00 per unit. Closing inventory was 2,500 units; this year's fixed overhead absorption rate is $7.20 per unit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the absorption costing profit for the year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why both the opening and closing inventory figures are needed for the reconciliation.
parts.answer: Absorption profit is reduced by fixed overhead brought forward in opening inventory (charged this year) and increased by fixed overhead carried forward in closing inventory; the net change, not just the closing figure, is the difference.
parts.working: 1 mark opening charged; 1 mark closing deferred

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the change in the absorption rate affects the comparison of profits between years.
parts.answer: Even with constant inventory volumes, a higher rate puts more overhead into closing inventory than came out of opening inventory, so absorption profit can rise without any improvement in trading.
parts.working: 1 mark effect of rate; 1 mark misleading comparison

author: HomiLabs

stem: The production manager of Neelum Furniture receives a bonus of 5% of the annual profit calculated using absorption costing. Demand is 10,000 chairs a year at $50 each. Variable cost is $30 per chair and fixed production overheads are $120,000 a year, absorbed on a normal output of 10,000 chairs. The factory can make up to 14,000 chairs. There was no opening inventory.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the absorption costing profit if (i) 10,000 chairs and (ii) 14,000 chairs are produced, with 10,000 sold in each case.
parts.working: Rate $12 per chair B1; (i) 80,000 A1; (ii) closing inventory 4,000 × $42; over-absorption 48,000 M1; 128,000 A1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the manager's bonus in each case.
parts.working: B1 each

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the marginal costing profit in each case.
parts.answer: $80,000 in both cases
parts.working: Contribution 200,000 − 120,000 B1

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why abnormal costs are excluded from the cost of inventory.
parts.answer: IAS 2 allows only normal costs of bringing inventory to its present condition; abnormal waste or idle time adds no value to the goods, and including it would overstate inventory and defer losses to a later period.

stem:
Sindh Pipes has two factories making the same pipe. Data for the year:
                         Lahore $    Karachi $
Units completed           40,000       25,000
Direct materials         480,000      312,500
Direct labour            360,000      200,000
Factory overheads        240,000      187,500
In both factories 75% of the factory overheads are fixed and the rest vary with output. The company wants to make an extra 10,000 units a year and both factories have enough spare capacity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the production cost per unit at each factory.
parts.answer: Lahore $27; Karachi $28
parts.working: B1 each

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the variable (marginal) production cost per unit at each factory, to three decimal places.
parts.answer: Lahore $22.500; Karachi $22.375

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the difference in total cost of making the extra 10,000 units at Karachi rather than Lahore.
parts.answer: Karachi is cheaper by $1,250.00

parts.label: d
parts.text: Advise the directors which factory should make the extra units. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Although Lahore has the lower full cost per unit, the extra units only add variable cost, and Karachi's is slightly lower ($1,250 a year), so Karachi on cost grounds; the difference is small, so other factors matter: distance to customers and transport costs, quality, labour availability, whether fixed costs would really stay the same, spreading risk. Decision.
parts.working: 1 mark relevant (marginal) comparison; 1 mark full cost misleading; up to 2 marks other factors; 1 mark decision
